"API endpoints"), or answer "where is X defined / which files reference Y." Do NOT use it for code review, design-doc auditing, cross-file consistency checks, or open-ended analysis — it reads excerpts rather than whole files and will miss content past its read window. 1	\documentclass[sigconf]{acmart}
2	
3	\setcopyright{none}
4	\settopmatter{printacmref=false}
5	\renewcommand\footnotetextcopyrightpermission[1]{}
6	\pagestyle{plain}
7	
8	\usepackage{booktabs}
9	\usepackage{array}
10	\usepackage{xspace}
11	\usepackage{url}
12	\usepackage{graphicx}
13	
14	\newcommand{\toolname}{\textsc{AgentPProf}\xspace}
15	\newcommand{\operation}{\texttt{operation}\xspace}
16	\newcommand{\opstack}{\texttt{operation stack}\xspace}
17	
18	\begin{document}
19	
20	\title{AgentPProf: Operation-Stack Profiling for AI Agent Traces}
21	
22	\begin{abstract}
23	AI-agent executions are no longer well described by one prompt, one session, or
24	one trace tree. A single run can contain prompts, tool calls, GUI actions,
25	browser actions, process events, plans, subagents, safety labels, failure
26	labels, and human subtask boundaries. Existing observability systems usually
27	make one boundary primary, such as a session, span, or prompt tree. Classic
28	profilers make another boundary primary, such as a function call stack. This
29	paper argues that agent profiling needs a smaller abstraction: an
30	\operation is a weighted record with fields, and an \opstack is a recursive
31	projection over those fields chosen at query time. Aggregation is not a separate
32	object or a fixed trace tree; it is the result of choosing a stack shape over the
33	same operations. This is not merely a claim about query-time aggregation, which
34	classic profilers and trace processors also support in different forms. The
35	scoped novelty is the combination of an agent-operation record model, recursive
36	multi-field operation-stack projections, and a hidden-label cross-dataset
37	localization benchmark.
38	
39	We implement this model in the Rust \toolname profiler and evaluate it through
40	three core empirical profiling experiments, RQ1/E1 through RQ3/E3, plus one
41	replayability/scope-control block, RQ4/E4, rather than a chronological run list.
42	RQ1/E1 tests generality and
43	recursive operation-stack formation: across 15 lightly sampled public labeled
44	sources, \toolname maps 47,590 samples into the same operation layer, and the
45	same 13,265 operations fold from 9 dataset stacks to 57 phase, 226 semantic, 455
46	action, or 3,757 fixed-session stacks without changing the input operations. RQ2/E2
47	is the main hidden-label localization benchmark. On AgentRewardBench,
48	SATraj-OS, AgentNet, and OSWorld-Human, we build six tasks over 34,539
49	operations and 3,699 positives, score 144 view/ranker policies, and find that
50	task-query operation-stack profiling inspects median 0.0937 top-five work versus
51	1.0 for flat summaries, improves top-five recall over fixed-session drilldown on
52	5 of 6 tasks, and reduces median group fragmentation from 285.0 to 157.5
53	groups.
54	RQ3/E3 isolates mechanisms and profile-configuration actionability. Rank-feature,
55	stack-depth, mapping, transfer, diagnostic-lens, case-packet, and counterfactual
56	analyses show that the useful configuration varies by task and objective:
57	operation-stack views are a Pareto point, not a universal default. Executable
58	profile-spec patches improve AP, top-five lift, and first-positive work on 5 of
59	6 tasks; a supervised held-out boundary-field ablation improves OSWorld-Human AP
60	from 0.2402 to 0.2583 and reduces groups from 108 to 74, while preserving work
61	counterpoints. A field-suitability synthesis further turns mapping, stack-depth,
62	rank-feature, and boundary-field evidence into guarded configuration decisions
63	with accept, caution, and reject outcomes. RQ4/E4 checks replayability, offline cost, and claim scope.
64	Deterministic replay covers 76 tracked profile specs, and profile-spec input
65	regressions cover local-session, agent-trace, and standard-trace replay. The
66	recorded source provenance, paper-number, rubric, and two-abstraction checks
67	constrain the paper's scope rather than forming a fourth empirical profiling
68	experiment.
69	
70	The supported claim is therefore a scoped profiling claim: operation-stack
71	profiling can localize, rank, and explain dataset-labeled failures, quality
72	problems, and semantic boundaries in public traces, with less inspection work
73	than flat summaries and a better median-fragmentation tradeoff than the
74	fixed-session drilldown proxy. Fixed-session drilldown is the current
75	trace-tree-shaped baseline; real
76	OpenTelemetry/OpenInference/Phoenix-style span-tree imports remain future
77	baselines. The paper does not claim human-productivity gains, automatic
78	discovery of all intent boundaries, metric dominance, or complete compatibility
79	with existing trace ecosystems.
80	\end{abstract}
81	
82	\maketitle
83	
84	\section{Introduction}
85	
86	AI-agent traces mix many objects that traditional profiling and tracing systems
87	keep separate. A coding agent may ask a model for a plan, call a shell tool,
88	launch a subagent, inspect a file, and retry a failing command. A web or desktop
89	agent may click, type, observe a page, repeat an action, and receive a benchmark
90	label saying that the action was unsafe, redundant, incorrect, or the start of
91	a human subtask. If the profiler fixes the hierarchy at prompt, session, or
92	span boundaries, these questions become hard to ask: which phases concentrate
93	unsafe operations, which action families cause redundant steps, and which
94	groups of operations cross sessions but share the same failure mode?
95	
96	\toolname takes the opposite position. The profiler stores a sequence as
97	operations, where prompts, tool calls, processes, syscalls, GUI actions, and
98	plan steps are operation records or derived fields. Session, span, task, and
99	trace identifiers are fields, exchange containers, or baseline shapes rather
100	than separate profiler objects. Users then choose an operation stack to fold the
101	same operations at different depths. One query may group by
102	\texttt{task,phase,action}; another may group by
103	\texttt{environment,safety}. Mapping and tagging are first-class field-derivation
104	steps, but they do not add a third profiler object. They only write fields
105	before the stack query runs. Thus the novelty is the abstraction that connects
106	stack shape to aggregation: changing the stack changes what is comparable,
107	localizable, and actionable without changing the underlying trace object model.
108	
109	This paper makes a profiling claim, not a human-productivity claim. A top-tier
110	profiling paper must show that the profiler attributes, localizes, and ranks
111	problems against explicit workload labels, and that the output leads to
112	optimization insight with better label-scored ranking or inspection cost than baselines. For agents, the
113	claim is:
114	\begin{quote}
115	\emph{Operation/operation-stack profiling provides label-scored localization
116	and ranking for task-relevant failures, quality problems, and dataset-provided
117	semantic boundaries in real labeled agent traces, while requiring less
118	inspection work than flat summaries and improving the median fragmentation
119	tradeoff relative to fixed-session drilldown.}
120	\end{quote}
121	
122	We evaluate this claim with public labeled traces rather than a human study. A
123	human or agent analyst study would be useful for productivity claims, but it is
124	not required to test label-scored profiler fidelity. Our evaluation therefore
125	uses hidden labels as the oracle for ranked profile groups and is organized
126	as three empirical profiling experiments plus one replayability/scope-control
127	block. RQ1/E1 tests operation generality, recursive stack folding, field
128	derivation, and human-boundary alignment under the same two-object model. RQ2/E2
129	is the main hidden-label localization and ranking benchmark. RQ3/E3 isolates
130	mechanisms and actionability through ranker, stack, mapping, transfer, case, and
131	profile-spec patch ablations. RQ4/E4 checks replayability, offline cost, and
132	claim scope. It is not treated as a fourth hidden-label accuracy result or a
133	fourth empirical profiling experiment. Supplementary results support these
134	blocks rather than defining the paper-facing structure.
135	
136	\section{Design}
137	
138	\subsection{Operations}
139	
140	An \operation is the only sample-level object in \toolname. It is a weighted
141	record with string fields. The same representation can encode a prompt, a tool
142	call, an API call, a browser action, a PyAutoGUI action, a process event, or a
143	derived label such as \texttt{looping=yes} or \texttt{step\_correct=incorrect}.
144	External datasets enter the system as operation JSONL. Local Codex or Claude
145	sessions can also be exported as an agent-session trace, imported back, or
146	converted to operation JSONL before profiling.
147	
148	\subsection{Operation Stacks}
149	
150	An \opstack is an ordered list of fields. Folding operations by that list yields
151	the usual folded-stack representation, but the stack is chosen at query time.
152	The same operation file can be folded as a flat task summary, a fixed-session
153	tree, a dataset-native hierarchy, a raw action stack, a semantic operation
154	stack, or an oracle label-drilldown. Fixed sessions and spans are therefore
155	baselines and exchange containers, not core profiler abstractions.
156	
157	\subsection{Mapping and Tagging}
158	
159	Mapping and tagging derive new operation fields before folding. For example,
160	desktop actions such as \texttt{type} and \texttt{key} can map to
161	\texttt{phase=input}, while tool/API rows can map to a tool phase before generic
162	action rules run. The Rust CLI exposes inline rules, rule files, profile specs,
163	operation predicates, and stack overrides. \texttt{--where} predicates run after
164	mapping and before stack construction, implementing the query predicate without
165	adding a profiler object. Profile specs record operation files, mappings,
166	predicates, views, stacks, and outputs for reproducibility, while command-line
167	flags can still override the stack query.
168	
169	\section{Evaluation Setup}
170	
171	Table~\ref{tab:datasets} summarizes the public trace families. We do not create
172	new test sets, sync complete image corpora, or depend on restricted data. The 15
173	sources establish generality, while the main hidden-label ranking results use the four
174	oracle-rich families with failure, safety, quality, and human-boundary labels.
175	
176	\begin{table*}[t]
177	\centering
178	\small
179	\caption{Public labeled trace families used by the evaluation. The main E2
180	hidden-label profiler benchmark uses the four oracle-rich rows in the bottom half.}
181	\label{tab:datasets}
182	\begin{tabular}{p{0.18\linewidth}p{0.29\linewidth}p{0.21\linewidth}p{0.22\linewidth}}
183	\toprule
184	Family & Native labels & Access path & Evaluation role \\
185	\midrule
186	WebLINX, Mind2Web, AgentTrek, WebShop & Web actions, demos, tasks, rewards, action history & Hugging Face viewer or public shards & Web navigation coverage \\
187	API-Bank, ToolBench, tau-bench & API calls, tool messages, solution paths, outcomes & Hugging Face rows or repo JSONL & Tool/API and dialogue coverage \\
188	SWE-agent & Issue trajectory, command actions, target outcome & Hugging Face viewer & Software-agent coverage \\
189	AndroidControl, GUI-Odyssey, ScaleCUA & Mobile or GUI actions, instructions, history context & Public/HF samples & Mobile and GUI coverage \\
190	AgentRewardBench & Expert success, side-effect, looping, optimality & HF annotations plus cleaned BrowserGym steps & Failure and looping tasks \\
191	SATraj-OS & Desktop actions, safety, reward, attack type & HF safety config & Safety task \\
192	OSWorld-Human & Human single-action and grouped-action traces & Public GitHub JSON & Human-boundary task \\
193	AgentNet & Human desktop PyAutoGUI, step correctness, redundancy & HF repo JSONL streaming & Step-quality tasks \\
194	\bottomrule
195	\end{tabular}
196	\end{table*}
197	
198	For the E2 hidden-label profiler benchmark, we build six tasks: AgentRewardBench looping, AgentRewardBench
199	side-effect, SATraj unsafe operation, AgentNet incorrect step, AgentNet
200	redundant step, and OSWorld-Human group start. Each task has an oracle-positive
201	field, but non-oracle rankers never read that field. We compare six views:
202	flat, fixed-session, dataset-native hierarchy, raw action stack, semantic
203	operation stack, and label-drilldown. We compare four rankers: width,
204	visible-risk, query-aware, and oracle upper bound. Label-drilldown and oracle
205	upper bound are marked as hidden upper bounds.
206

309	
310	\subsection{RQ1/E1: Generality and Recursive Folding}
311	
312	RQ1/E1 tests whether one operation layer can represent heterogeneous agent
313	traces without making prompt, session, tool, process, or syscall records into
314	separate profiler objects. The evaluation folds the same operation records into
315	task, phase, action, human-boundary, and fixed-session-shaped stacks by changing
316	only mappings and stack fields. Public dataset labels and native trajectory
317	fields provide the oracle signal, with OSWorld-Human boundaries and AgentNet
318	quality labels as the strongest structure labels. The comparison uses
319	dataset-native, no-map, fixed-session, replay, and trace round-trip views. The
320	metrics are coverage, stack range, compression, boundary F1, V-measure, and
321	round-trip equality. The scoped conclusion is configurable operation-stack
322	folding, not complete ecosystem compatibility or latent-intent recovery.
323	
324	The 14 core public sources produce 42,590 operations. Adding the supplemental
325	ScaleCUA stream brings the smoke set to 47,590 operations. These operations
326	cover web, mobile, desktop, software, API, tool-agent-user dialogue, expert
327	failure labels, safety labels, human grouped-action labels, and desktop
328	step-quality labels. No source required a prompt-specific, GUI-specific, or
329	safety-specific profiler object.
330

375	\paragraph{Recursive stack-depth sweep.}
376	
377	On the same 13,265 operations, a depth sweep folds to 9 dataset stacks, 57
378	phase stacks, 226 tool/semantic stacks, 455 action stacks, and 3,757
379	fixed-session stacks. A fixed session boundary therefore increases stack count
380	by 417.4$\times$ relative to dataset depth. On AgentNet, a tracked profile spec
381	folds 16,741 operations into 608 diagnostic stacks, while a CLI stack override
382	changes the output to 83 stacks without changing the operation input. The
383	result supports query-time recursive stack choice rather than a fixed
384	prompt/session hierarchy.
385	
386	The implementation probes are grouped as interface evidence, not additional
387	main experiments. They show that profile specs can select mapped subsets before
388	folding (729/729, 714/714, and 4,285/4,285 expected operations), compose
389	operation files, predicates, visible ranking rules, rank modes, and explicit
390	stack depths without prompt/session frames (12/12 specs), and round-trip a real
391	operation-file prefix through a standard trace container while preserving 512
392	samples and 11 folded stacks. These interface checks are provenance for E1: they
393	test whether the operation layer stays fixed while views change; the
394	localization and ranker gains from those specs are evaluated under E2/E3.
395	
396	\paragraph{Field derivation and boundary probes.}
397	
398	Held-out mapping rules improve compression from 14.049 to 19.091 on 3,990
399	operations. Leave-dataset-out mapping reduces unique stacks on 6 of 9 held-out
400	datasets with no negative stack-reduction regressions after API/tool phase
401	precedence is fixed. A supervised OSWorld-Human boundary backend reaches F1
402	0.7735 on held-out adjacent pairs and writes predicted boundary fields that the
403	Rust profiler folds as ordinary operation fields. Boundary backends therefore
404	extend field derivation, not the profiler object model.
405	The field-derivation audit keeps both support and counterpoints visible:
406	held-out mapping improves compression but coarsens action-to-phase V-measure
407	from 0.9343 to 0.7416; profile-spec composition stays prompt/session-free on
408	12/12 variants; and learned boundary backends beat the best simple baseline on
409	4/5 rows, while AgentRewardBench looping is fully explained by
410	\texttt{repeat\_signal\_change}. This supports first-class field derivation and
411	suitability checks, not automatic intent boundary discovery and not a new
412	profiler object. Rank-feature criticality from the same audit belongs to
413	RQ3/E3's mechanism/actionability evidence, not to RQ1/E1's abstraction claim.
414	The suitability check makes the extension policy explicit. Deterministic
415	mappings are useful for compression but can coarsen action boundaries. Rank
416	features require ablation guards because both critical and misleading feature
417	rows appear. Boundary-derived fields require family-specific evidence. The
418	tested boundary families produce accept, caution, and reject outcomes, so field
419	derivation remains a guarded profile-configuration loop rather than a universal
420	selector.
421	
422	\paragraph{Human-boundary oracle.}
423	
424	OSWorld-Human gives the strongest direct boundary oracle. On 320 exact-aligned
425	tasks with 4,011 operations and 2,075 human groups, grouped-depth stacks reduce
426	482 action stacks to 106 grouped stacks. A conservative \texttt{group\_pattern}
427	projection has human-group boundary F1 0.627 with precision 1.0 and recall
428	0.456. This is not complete intent discovery, but it shows that the same
429	single-action sequence can be folded at action depth or human-group depth and
430	scored against a human boundary oracle.

432	\subsection{RQ2/E2: Hidden-Label Localization and Ranking}
433	
434	RQ2/E2 treats profiling as a ranked localization problem. The benchmark marks
435	3,699 positive operations among 34,539 operations and asks whether hot stacks
436	and top-ranked groups correspond to those hidden positives. The comparison
437	covers flat summaries, fixed-session drilldown, dataset-native hierarchy,
438	raw-action stacks, operation stacks, label drilldown, and oracle upper bounds.
439	The metrics are precision@k, recall, F1, AP as an AUPRC-style score, nDCG,
440	budget recall and F1, work-to-first-positive, and group count. The scoped claim
441	is a Pareto tradeoff: operation stacks should reduce flat inspection work and
442	improve a useful fixed-session localization or fragmentation objective, while
443	flat and dataset-native views may still win broad-recall or nDCG goals.
444	
445	Primary comparison and success criterion. E2 treats every profile group as an
446	inspection target and asks whether the ranked targets find hidden positives
447	with less work than flat summaries and less fragmentation than a fixed-session
448	trace-tree proxy. Success is therefore a Pareto condition, not a single winning
449	metric: operation stacks must reduce flat inspection work, improve a meaningful
450	fixed-session localization or fragmentation objective, and keep fixed-session
451	early-hit counterpoints visible. Table~\ref{tab:e2-localization} is the main E2
452	localization display; supporting case views explain the result without becoming
453	separate paper experiments. Flat summaries recover all positives, but only by inspecting the
454	whole task, so their median work@5 and work-to-first-positive are both 1.0.
455	Fixed-session drilldown finds an early
456	positive with median work-to-first-positive 0.0044 and median work@5 0.0163,
457	but its median recall@5 is only 0.0233 and it fragments the workload into 285.0
458	groups. Query-aware operation stacks inspect median 0.0937 work in the top five
459	groups, reach median recall@budget30 of 0.3900, and reduce the median group
460	count to 157.5.
461	
462	Failure interpretation and baseline scope are part of the result.
463	Fixed-session drilldown is the evaluated trace-tree-shaped baseline, not
464	evidence of full OpenTelemetry/Phoenix/LangSmith/Perfetto compatibility. On the
465	same scored rows, operation-stack query-aware improves fixed-session top-five
466	recall and F1 on 5/6 tasks, budget-30 recall on 4/6, and group count on 4/6,
467	while fixed-session retains lower top-five work and first-positive work on 4/6.
468	The depth-aware slice gives the finer version of the same claim: operation-stack rankings
469	beat fixed-session on budget-30 positive-unit recall for 20/24 task-depth rows
470	and use fewer groups to reach 50\% positive units on 22/24 rows. If these
471	counterpoints disappeared from the paper, the result would be overstated; with
472	them, E2 supports a better localization-budget/fragmentation tradeoff, not
473	dominance over every trace-tree-shaped objective.

558	\subsection{RQ3/E3: Mechanism and Actionability}
559	
560	RQ3/E3 asks why the E2 rankings improve and whether the profiler points to
561	concrete configuration changes. The candidate mechanisms are stack fields,
562	mapping and tagging rules, rankers, profile specs, and boundary-derived
563	operation fields. Hidden labels score the output only after profiling, and
564	held-out OSWorld-Human boundary positives score boundary-derived fields. The
565	comparison covers default and patched specs, visible rankers, transfer
566	policies, learned-boundary fields, fixed-session drilldown, and semantic-width
567	stacks. The metrics are accepted patches, AP delta, top-five lift,
568	first-positive work, group reduction, and top-five-work counterpoints. The
569	scoped conclusion is profile-configuration actionability, not automatic
570	boundary discovery, automatic patch selection, or a universal selector.
571	
572	Primary mechanism question. E3 starts from the E2 ranked outputs and asks
573	whether the profiler can explain what to change in the profile configuration.
574	Hidden labels are used only after profiling to score a configuration; the
575	visible inputs are stack fields, mapping/tagging rules, rank features, profile
576	specs, and boundary-derived operation fields. The success criterion is an
577	actionable, replayable diagnosis: a task should point to a concrete stack,
578	field, ranker, mapping, profile-spec, or drilldown change, and executable
579	patches should improve the scored output without turning into an automatic
580	selector.
581	
582	Table~\ref{tab:actionability} is the main E3 display. It compresses the
583	task-card evidence into a paper-facing diagnosis table; the supporting case
584	views remain provenance rather than additional main experiments.
585	SATraj unsafe is the cleanest operation-stack win: environment, phase, and
586	action fields plus query-aware risk ranking give the best visible top-five F1.
587	Looping exposes the value and limit of \texttt{repeat\_signal}: it helps
588	ranking, but positives are prevalent, so prevalence-aware ranking remains the
589	optimization. Side-effect has large oracle headroom and points to deeper
590	write/input mappings. AgentNet step-quality tasks need action-family
591	localization followed by fixed-session examples. OSWorld-Human needs
592	boundary-derived fields rather than action depth alone. Thus the first
593	actionability result is not that one view wins; it is that the profiler
594	identifies which stack field, mapping, ranker, or drilldown should change for
595	each task family.
596	The task-level verdict synthesis clarifies the claim boundary: all six tasks
597	support E3 with counterpoints, not as unconditional wins. Five of six tasks have
598	accepted executable profile-spec patches; the remaining OSWorld-Human row points
599	to boundary-derived fields and keeps top-five and first-positive work
600	counterpoints.
601	The six rows resolve into three reusable optimization patterns. Safety and
602	side-effect tasks point to field and ranker changes because environment,
603	phase/action, and write/input fields move relevant positives into smaller
604	inspected regions. Step-quality tasks point to a drilldown workflow because
605	desktop phase, repeat, and action fields locate suspicious regions before
606	fixed-session examples explain individual traces. Human-boundary tasks point to
607	representation repair because action-depth stacks are insufficient, while
608	boundary-derived operation fields improve AP and reduce groups with explicit
609	inspection-work counterpoints. These patterns are configuration guidance over
610	profile inputs, stack fields, and rankers, not labels predicted by the profiler.
611	
612	The Rust mechanism ablations isolate where those diagnoses come from without
613	turning the paper into a run list. First, stack-text rules and rank-mode
614	variants are replayable from profile specs but too coarse for safety and
615	side-effect tasks. Second, operation-level rank features close that gap by
616	matching visible mapped operation tokens before folding: semantic-stack feature
617	ranking improves AP over width on 5 of 6 tasks, top-five lift on 4 of 6, and
618	first-positive work on 5 of 6; coarse depth improves AP on 4 of 6 while
619	reducing groups. Third, leave-one-feature and robustness ablations make the
620	knobs concrete: \texttt{repeat\_signal}, write-action features, and
621	\texttt{status=success} are critical in different families, while misleading
622	safety-like or input-phase features can hurt AP or first-positive work.
623	Equal/global feature banks often preserve the gains, and guided repairs improve
624	AP on 2 of 3 misleading-feature cases, but these repairs use offline scored
625	feedback and are not an automatic learned ranker. These audits are provenance
626	for this single E3 mechanism block.
627	
628	The view and policy audits show the same mechanism at the analysis-surface
629	level. Best AP and best top-five F1 are split across operation-stack,
630	fixed-session, dataset-native, raw-action, and flat views; leave-task source
631	selection cannot reliably pick the best visible view. Nevertheless, the
632	operation-stack query-aware policy remains Pareto-frontier on all six tasks,
633	beats flat top-five work on all six, beats fixed-session top-five recall on 5
634	of 6, and reaches fewer groups-to-50\% positives than fixed-session on 5 of 6.
635	At a 25\% recall target it covers all six tasks with median work 0.2000 versus
636	flat 1.0000 and median 16.0 groups versus fixed-session 50.0; at 50\% recall,
637	other depths or views become the best-work counterpoints. Sequence and
638	oracle-depth audits add the inspection unit below and above individual groups.
639	Sequence and oracle-depth scoring show that
640	at a 30\% operation budget, operation-stack query-aware reaches median 0.4669
641	positive-session recall versus fixed-session 0.3230, and across 24 oracle-depth
642	rows it has median 0.4342 budget-30 positive-unit recall, beats fixed-session
643	unit recall on 20/24 rows, and reaches 50\% positive units with fewer groups on
644	22/24. Positive-run proxy units are derived episode units, not human intent
645	boundaries. The fixed-session depth-gap counterpoint remains, so this is
646	depth-aware triage, not complete intent-boundary recovery.
647	The multi-metric audit also keeps the metric surface honest: it records 30
648	supporting baseline-metric comparisons, 16 explicit counterpoints, and nDCG
649	cases where flat or dataset-native views can win.
650	
651	The actionability portfolio turns those comparisons into reviewer-auditable
652	profile-configuration tuning insight. Across 36 objective rows, every row has a
653	concrete configuration action, but 27/36 best visible policies are not the
654	default operation-stack query-aware view; transfer misses are mostly view or
655	ranker changes rather than opaque errors. The same evidence is presented as
656	diagnostic lenses, case packets, and baseline contrasts: six lenses cover 36
657	objectives, top-five case groups contain positives on 6/6 tasks, top-one groups
658	on 5/6, median top-five lift is 1.6508 at 0.0937 work, and operation stacks beat
659	flat top-five work on 6/6 and fixed-session top-five recall on 5/6 while
660	preserving fixed-session first-positive and flat full-recall counterpoints.
661	Counterfactual and held-out transfer checks separate visible actions from
662	target-label leakage: 36/36 best rows are visible non-oracle, 27/36 require a
663	non-default action, 25/36 require a view change, held-out action transfer stays
664	within tolerance on 35/60 aligned decisions, but exact action-class transfer is
665	only 7/60 overall and 2/42 on non-default target actions. These support audits
666	form one E3 actionability block. The actionable claim is therefore a tunable
667	diagnosis surface, not a label-free automatic selector.
668	Field-suitability decisions make that guard concrete. Deterministic mapping,
669	stack-depth and predicate choices, operation-level rank features, supervised
670	boundary fields, and boundary-profile repair are useful only under different
671	conditions. The boundary-family matrix has one accept, three caution, and one
672	reject outcome, which means the profiler can guide configuration but should not
673	present boundary fields as a universal automatic selector.
674	
675	Finally, executable patches close one loop from diagnosis to profiler
676	configuration. Default and profile-guided Rust profile specs run over the same
677	visible operation input, and hidden labels are scored only after
678	\texttt{agentpprof --profile-spec}. Five of six patches improve AP, top-five
679	lift, and first-positive work, with median AP delta 0.0376 and median top-five
680	lift delta 0.5750. The failure interpretation matters here too: the rejected
681	OSWorld-Human patch shows that visible phase/action rank features are
682	insufficient for a human-boundary objective. Folding held-out boundary-derived
683	operation fields then improves AP to 0.2583 versus 0.2402 for semantic width
684	and reduces groups to 74 versus 108, while top-five work and first-positive
685	work increase. These patch and boundary-field results support boundary fields
686	as an actionable operation-field knob, not automatic boundary
687	discovery or automatic patch selection. The result belongs to
688	mechanism/actionability, not a fifth core experiment.

713	\subsection{RQ4/E4: Reproducibility, Offline Cost, and Scope Control}
714	
715	RQ4/E4 asks a narrower question than E2/E3: can reviewers replay the
716	offline profile-spec path at low local cost while checking that source
717	provenance, paper numbers, two-abstraction wording, and non-claims remain
718	aligned? The evidence is the tracked specs and inputs, profile-spec input
719	replay regressions, repeated profile outputs, runtime logs, and recorded source
720	provenance. We compare default output with deterministic-output replay, semantic
721	profile hashes with raw-byte hashes, and effective input metadata with silently
722	ignored source paths. The measured quantities are deterministic spec pass rate,
723	profiler invocations, median and p95 runtime, sample equality, stack equality,
724	raw-byte output equality, and input-source replay coverage. These checks bound
725	the paper claim. They are not a hidden-label accuracy result, live eBPF
726	overhead, human utility, complete ecosystem compatibility, or a universal
727	selector.
728	
729	The empirical content of this subsection is only one replayability/cost block. It
730	reruns the profile specs used by the labeled-trace experiments: 76
731	tracked specs over tracked operation JSONL inputs, executed twice for 152
732	profiler invocations. The semantic profile content is stable for 76/76 specs in
733	both modes; deterministic output also makes raw-byte profile files stable for
734	76/76 specs by fixing profile timestamps. The clean deterministic rerun reports
735	median runtime 1.601s and p95 2.767s per spec. The replayed files provide
736	provenance for this E4 block. This supports replayable offline
737	profiler outputs, not live eBPF overhead or analyst productivity, or another
738	empirical profiling experiment.
739	
740	Input-source replay checks belong to the same E4 block. The Rust
741	profile-spec path carries \texttt{session\_files}, \texttt{trace\_files},
742	\texttt{standard\_trace\_files}, regex tag rules, predicates, rank rules, stack
743	overrides, and \texttt{include\_standard\_trace\_args}. The regressions replay
744	the public Codex fixture as a local session and as an exported agent-session
745	trace, then replay a generic Chrome Trace Event import whose non-AgentSight
746	\texttt{protocol} argument becomes an operation field before folding. These
747	checks keep local sessions and trace containers inside the same operation /
748	operation-stack path. They do not add a new accuracy experiment, a third
749	profiler object, or an ecosystem-compatibility claim.
750	
751	Tables~\ref{tab:e4-replay-cost} and~\ref{tab:e4-determinism} are the two E4 main displays: they
752	summarize the replayability/cost result and the deterministic-output repair,
753	while their row labels name source-spec families rather than additional
754	accuracy experiments.
755	
756	The remaining consistency checks support reproducibility and scope control, not
757	new empirical evidence. They reuse tracked inputs, tracked outputs, and the current paper text
758	without reranking, downloading, syncing, creating, relabeling, rerunning the
759	profiler, or running a human or agent analyst task. The checks verify replay
760	paths, source provenance, paper-number alignment, two-abstraction wording, and
761	non-claim consistency. They let reviewers audit whether the paper is faithful to
762	tracked outputs, but they do not increase the localization, actionability, or
763	overhead claims.
764	
765	\paragraph{Profile-spec determinism and local cost.}
766	
767	The replay workload reruns the existing profile specs used by the E2
768	and E3 views, rankers, and robustness checks.
769	The workload contains 76 tracked specs: four view specs, 12 operation-feature
770	rank specs, and 60 robustness specs. Each spec is executed twice by the Rust
771	profiler against tracked operation JSONL inputs, for 152 profiler invocations.
772	No dataset is downloaded or synced. The replay check hashes the semantic
773	profile content after removing the JSON \texttt{generated\_at} timestamp, and
774	separately reports raw-byte hashes.

830	\section{Related Work and Novelty}
831	
832	\textbf{Classic profiling and trace analysis.}
833	Flame graphs and pprof establish the folded-stack lineage for profiling:
834	profiles consist of weighted samples attached to a location hierarchy, can carry
835	sample labels, and pprof can visualize labels as pseudo stack frames through
836	tag-root or tag-leaf options~\cite{flamegraphs,pprof}. Perfetto generalizes
837	trace ingestion and SQL analysis over many trace formats and can derive new
838	events from trace contents~\cite{perfetto}. These systems are closer than a
839	simple ``fixed hierarchy'' baseline. \toolname therefore does not claim novelty
840	for query-time aggregation alone. The difference is the domain object and
841	evaluation target: the sample is an agent operation, the frames are recursive
842	multi-field operation projections, and the groups are scored against hidden
843	agent-trajectory labels across datasets.
844	
845	\textbf{Agent tracing and LLM observability.}
846	OpenTelemetry GenAI and OpenInference standardize GenAI spans, LLM calls, agent
847	reasoning steps, tool invocations, retrieval operations, MCP, and
848	provider-specific telemetry~\cite{otel,openinference}. LangSmith, Langfuse, and
849	Phoenix expose traces, sessions, observations, evaluations, dashboards, datasets,
850	and prompt iteration workflows~\cite{langsmith,langfuse,phoenix}. AgentOps gives
851	the closest academic same-problem framing by arguing that agent observability
852	should trace goals, plans, tools, artifacts, and associated data~\cite{agentops}.
853	These systems are strong prior work, so the safe novelty claim is not generic
854	``agent observability.'' In this paper, traces, spans, sessions, and observations
855	are exchange containers or baseline shapes. E2 evaluates fixed-session
856	drilldown as the current trace-tree-shaped baseline; real
857	OpenTelemetry/OpenInference or Phoenix span-tree imports remain future
858	interoperability baselines. The profiler
859	abstractions are only operations and operation stacks, and the central mechanism
860	is that stack shape determines semantic aggregation at query time.
861	
862	\textbf{Agent failure and span localization.}
863	Recent agent-diagnosis work is the closest same-problem threat. AgentRx releases
864	failed trajectories with critical-failure-step and failure-category annotations
865	and uses constraint checking plus an LLM judge to localize root causes
866	~\cite{agentrx}. TELBench/DRIFT builds a deep-research span-localization
867	benchmark from semantic spans annotated for harmful errors~\cite{telbench}.
868	Holistic Evaluation and Failure Diagnosis pairs agent-level diagnosis with
869	per-span evaluation over long traces~\cite{holistic}. AgentAtlas argues that
870	outcome leaderboards miss trajectory and control-decision quality~\cite{agentatlas}.
871	These works make clear that failure localization and trajectory diagnosis are
872	not novel by themselves. The narrower difference here is that \toolname treats
873	profile groups as profiler outputs: the same operations are folded into flat,
874	fixed-session drilldown, dataset-native, raw-action, and operation-stack views, then
875	scored with AP, nDCG, recall under inspection budgets, work-to-first-positive,
876	fragmentation, and profile-configuration actionability across heterogeneous
877	public labeled traces. AgentRx- or TELBench-style traces are therefore future
878	oracle/baseline candidates, not current evidence for a broader span-localization
879	claim.
880	
881	\textbf{Public labeled agent trajectories.}
882	AgentRewardBench, OSWorld-Human, OpenCUA/AgentNet, SATraj-OS, and OSWorld
883	provide the labels and workloads that make the hidden-label profiler benchmark possible~\cite{agentrewardpaper,
884	osworldhuman,opencua,safactory,osworld}. Prior benchmark papers use these labels
885	to evaluate agents, reward models, safety behavior, or efficiency. We use them
886	as hidden oracles for a profiler benchmark: different stack-shaped aggregates
887	become ranked outputs, and the evaluation measures precision, recall, AP, nDCG,
888	inspection work, fragmentation, and profile-configuration tuning insight. This is the paper's
889	scoped novelty.
890	
891	\section{Discussion}
892	
893	The result scope is deliberately narrow. The main claim is a profiler claim:
894	on six real labeled tasks, operation-stack profiles can be scored as ranked
895	localization outputs against dataset-provided labels, and they expose a
896	work/fragmentation/actionability tradeoff against flat summaries,
897	fixed-session drilldown, dataset-native hierarchy, and raw-action stacks. The
898	supporting audits add uncertainty checks, label-permutation negative controls,
899	view/depth task-fit checks, fixed-recall target costs, sequence-scope scoring,
900	oracle-depth scoring, action counterfactuals, transfer checks, and
901	replayability checks. They do not add a new empirical claim; they explain when
902	the headline comparison should be trusted and when it should be narrowed.
903	
904	The strongest negative results define the useful boundary. Operation-stack
905	query-aware ranking improves AP over width on all six E2 tasks, but top-five
906	F1, first-positive work, and high-recall targets remain task dependent.
907	Mapping helps some tasks and hurts others; feature ablations find both critical
908	and misleading fields; held-out action transfer is often within tolerance but
909	rarely transfers the exact action class for non-default targets. Fixed-session
910	drilldown remains a real first-positive counterpoint, raw-action stacks can
911	cover broader session scope, and OSWorld-Human needs boundary-derived fields.
912	These counterpoints are why the design exposes stack fields, mapping rules,
913	rank modes, operation-level rank features, profile specs, and task-specific
914	policies instead of hard-coding one hierarchy.
915	
916	These results do not show that humans or agents answer questions faster with
917	the tool, nor do they measure live eBPF overhead. They also do not show
918	automatic discovery of all intent boundaries, a label-free automatic selector,
919	or complete compatibility with OpenTelemetry, Phoenix, LangSmith, Langfuse, or
920	Perfetto producers. Those systems remain related work and baselines. In this
921	paper, trace formats are containers; fixed sessions are the evaluated drilldown
922	baseline, while real span-tree imports remain future baselines. The profiler
923	abstractions remain only operations and operation stacks.
924	
925	\section{Conclusion}
926	
927	\toolname reduces agent profiling to two abstractions. Operations carry all
928	observed and derived fields; operation stacks fold those fields at the depth
929	chosen by the query. Mapping, predicates, rank rules, profile specs, trace
930	exchange, and boundary backends are mechanisms around those two objects, not
931	additional profiler abstractions.
932	
933	Across 15 public labeled trace sources, the model covers web, mobile, desktop,
934	software, API, dialogue, failure, safety, human-boundary, and step-quality
935	trajectories. On the four oracle-rich families, operation-stack profiling
936	localizes and ranks labeled problems with less inspection work than flat
937	summaries and a better median-fragmentation tradeoff than fixed-session
938	drilldown, while the
939	mechanism audits show which fields, mappings, rankers, depths, and profile-spec
940	patches produce the gains. The paper's central claim is therefore a profiler
941	claim: operation/operation-stack profiling exposes dataset-labeled
942	task-relevant failures, quality problems, and semantic boundaries, and produces
943	profile-configuration actionability without relying on prompt/session/span
944	boundaries.
945	The novelty is not a new renderer, trace schema, or generic query engine; it is
946	the combination of agent-operation records, recursive multi-field stack
947	projections, and hidden-label profile-group scoring.
948	
949	The evidence remains scoped. The profile-spec and deterministic-output audits
950	make the offline outputs reproducible, and the claim-scope checks keep the
951	paper aligned with tracked results. They do not claim human or agent
952	analyst productivity, live eBPF overhead, automatic discovery of all intent
953	boundaries, a label-free universal selector, or complete compatibility with
954	OpenTelemetry, Phoenix, LangSmith, Langfuse, or Perfetto producers.

\documentclass[sigconf]{acmart}

\setcopyright{none}
\settopmatter{printacmref=false}
\renewcommand\footnotetextcopyrightpermission[1]{}
\pagestyle{plain}

\usepackage{booktabs}
\usepackage{array}
\usepackage{xspace}
\usepackage{url}
\usepackage{graphicx}

\newcommand{\toolname}{\textsc{AgentPProf}\xspace}
\newcommand{\operation}{\texttt{operation}\xspace}
\newcommand{\opstack}{\texttt{operation stack}\xspace}

\begin{document}

\title{AgentPProf: Operation-Stack Profiling for AI Agent Traces}

\begin{abstract}
AI-agent executions are no longer well described by one prompt, one session, or
one trace tree. A single run can contain prompts, tool calls, GUI actions,
browser actions, process events, plans, subagents, safety labels, failure
labels, and human subtask boundaries. Existing observability systems usually
make one boundary primary, such as a session, span, or prompt tree. Classic
profilers make another boundary primary, such as a function call stack. This
paper argues that agent profiling needs a smaller abstraction: an
\operation is a weighted record with fields, and an \opstack is a recursive
projection over those fields chosen at query time. Aggregation is not a separate
object or a fixed trace tree; it is the result of choosing a stack shape over the
same operations. This is not merely a claim about query-time aggregation, which
classic profilers and trace processors also support in different forms. The
scoped novelty is the combination of an agent-operation record model, recursive
multi-field operation-stack projections, and a hidden-label cross-dataset
localization benchmark.

We implement this model in the Rust \toolname profiler and evaluate it through
three core empirical profiling experiments, RQ1/E1 through RQ3/E3, plus one
replayability/scope-control block, RQ4/E4, rather than a chronological run list.
RQ1/E1 tests generality and
recursive operation-stack formation: across 15 lightly sampled public labeled
sources, \toolname maps 47,590 samples into the same operation layer, and the
same 13,265 operations fold from 9 dataset stacks to 57 phase, 226 semantic, 455
action, or 3,757 fixed-session stacks without changing the input operations. RQ2/E2
is the main hidden-label localization benchmark. On AgentRewardBench,
SATraj-OS, AgentNet, and OSWorld-Human, we build six tasks over 34,539
operations and 3,699 positives, score 144 view/ranker policies, and find that
task-query operation-stack profiling inspects median 0.0937 top-five work versus
1.0 for flat summaries, improves top-five recall over fixed-session drilldown on
5 of 6 tasks, and reduces median group fragmentation from 285.0 to 157.5
groups.
RQ3/E3 isolates mechanisms and profile-configuration actionability. Rank-feature,
stack-depth, mapping, transfer, diagnostic-lens, case-packet, and counterfactual
analyses show that the useful configuration varies by task and objective:
operation-stack views are a Pareto point, not a universal default. Executable
profile-spec patches improve AP, top-five lift, and first-positive work on 5 of
6 tasks; a supervised held-out boundary-field ablation improves OSWorld-Human AP
from 0.2402 to 0.2583 and reduces groups from 108 to 74, while preserving work
counterpoints. A field-suitability synthesis further turns mapping, stack-depth,
rank-feature, and boundary-field evidence into guarded configuration decisions
with accept, caution, and reject outcomes. RQ4/E4 checks replayability, offline cost, and claim scope.
Deterministic replay covers 76 tracked profile specs, and profile-spec input
regressions cover local-session, agent-trace, and standard-trace replay. The
recorded source provenance, paper-number, rubric, and two-abstraction checks
constrain the paper's scope rather than forming a fourth empirical profiling
experiment.

The supported claim is therefore a scoped profiling claim: operation-stack
profiling can localize, rank, and explain dataset-labeled failures, quality
problems, and semantic boundaries in public traces, with less inspection work
than flat summaries and a better median-fragmentation tradeoff than the
fixed-session drilldown proxy. Fixed-session drilldown is the current
trace-tree-shaped baseline; real
OpenTelemetry/OpenInference/Phoenix-style span-tree imports remain future
baselines. The paper does not claim human-productivity gains, automatic
discovery of all intent boundaries, metric dominance, or complete compatibility
with existing trace ecosystems.
\end{abstract}

\maketitle

\section{Introduction}

AI-agent traces mix many objects that traditional profiling and tracing systems
keep separate. A coding agent may ask a model for a plan, call a shell tool,
launch a subagent, inspect a file, and retry a failing command. A web or desktop
agent may click, type, observe a page, repeat an action, and receive a benchmark
label saying that the action was unsafe, redundant, incorrect, or the start of
a human subtask. If the profiler fixes the hierarchy at prompt, session, or
span boundaries, these questions become hard to ask: which phases concentrate
unsafe operations, which action families cause redundant steps, and which
groups of operations cross sessions but share the same failure mode?

\toolname takes the opposite position. The profiler stores a sequence as
operations, where prompts, tool calls, processes, syscalls, GUI actions, and
plan steps are operation records or derived fields. Session, span, task, and
trace identifiers are fields, exchange containers, or baseline shapes rather
than separate profiler objects. Users then choose an operation stack to fold the
same operations at different depths. One query may group by
\texttt{task,phase,action}; another may group by
\texttt{environment,safety}. Mapping and tagging are first-class field-derivation
steps, but they do not add a third profiler object. They only write fields
before the stack query runs. Thus the novelty is the abstraction that connects
stack shape to aggregation: changing the stack changes what is comparable,
localizable, and actionable without changing the underlying trace object model.

This paper makes a profiling claim, not a human-productivity claim. A top-tier
profiling paper must show that the profiler attributes, localizes, and ranks
problems against explicit workload labels, and that the output leads to
optimization insight with better label-scored ranking or inspection cost than baselines. For agents, the
claim is:
\begin{quote}
\emph{Operation/operation-stack profiling provides label-scored localization
and ranking for task-relevant failures, quality problems, and dataset-provided
semantic boundaries in real labeled agent traces, while requiring less
inspection work than flat summaries and improving the median fragmentation
tradeoff relative to fixed-session drilldown.}
\end{quote}

We evaluate this claim with public labeled traces rather than a human study. A
human or agent analyst study would be useful for productivity claims, but it is
not required to test label-scored profiler fidelity. Our evaluation therefore
uses hidden labels as the oracle for ranked profile groups and is organized
as three empirical profiling experiments plus one replayability/scope-control
block. RQ1/E1 tests operation generality, recursive stack folding, field
derivation, and human-boundary alignment under the same two-object model. RQ2/E2
is the main hidden-label localization and ranking benchmark. RQ3/E3 isolates
mechanisms and actionability through ranker, stack, mapping, transfer, case, and
profile-spec patch ablations. RQ4/E4 checks replayability, offline cost, and
claim scope. It is not treated as a fourth hidden-label accuracy result or a
fourth empirical profiling experiment. Supplementary results support these
blocks rather than defining the paper-facing structure.

\section{Design}

\subsection{Operations}

An \operation is the only sample-level object in \toolname. It is a weighted
record with string fields. The same representation can encode a prompt, a tool
call, an API call, a browser action, a PyAutoGUI action, a process event, or a
derived label such as \texttt{looping=yes} or \texttt{step\_correct=incorrect}.
External datasets enter the system as operation JSONL. Local Codex or Claude
sessions can also be exported as an agent-session trace, imported back, or
converted to operation JSONL before profiling.

\subsection{Operation Stacks}

An \opstack is an ordered list of fields. Folding operations by that list yields
the usual folded-stack representation, but the stack is chosen at query time.
The same operation file can be folded as a flat task summary, a fixed-session
tree, a dataset-native hierarchy, a raw action stack, a semantic operation
stack, or an oracle label-drilldown. Fixed sessions and spans are therefore
baselines and exchange containers, not core profiler abstractions.

\subsection{Mapping and Tagging}

Mapping and tagging derive new operation fields before folding. For example,
desktop actions such as \texttt{type} and \texttt{key} can map to
\texttt{phase=input}, while tool/API rows can map to a tool phase before generic
action rules run. The Rust CLI exposes inline rules, rule files, profile specs,
operation predicates, and stack overrides. \texttt{--where} predicates run after
mapping and before stack construction, implementing the query predicate without
adding a profiler object. Profile specs record operation files, mappings,
predicates, views, stacks, and outputs for reproducibility, while command-line
flags can still override the stack query.

\section{Results}

\subsection{RQ1/E1: Generality and Recursive Folding}

RQ1/E1 tests whether one operation layer can represent heterogeneous agent
traces without making prompt, session, tool, process, or syscall records into
separate profiler objects. The evaluation folds the same operation records into
task, phase, action, human-boundary, and fixed-session-shaped stacks by changing
only mappings and stack fields. Public dataset labels and native trajectory
fields provide the oracle signal, with OSWorld-Human boundaries and AgentNet
quality labels as the strongest structure labels. The comparison uses
dataset-native, no-map, fixed-session, replay, and trace round-trip views. The
metrics are coverage, stack range, compression, boundary F1, V-measure, and
round-trip equality. The scoped conclusion is configurable operation-stack
folding, not complete ecosystem compatibility or latent-intent recovery.

The 14 core public sources produce 42,590 operations. Adding the supplemental
ScaleCUA stream brings the smoke set to 47,590 operations. These operations
cover web, mobile, desktop, software, API, tool-agent-user dialogue, expert
failure labels, safety labels, human grouped-action labels, and desktop
step-quality labels. No source required a prompt-specific, GUI-specific, or
safety-specific profiler object.

\paragraph{Recursive stack-depth sweep.}

On the same 13,265 operations, a depth sweep folds to 9 dataset stacks, 57
phase stacks, 226 tool/semantic stacks, 455 action stacks, and 3,757
fixed-session stacks. A fixed session boundary therefore increases stack count
by 417.4$\times$ relative to dataset depth. On AgentNet, a tracked profile spec
folds 16,741 operations into 608 diagnostic stacks, while a CLI stack override
changes the output to 83 stacks without changing the operation input. The
result supports query-time recursive stack choice rather than a fixed
prompt/session hierarchy.

The implementation probes are grouped as interface evidence, not additional
main experiments. They show that profile specs can select mapped subsets before
folding (729/729, 714/714, and 4,285/4,285 expected operations), compose
operation files, predicates, visible ranking rules, rank modes, and explicit
stack depths without prompt/session frames (12/12 specs), and round-trip a real
operation-file prefix through a standard trace container while preserving 512
samples and 11 folded stacks. These interface checks are provenance for E1: they
test whether the operation layer stays fixed while views change; the
localization and ranker gains from those specs are evaluated under E2/E3.

\paragraph{Field derivation and boundary probes.}

Held-out mapping rules improve compression from 14.049 to 19.091 on 3,990
operations. Leave-dataset-out mapping reduces unique stacks on 6 of 9 held-out
datasets with no negative stack-reduction regressions after API/tool phase
precedence is fixed. A supervised OSWorld-Human boundary backend reaches F1
0.7735 on held-out adjacent pairs and writes predicted boundary fields that the
Rust profiler folds as ordinary operation fields. Boundary backends therefore
extend field derivation, not the profiler object model.
The field-derivation audit keeps both support and counterpoints visible:
held-out mapping improves compression but coarsens action-to-phase V-measure
from 0.9343 to 0.7416; profile-spec composition stays prompt/session-free on
12/12 variants; and learned boundary backends beat the best simple baseline on
4/5 rows, while AgentRewardBench looping is fully explained by
\texttt{repeat\_signal\_change}. This supports first-class field derivation and
suitability checks, not automatic intent boundary discovery and not a new
profiler object. Rank-feature criticality from the same audit belongs to
RQ3/E3's mechanism/actionability evidence, not to RQ1/E1's abstraction claim.
The suitability check makes the extension policy explicit. Deterministic
mappings are useful for compression but can coarsen action boundaries. Rank
features require ablation guards because both critical and misleading feature
rows appear. Boundary-derived fields require family-specific evidence. The
tested boundary families produce accept, caution, and reject outcomes, so field
derivation remains a guarded profile-configuration loop rather than a universal
selector.

\paragraph{Human-boundary oracle.}

OSWorld-Human gives the strongest direct boundary oracle. On 320 exact-aligned
tasks with 4,011 operations and 2,075 human groups, grouped-depth stacks reduce
482 action stacks to 106 grouped stacks. A conservative \texttt{group\_pattern}
projection has human-group boundary F1 0.627 with precision 1.0 and recall
0.456. This is not complete intent discovery, but it shows that the same
single-action sequence can be folded at action depth or human-group depth and
scored against a human boundary oracle.

\subsection{RQ2/E2: Hidden-Label Localization and Ranking}

RQ2/E2 treats profiling as a ranked localization problem. The benchmark marks
3,699 positive operations among 34,539 operations and asks whether hot stacks
and top-ranked groups correspond to those hidden positives. The comparison
covers flat summaries, fixed-session drilldown, dataset-native hierarchy,
raw-action stacks, operation stacks, label drilldown, and oracle upper bounds.
The metrics are precision@k, recall, F1, AP as an AUPRC-style score, nDCG,
budget recall and F1, work-to-first-positive, and group count. The scoped claim
is a Pareto tradeoff: operation stacks should reduce flat inspection work and
improve a useful fixed-session localization or fragmentation objective, while
flat and dataset-native views may still win broad-recall or nDCG goals.

Primary comparison and success criterion. E2 treats every profile group as an
inspection target and asks whether the ranked targets find hidden positives
with less work than flat summaries and less fragmentation than a fixed-session
trace-tree proxy. Success is therefore a Pareto condition, not a single winning
metric: operation stacks must reduce flat inspection work, improve a meaningful
fixed-session localization or fragmentation objective, and keep fixed-session
early-hit counterpoints visible. Table~\ref{tab:e2-localization} is the main E2
localization display; supporting case views explain the result without becoming
separate paper experiments. Flat summaries recover all positives, but only by inspecting the
whole task, so their median work@5 and work-to-first-positive are both 1.0.
Fixed-session drilldown finds an early
positive with median work-to-first-positive 0.0044 and median work@5 0.0163,
but its median recall@5 is only 0.0233 and it fragments the workload into 285.0
groups. Query-aware operation stacks inspect median 0.0937 work in the top five
groups, reach median recall@budget30 of 0.3900, and reduce the median group
count to 157.5.

Failure interpretation and baseline scope are part of the result.
Fixed-session drilldown is the evaluated trace-tree-shaped baseline, not
evidence of full OpenTelemetry/Phoenix/LangSmith/Perfetto compatibility. On the
same scored rows, operation-stack query-aware improves fixed-session top-five
recall and F1 on 5/6 tasks, budget-30 recall on 4/6, and group count on 4/6,
while fixed-session retains lower top-five work and first-positive work on 4/6.
The depth-aware slice gives the finer version of the same claim: operation-stack rankings
beat fixed-session on budget-30 positive-unit recall for 20/24 task-depth rows
and use fewer groups to reach 50\% positive units on 22/24 rows. If these
counterpoints disappeared from the paper, the result would be overstated; with
them, E2 supports a better localization-budget/fragmentation tradeoff, not
dominance over every trace-tree-shaped objective.

\subsection{RQ3/E3: Mechanism and Actionability}

RQ3/E3 asks why the E2 rankings improve and whether the profiler points to
concrete configuration changes. The candidate mechanisms are stack fields,
mapping and tagging rules, rankers, profile specs, and boundary-derived
operation fields. Hidden labels score the output only after profiling, and
held-out OSWorld-Human boundary positives score boundary-derived fields. The
comparison covers default and patched specs, visible rankers, transfer
policies, learned-boundary fields, fixed-session drilldown, and semantic-width
stacks. The metrics are accepted patches, AP delta, top-five lift,
first-positive work, group reduction, and top-five-work counterpoints. The
scoped conclusion is profile-configuration actionability, not automatic
boundary discovery, automatic patch selection, or a universal selector.

Primary mechanism question. E3 starts from the E2 ranked outputs and asks
whether the profiler can explain what to change in the profile configuration.
Hidden labels are used only after profiling to score a configuration; the
visible inputs are stack fields, mapping/tagging rules, rank features, profile
specs, and boundary-derived operation fields. The success criterion is an
actionable, replayable diagnosis: a task should point to a concrete stack,
field, ranker, mapping, profile-spec, or drilldown change, and executable
patches should improve the scored output without turning into an automatic
selector.

Table~\ref{tab:actionability} is the main E3 display. It compresses the
task-card evidence into a paper-facing diagnosis table; the supporting case
views remain provenance rather than additional main experiments.
SATraj unsafe is the cleanest operation-stack win: environment, phase, and
action fields plus query-aware risk ranking give the best visible top-five F1.
Looping exposes the value and limit of \texttt{repeat\_signal}: it helps
ranking, but positives are prevalent, so prevalence-aware ranking remains the
optimization. Side-effect has large oracle headroom and points to deeper
write/input mappings. AgentNet step-quality tasks need action-family
localization followed by fixed-session examples. OSWorld-Human needs
boundary-derived fields rather than action depth alone. Thus the first
actionability result is not that one view wins; it is that the profiler
identifies which stack field, mapping, ranker, or drilldown should change for
each task family.
The task-level verdict synthesis clarifies the claim boundary: all six tasks
support E3 with counterpoints, not as unconditional wins. Five of six tasks have
accepted executable profile-spec patches; the remaining OSWorld-Human row points
to boundary-derived fields and keeps top-five and first-positive work
counterpoints.
The six rows resolve into three reusable optimization patterns. Safety and
side-effect tasks point to field and ranker changes because environment,
phase/action, and write/input fields move relevant positives into smaller
inspected regions. Step-quality tasks point to a drilldown workflow because
desktop phase, repeat, and action fields locate suspicious regions before
fixed-session examples explain individual traces. Human-boundary tasks point to
representation repair because action-depth stacks are insufficient, while
boundary-derived operation fields improve AP and reduce groups with explicit
inspection-work counterpoints. These patterns are configuration guidance over
profile inputs, stack fields, and rankers, not labels predicted by the profiler.

The Rust mechanism ablations isolate where those diagnoses come from without
turning the paper into a run list. First, stack-text rules and rank-mode
variants are replayable from profile specs but too coarse for safety and
side-effect tasks. Second, operation-level rank features close that gap by
matching visible mapped operation tokens before folding: semantic-stack feature
ranking improves AP over width on 5 of 6 tasks, top-five lift on 4 of 6, and
first-positive work on 5 of 6; coarse depth improves AP on 4 of 6 while
reducing groups. Third, leave-one-feature and robustness ablations make the
knobs concrete: \texttt{repeat\_signal}, write-action features, and
\texttt{status=success} are critical in different families, while misleading
safety-like or input-phase features can hurt AP or first-positive work.
Equal/global feature banks often preserve the gains, and guided repairs improve
AP on 2 of 3 misleading-feature cases, but these repairs use offline scored
feedback and are not an automatic learned ranker. These audits are provenance
for this single E3 mechanism block.

The view and policy audits show the same mechanism at the analysis-surface
level. Best AP and best top-five F1 are split across operation-stack,
fixed-session, dataset-native, raw-action, and flat views; leave-task source
selection cannot reliably pick the best visible view. Nevertheless, the
operation-stack query-aware policy remains Pareto-frontier on all six tasks,
beats flat top-five work on all six, beats fixed-session top-five recall on 5
of 6, and reaches fewer groups-to-50\% positives than fixed-session on 5 of 6.
At a 25\% recall target it covers all six tasks with median work 0.2000 versus
flat 1.0000 and median 16.0 groups versus fixed-session 50.0; at 50\% recall,
other depths or views become the best-work counterpoints. Sequence and
oracle-depth audits add the inspection unit below and above individual groups.
Sequence and oracle-depth scoring show that
at a 30\% operation budget, operation-stack query-aware reaches median 0.4669
positive-session recall versus fixed-session 0.3230, and across 24 oracle-depth
rows it has median 0.4342 budget-30 positive-unit recall, beats fixed-session
unit recall on 20/24 rows, and reaches 50\% positive units with fewer groups on
22/24. Positive-run proxy units are derived episode units, not human intent
boundaries. The fixed-session depth-gap counterpoint remains, so this is
depth-aware triage, not complete intent-boundary recovery.
The multi-metric audit also keeps the metric surface honest: it records 30
supporting baseline-metric comparisons, 16 explicit counterpoints, and nDCG
cases where flat or dataset-native views can win.

The actionability portfolio turns those comparisons into reviewer-auditable
profile-configuration tuning insight. Across 36 objective rows, every row has a
concrete configuration action, but 27/36 best visible policies are not the
default operation-stack query-aware view; transfer misses are mostly view or
ranker changes rather than opaque errors. The same evidence is presented as
diagnostic lenses, case packets, and baseline contrasts: six lenses cover 36
objectives, top-five case groups contain positives on 6/6 tasks, top-one groups
on 5/6, median top-five lift is 1.6508 at 0.0937 work, and operation stacks beat
flat top-five work on 6/6 and fixed-session top-five recall on 5/6 while
preserving fixed-session first-positive and flat full-recall counterpoints.
Counterfactual and held-out transfer checks separate visible actions from
target-label leakage: 36/36 best rows are visible non-oracle, 27/36 require a
non-default action, 25/36 require a view change, held-out action transfer stays
within tolerance on 35/60 aligned decisions, but exact action-class transfer is
only 7/60 overall and 2/42 on non-default target actions. These support audits
form one E3 actionability block. The actionable claim is therefore a tunable
diagnosis surface, not a label-free automatic selector.
Field-suitability decisions make that guard concrete. Deterministic mapping,
stack-depth and predicate choices, operation-level rank features, supervised
boundary fields, and boundary-profile repair are useful only under different
conditions. The boundary-family matrix has one accept, three caution, and one
reject outcome, which means the profiler can guide configuration but should not
present boundary fields as a universal automatic selector.

Finally, executable patches close one loop from diagnosis to profiler
configuration. Default and profile-guided Rust profile specs run over the same
visible operation input, and hidden labels are scored only after
\texttt{agentpprof --profile-spec}. Five of six patches improve AP, top-five
lift, and first-positive work, with median AP delta 0.0376 and median top-five
lift delta 0.5750. The failure interpretation matters here too: the rejected
OSWorld-Human patch shows that visible phase/action rank features are
insufficient for a human-boundary objective. Folding held-out boundary-derived
operation fields then improves AP to 0.2583 versus 0.2402 for semantic width
and reduces groups to 74 versus 108, while top-five work and first-positive
work increase. These patch and boundary-field results support boundary fields
as an actionable operation-field knob, not automatic boundary
discovery or automatic patch selection. The result belongs to
mechanism/actionability, not a fifth core experiment.

\subsection{RQ4/E4: Reproducibility, Offline Cost, and Scope Control}

RQ4/E4 asks a narrower question than E2/E3: can reviewers replay the
offline profile-spec path at low local cost while checking that source
provenance, paper numbers, two-abstraction wording, and non-claims remain
aligned? The evidence is the tracked specs and inputs, profile-spec input
replay regressions, repeated profile outputs, runtime logs, and recorded source
provenance. We compare default output with deterministic-output replay, semantic
profile hashes with raw-byte hashes, and effective input metadata with silently
ignored source paths. The measured quantities are deterministic spec pass rate,
profiler invocations, median and p95 runtime, sample equality, stack equality,
raw-byte output equality, and input-source replay coverage. These checks bound
the paper claim. They are not a hidden-label accuracy result, live eBPF
overhead, human utility, complete ecosystem compatibility, or a universal
selector.

The empirical content of this subsection is only one replayability/cost block. It
reruns the profile specs used by the labeled-trace experiments: 76
tracked specs over tracked operation JSONL inputs, executed twice for 152
profiler invocations. The semantic profile content is stable for 76/76 specs in
both modes; deterministic output also makes raw-byte profile files stable for
76/76 specs by fixing profile timestamps. The clean deterministic rerun reports
median runtime 1.601s and p95 2.767s per spec. The replayed files provide
provenance for this E4 block. This supports replayable offline
profiler outputs, not live eBPF overhead or analyst productivity, or another
empirical profiling experiment.

Input-source replay checks belong to the same E4 block. The Rust
profile-spec path carries \texttt{session\_files}, \texttt{trace\_files},
\texttt{standard\_trace\_files}, regex tag rules, predicates, rank rules, stack
overrides, and \texttt{include\_standard\_trace\_args}. The regressions replay
the public Codex fixture as a local session and as an exported agent-session
trace, then replay a generic Chrome Trace Event import whose non-AgentSight
\texttt{protocol} argument becomes an operation field before folding. These
checks keep local sessions and trace containers inside the same operation /
operation-stack path. They do not add a new accuracy experiment, a third
profiler object, or an ecosystem-compatibility claim.

The remaining consistency checks support reproducibility and scope control, not
new empirical evidence. They reuse tracked inputs, tracked outputs, and the current paper text
without reranking, downloading, syncing, creating, relabeling, rerunning the
profiler, or running a human or agent analyst task. The checks verify replay
paths, source provenance, paper-number alignment, two-abstraction wording, and
non-claim consistency. They let reviewers audit whether the paper is faithful to
tracked outputs, but they do not increase the localization, actionability, or
overhead claims.

The workload contains 76 tracked specs: four view specs, 12 operation-feature
