\documentclass[sigconf]{acmart}

\setcopyright{none}
\settopmatter{printacmref=false}
\renewcommand\footnotetextcopyrightpermission[1]{}
\pagestyle{plain}

\usepackage{booktabs}
\usepackage{array}
\usepackage{xspace}
\usepackage{url}
\usepackage{graphicx}

\newcommand{\toolname}{\textsc{AgentPProf}\xspace}
\newcommand{\operation}{\texttt{operation}\xspace}
\newcommand{\opstack}{\texttt{operation stack}\xspace}

\begin{document}

\title{AgentPProf: Semantic Profiling for AI Agent Traces}

\begin{abstract}
AI agent observability tools can show every span, every LLM call, and every
tool invocation---but they cannot answer aggregate questions: which categories
of work consumed the most tokens, where did the budget go, and which task
families produce repeated failures? These tools are debuggers; agents also
need a profiler.

CPU profilers solved the equivalent problem for programs: flame graphs fold
millions of function calls into a single chart where width equals cost.
The key enabler is that function names are deterministic---identical code
paths produce identical stack frames that merge on contact.
Agent traces break this assumption. Prompts are natural language:
nondeterministic, variable-length, multilingual. Two prompts expressing the
same intent produce different strings and cannot be folded.

\toolname restores the aggregation ability that natural-language prompts
break. It maps free-form prompts to stable semantic labels
(\texttt{debug}, \texttt{review}, \texttt{test}), then folds agent traces
into flame graphs where width represents token count, wall-clock time, or
operation count. The profiler retains only two core abstractions:
an \emph{operation} (a weighted record carrying semantic and
mechanism fields) and an \emph{operation stack} (an ordered field
projection chosen at query time). Sessions, spans, and trace identifiers
are operation fields, not separate profiler objects; changing the stack
changes the aggregation without changing the underlying data.

We evaluate \toolname on 15 public labeled trace families (47{,}590
operations) and on hundreds of real Codex/Claude sessions (183{,}714
system observations). On real sessions, removing semantic labels leaves
90.4\% of system-effect weight in mixed-intent buckets; adding prompt
labels reduces this to 36.7\%. On four oracle-rich public datasets (6
tasks, 34{,}539 operations, 3{,}699 positives), operation-stack profiling
inspects 9.4\% of the work to cover the top five groups versus 100\% for
flat summaries, and reduces median group fragmentation from 285 to 158
compared to fixed-session drilldown. Case studies on real flame graphs
show actionable budget, duplication, and security-audit insights that
timeline views cannot surface.
\end{abstract}

\maketitle

%% ===================================================================
\section{Introduction}

AI agent systems produce execution traces that interleave prompts, LLM
calls, tool invocations, GUI actions, process events, and benchmark
labels. As agent deployments scale to hundreds of sessions and tens of
thousands of calls, developers need to answer aggregate questions: which
categories of work consume the most tokens, where do repeated failures
concentrate, and how does cost distribute across semantic task families?
Existing observability tools---LangSmith~\cite{langsmith},
Langfuse~\cite{langfuse}, Phoenix~\cite{phoenix}, OpenTelemetry
GenAI~\cite{otel}---organize events into per-execution timelines and
span trees, enabling developers to debug individual runs. But no existing
tool provides an aggregate view that folds heterogeneous events across
sessions into a cost or frequency distribution grouped by semantic work
category.

This gap has a precise analogy in traditional software.
Before CPU profilers, developers diagnosed performance by reading logs
and instrumenting individual functions. Flame
graphs~\cite{flamegraphs} and profiling tools like pprof~\cite{pprof}
changed the practice: they compress millions of function-call samples
into a single chart where width represents cost, and identical call
stacks merge automatically. The key enabler is that function names are
\emph{deterministic}---the same code path always produces the same stack
frames. Agent traces break this assumption. Prompts are natural language:
nondeterministic, variable-length, and multilingual.
``Fix the bug'' and ``修一下这个 error'' express the same intent but
share no characters. If prompt text is used directly as a flame-graph
frame label, every prompt becomes a unique bar and no aggregation occurs.
The same problem affects tool calls, GUI actions, and process events,
which are named heterogeneously across agent families and trace formats.

This paper presents \toolname, a profiler that restores aggregate
flame-graph analysis for agent traces. The core mechanism is
\emph{intent recognition}: mapping free-form prompts and heterogeneous
actions to stable semantic labels through pluggable backends (regex rules,
local LLM tagging, or unsupervised clustering). Once labeled, agent
events fold into flame graphs using the same folded-stack aggregation
that CPU profilers use. The profiler is built on two abstractions:
an \emph{operation} (a weighted record representing any measurable agent
activity) and an \emph{operation stack} (an ordered field projection
chosen at query time). Sessions, spans, and trace identifiers are
operation fields, not separate profiler objects; changing the stack
projection changes the aggregation shape without changing the underlying
data.

This paper makes three contributions:

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Problem: the aggregation gap.}
  We identify a structural gap in agent observability: existing tools
  provide per-execution trace debugging but not cross-session aggregate
  profiling. The key obstacle is that natural-language prompts lack the
  deterministic identifiers that enable flame-graph folding
  (\S\ref{sec:design}).
\item \textbf{Design: semantic agent profiling.}
  We design a profiler around two abstractions---operations and operation
  stacks---with pluggable intent recognition that restores flame-graph
  aggregation for agent traces. Four built-in views answer distinct
  aggregate questions about token budget, time, file access, and network
  activity (\S\ref{sec:design}--\S\ref{sec:impl}).
\item \textbf{Evaluation.}
  On real agent sessions, semantic labels separate 90\% of the
  system-effect weight that unsemantic summaries merge. On public labeled
  benchmarks, operation-stack profiling reduces inspection work by 90\%
  versus flat summaries and fragmentation by 45\% versus fixed-session
  drilldown. Case studies demonstrate budget, duplication, and
  security-audit insights invisible to timeline views
  (\S\ref{sec:eval}).
\end{enumerate}

%% ===================================================================
\section{Design}
\label{sec:design}

\subsection{Operations and Operation Stacks}

A CPU flame graph has two objects: a \emph{sample} (a weighted snapshot of
the call stack) and a \emph{stack} (the sequence of function frames).
\toolname adapts these to agent traces.

An \operation is a weighted record representing one measurable activity in
an agent's history: a user prompt, an LLM call, a tool invocation, a file
read, or a network request. Each operation carries string fields
(\texttt{project}, \texttt{agent}, \texttt{session}, \texttt{prompt\_tag},
\texttt{kind}, \texttt{model}, \texttt{path}, \texttt{domain},
\texttt{status}, \ldots) and additive measures (token count, duration,
occurrence count). Different agent families and trace formats produce
different fields, but every entry is an operation record.

An \opstack is an ordered list of fields chosen at query time. Folding
operations by that list produces the standard folded-stack representation:

\begin{small}
\begin{verbatim}
CPU:   main;parse;tokenize          42
Agent: prompt:debug;call:llm;tool:bash  4200
\end{verbatim}
\end{small}

\noindent The critical difference from CPU profiling is that the stack is
not determined by execution---it is chosen by the analyst. The same
operations can be folded as a flat task summary, a fixed-session tree, a
semantic phase/action hierarchy, or a dataset-native trajectory. Changing
the fields changes the aggregation shape without changing the underlying
operations.

A \emph{view} is a triple $(\varphi, \sigma, w)$: a predicate $\varphi$
selects which operations participate, a stack function $\sigma$ maps each
operation to a frame sequence, and a weight function $w$ assigns a
nonnegative measure. Evaluation produces folded stacks grouped by
$\sigma$ with weights summed by $w$. Four built-in views answer four
different questions:

\begin{table}[t]
\centering\small
\caption{Built-in views. Each shares the same operation set
but selects different activities, stack structures, and weights.}
\label{tab:views}
\begin{tabular}{llll}
\toprule
View & $\varphi$ (select) & $w$ (width) & Question \\
\midrule
\texttt{tokens} & LLM calls & token count & Budget distribution? \\
\texttt{time} & All timed ops & duration (s) & Time distribution? \\
\texttt{files} & File-effect ops & event count & Repo coverage? \\
\texttt{network} & Net-effect ops & event count & External contacts? \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Sessions and spans deserve explicit discussion. In existing observability
tools, sessions and spans define the fixed hierarchy. In \toolname, they
are optional operation fields. An analyst can include \texttt{session} in
the stack (producing a per-session drilldown equivalent to a trace tree),
or exclude it (producing a cross-session aggregate that no trace tool
provides). This is the design's central point: the same data supports
both debugging and profiling views, selected at query time.

\subsection{Intent Recognition: From Prompts to Labels}

Operations and stacks are conventional engineering; the hard problem is
\emph{intent recognition}. A flame graph requires short, stable,
repeatable frame labels. Function names provide this for CPU profiles.
Agent prompts do not: they are free-form, multilingual, variable-length,
and often contain sensitive content.

\toolname provides a pluggable tagger framework with three backends:

\paragraph{Regex rules with agent-assisted iteration.}
The production default. Rules have the form
\texttt{KIND:TAG=REGEX}, where \texttt{KIND} is \texttt{prompt},
\texttt{llm}, or \texttt{all}, \texttt{TAG} is a short lowercase label,
and \texttt{REGEX} is a pattern. Rules are evaluated in order; the first
match wins. The workflow is human--agent collaborative: run \toolname,
observe the unmatched rate and sample prompts, add rules, re-run, and
iterate until unmatched drops below 5\% with a reasonable distribution
(10--20 categories, no single category exceeding 50\%). This typically
takes 5--10 rounds of 1--2 minutes each. The resulting rule set is
deterministic, reproducible, and version-controllable.

\paragraph{Local LLM tagger.}
For exploration or complex multilingual prompts, a local model
(e.g., a 3B-parameter GGUF via llama.cpp) generates a single-word label
per prompt. Grammar-constrained decoding ensures output validity.
Labels are cached; re-runs with unchanged prompts incur zero LLM calls.
The LLM tagger's output serves as a starting point for writing regex
rules.

\paragraph{Unsupervised clustering.}
TF-IDF vectorization followed by K-Means discovers natural prompt groups
without predefined rules. This backend identifies ``what categories exist
in my prompt distribution'' and feeds rule authoring.

The one-word label design is deliberate. Flame-graph frames must be
short; long summaries make charts unreadable. Labels serve navigation
and aggregation, not correctness verdicts. A label like \texttt{debug}
does not certify that the prompt is a debugging task; it groups prompts
that share debugging-related tokens so that their downstream
activities fold together.

\subsection{Mapping for Structured Traces}

For public benchmark datasets and structured trace formats, prompts are
already structured: action types, tool names, environment labels, and
quality annotations are explicit fields. \toolname supports deterministic
\emph{mapping rules} that derive new operation fields from existing ones
before stack construction. For example, desktop actions \texttt{type} and
\texttt{key} can map to \texttt{phase=input}, while API tool rows can map
to a tool-phase field. A \emph{profile spec} records the complete
analysis configuration---data sources, mappings, predicates, stack
fields, and outputs---for deterministic replay.

This mechanism explains why \toolname handles both real agent sessions
(which need intent recognition) and public benchmarks (which need
mapping rules): both paths produce operations with fields, and the
stack query works identically on both.

%% ===================================================================
\section{Implementation}
\label{sec:impl}

\toolname is a Rust CLI. It reads Codex and Claude Code local JSONL
history files through the shared \texttt{agent-session} parser crate,
which recovers prompts, LLM calls, tool invocations, and their triggered
file and network effects. External datasets enter as operation JSONL.
Output formats include pprof protobuf (compatible with
\texttt{go tool pprof}), folded-stack text, standalone SVG flame graphs,
and JSON summaries. Profile specs support deterministic replay: the same
spec and input always produce the same output.

%% ===================================================================
\section{Evaluation}
\label{sec:eval}

We evaluate four questions: (1)~can the two-abstraction model represent
diverse agent traces? (2)~does semantic folding separate what flat
summaries mix? (3)~can profiler groups find hidden labeled problems?
(4)~do real flame graphs surface actionable insights?

\subsection{E1: Generality---Can Two Abstractions Cover Heterogeneous
Agent Traces?}

We import 15 public labeled trace families covering web navigation
(WebLINX, Mind2Web, AgentTrek, WebShop), tool and API interaction
(API-Bank, ToolBench, tau-bench), software engineering (SWE-agent),
mobile and GUI (AndroidControl, GUI-Odyssey, ScaleCUA), expert failure
labels (AgentRewardBench), safety labels (SATraj-OS), human-boundary
labels (OSWorld-Human), and desktop step quality (AgentNet).
Table~\ref{tab:datasets} summarizes the families.

\begin{table*}[t]
\centering\small
\caption{Public labeled trace families. The bottom four rows provide
oracle labels used for the E3 hidden-label benchmark.}
\label{tab:datasets}
\begin{tabular}{p{0.18\linewidth}p{0.28\linewidth}p{0.20\linewidth}p{0.24\linewidth}}
\toprule
Family & Native labels & Access & Evaluation role \\
\midrule
WebLINX, Mind2Web, AgentTrek, WebShop & Web actions, tasks, rewards & HF / public shards & Web coverage \\
API-Bank, ToolBench, tau-bench & API calls, tool messages, outcomes & HF / repo JSONL & Tool/API coverage \\
SWE-agent & Issue trajectories, commands & HF viewer & Software coverage \\
AndroidControl, GUI-Odyssey, ScaleCUA & Mobile/GUI actions, history & Public/HF samples & Mobile/GUI coverage \\
\midrule
AgentRewardBench & Success, side-effect, looping, optimality & HF annotations & Failure/looping tasks \\
SATraj-OS & Safety, reward, attack type & HF safety config & Safety task \\
OSWorld-Human & Human single/grouped-action traces & GitHub JSON & Human-boundary task \\
AgentNet & Step correctness, redundancy & HF repo JSONL & Step-quality tasks \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table*}

All 15 sources produce 47{,}590 operations through mapping rules. No
source requires a prompt-specific, GUI-specific, or safety-specific
profiler object. The same 13{,}265 operations (from the four oracle-rich
families) fold into 9 dataset stacks, 57 phase stacks, 226 semantic
stacks, 455 action stacks, or 3{,}757 fixed-session stacks by changing
only the stack fields. A fixed-session boundary increases stack count by
$417\times$ relative to dataset depth. On AgentNet, a profile-spec stack
override folds 16{,}741 operations from 608 stacks to 83 stacks without
changing any input operation.

These results support a narrow claim: the two abstractions are sufficient
to represent heterogeneous agent traces and to produce recursive folding
at multiple depths. They do not claim complete ecosystem compatibility or
automatic intent-boundary discovery.

\subsection{E2: Separation---Does Semantic Folding Add Value?}

The strongest argument against semantic profiling is that traditional
tools ``can already see the same information.'' We test this directly.

On real Codex and Claude sessions (325 readable sessions, 183{,}714
system observations including tool calls, process events, and
file/network effects), we fold observations into semantic system stacks
and measure how many observations land in \emph{mixed-intent} buckets
under different projections. A bucket is mixed if it contains observations
from more than one semantic region.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering\small
\caption{Semantic-axis ablation on 183{,}714 system observations.
All rows preserve the same total weight.}
\label{tab:mixing}
\begin{tabular}{lrrr}
\toprule
Projection & Unique stacks & Mixed weight & Residual mixed \\
\midrule
No semantic labels & 11{,}967 & 90.4\% & 44.7\% \\
Session label only & 15{,}027 & 84.4\% & 33.4\% \\
Prompt label only & 24{,}703 & 36.7\% & 7.5\% \\
Session + prompt & 26{,}829 & 0.0\% & 0.0\% \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:mixing} shows the result. Without semantic labels,
90.4\% of system-effect weight falls into mixed buckets: a flat
\texttt{cargo~test} counter shows 2{,}903 executions but cannot
distinguish whether they were triggered by a \texttt{review},
\texttt{debug}, \texttt{refactor}, or \texttt{test} prompt. Adding
only the prompt semantic label reduces mixed weight to 36.7\% and
residual mixed weight to 7.5\%. The session label alone barely helps
(84.4\% mixed), because many sessions contain multiple intent phases.

A concrete example: the process/effect stack
\texttt{process:cargo; effect:test; status:ok} appears under 48
distinct prompt tags. The top tag (\texttt{refactor}) accounts for only
32.0\% of the weight; the remaining 68.0\% comes from \texttt{review},
\texttt{research}, \texttt{test}, \texttt{explain}, and others. A flat
summary or a traditional process audit would merge all of these into
a single ``cargo test'' bar.

A label-permutation test confirms that the separation is not random.
Shuffling prompt tags 1{,}000 times within each session and recomputing
separation gives a null-distribution p95 information gain of 1.9\%; the
real tags achieve 8.4\% ($p = 0.001$). This supports a weighted
association between semantic labels and system behavior, not a claim of
human-verified semantic adequacy.

\subsection{E3: Localization---Can Profiler Groups Find Hidden Problems?}

How does one objectively evaluate a profiler without a user study? For
CPU profilers, one can inject known bottlenecks and check whether the
profiler finds them. For agent profilers, we adopt an analogous strategy:
public benchmark datasets provide ground-truth labels (failure, safety
violation, redundant step, human-task boundary). We \emph{hide} these
labels, run the profiler with different view configurations, rank the
resulting groups, and check whether the top-ranked groups contain the
hidden positives.

We build six tasks: AgentRewardBench looping and side-effect, SATraj-OS
unsafe operation, AgentNet incorrect and redundant step, and
OSWorld-Human group start. Together these cover 34{,}539 operations with
3{,}699 positives. We compare six views: flat summary, fixed-session
drilldown, dataset-native hierarchy, raw-action stacks, operation stacks,
and label-drilldown (hidden upper bound). Four rankers score groups:
width, visible-risk, query-aware, and oracle upper bound. Metrics include
precision@5, recall@5, F1@5, average precision (AP), nDCG,
work-to-first-positive (WTFP), and group count.

\begin{table*}[t]
\centering\small
\caption{E3 hidden-label localization results (medians across six tasks).
Hidden policies read oracle labels and serve only as upper bounds.}
\label{tab:localization}
\begin{tabular}{lrrrrrrrr}
\toprule
Policy & Hidden & AP & R@5 & F1@5 & Work@5 & R@30\% & WTFP & Groups \\
\midrule
flat:width & 0 & 0.168 & 1.000 & 0.287 & 1.000 & 0.000 & 1.000 & 1.0 \\
fixed-session:query-aware & 0 & 0.348 & 0.023 & 0.043 & 0.016 & 0.356 & 0.004 & 285.0 \\
dataset-native:query-aware & 0 & 0.357 & 0.867 & 0.282 & 0.854 & 0.338 & 0.058 & --- \\
raw-action:query-aware & 0 & 0.274 & 0.244 & 0.220 & 0.151 & 0.333 & 0.037 & --- \\
op-stack:query-aware & 0 & 0.312 & 0.188 & 0.198 & 0.094 & 0.390 & 0.038 & 157.5 \\
op-stack:oracle-upper & 1 & 0.599 & 0.300 & 0.403 & 0.044 & 0.564 & 0.012 & --- \\
label-drilldown:oracle & 1 & 1.000 & 0.670 & 0.797 & 0.115 & 1.000 & 0.038 & --- \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table*}

Table~\ref{tab:localization} summarizes the results.
Flat summaries recover all positives but only by inspecting
everything (Work@5\,=\,1.0).
Fixed-session drilldown finds a first positive quickly
(WTFP\,=\,0.004) but fragments the workload into 285 groups and
achieves only 2.3\% top-five recall.
Operation-stack query-aware profiling inspects 9.4\% of the work in
the top five groups, achieves 39.0\% budget-30 recall, and reduces
groups to 157.5.

The result is a Pareto tradeoff, not dominance. Operation stacks improve
top-five recall over fixed-session drilldown on 5 of 6 tasks, reduce
median group count by 45\%, and save 90\% of inspection work versus flat
summaries. But fixed-session drilldown retains lower
work-to-first-positive on 4 of 6 tasks. The profiler and the
debugger are complementary, not competing.

Bootstrap (10{,}000 resamples) and label-permutation (2{,}000 trials)
audits confirm that AP deltas are stable and that AP exceeds the 95\%
prevalence/group-size null on all six tasks.

\subsection{E4: Qualitative Analysis---Aggregate Insights from Flame Graphs}

E1--E3 evaluate mechanism and label-scored fidelity. This subsection
examines whether semantic flame graphs reveal aggregate patterns that
per-event timeline views structurally cannot surface. We profile a
real multi-month development project (the AgentSight repository) with
325 Codex and Claude sessions, and report four representative
observations.

\paragraph{Observation 1: Budget distribution across intent categories.}
The \texttt{tokens} view (Figure~\ref{fig:flamegraphs}, top) reveals that
\texttt{review}-tagged prompts consume the largest share of the model
budget, followed by \texttt{git}, \texttt{code}, \texttt{edit}, and
\texttt{debug}. A timeline of 80{,}000 individual LLM calls cannot
produce this distribution without external aggregation; the flame graph
produces it directly. The stack structure further decomposes each
category: under \texttt{prompt:review}, the dominant sub-frames are
\texttt{call:llm/code} and \texttt{call:llm/tool}, indicating that
review prompts trigger both code-generation and tool-use responses.

\paragraph{Observation 2: Cross-session duplication.}
The \texttt{files} view shows that \texttt{debug}-tagged prompts
across different sessions repeatedly access the same source files under
\texttt{collector/src/}. The flame graph aggregates these accesses
into a single wide bar whose width reflects total cross-session
frequency. A timeline displays each file read as an individual event in
its session; only the folded view makes the repetition pattern visible.

\paragraph{Observation 3: Metric divergence across views.}
The \texttt{time} and \texttt{tokens} views of the same sessions share
only 7 of the top 10 prompt categories. \texttt{network}-tagged prompts
rank 8th by wall-clock time (due to I/O wait) but 93rd by token count;
\texttt{benchmark}-tagged prompts show the opposite pattern. This
divergence motivates the multi-view design: a single cost metric cannot
represent the full resource picture.

\paragraph{Observation 4: External-contact and path auditing.}
The \texttt{network} view attributes external domain contacts to prompt
categories: \texttt{anthropic.com} (model inference),
\texttt{crates.io} (dependency resolution), \texttt{github.com} (version
control). The \texttt{files} view identifies accesses outside the project
root, bucketed as \texttt{external/home}, \texttt{external/tmp}, and
\texttt{external/codex}. These cross-session access patterns are
invisible in per-span timelines but appear as distinct flame-graph
branches, supporting security and compliance auditing use cases.

% Placeholder for actual flame-graph figure
\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
% \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/flamegraph-tokens.png}
\fbox{\parbox{0.93\linewidth}{\centering\small
[Flame-graph screenshots: tokens view (top) and files view (bottom)
showing budget distribution and file-access patterns across sessions]}}
\caption{Real flame graphs from a development project. Top:
\texttt{tokens} view showing budget distribution by prompt category.
Bottom: \texttt{files} view showing which prompt categories touch
which repository regions. Width represents token count and file-operation
count, respectively.}
\Description{Two flame graphs showing token budget and file access
distribution across semantic prompt categories.}
\label{fig:flamegraphs}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Reproducibility and Cost}

All evaluation results are backed by profile specs that support
deterministic replay. We re-execute all 76 tracked specs twice (152
invocations); all 76 produce identical semantic output. Median runtime is
1.6\,s per spec (p95: 2.8\,s). Deterministic-output mode
(\texttt{--deterministic-output}) additionally stabilizes raw-byte output
by replacing timestamps with fixed values: 76/76 specs achieve both
semantic and raw-byte determinism.

%% ===================================================================
\section{Related Work}

\textbf{Profiling and flame graphs.}
Flame graphs and pprof establish the folded-stack lineage: profiles are
weighted samples attached to location hierarchies, with optional sample
labels that pprof can visualize as pseudo stack frames~\cite{flamegraphs,
pprof}. Perfetto generalizes trace ingestion and SQL-based analysis over
many formats and can derive new events from trace
contents~\cite{perfetto}. These systems are closer than a simple
``fixed hierarchy'' baseline. \toolname therefore does not claim novelty
for query-time aggregation alone. The difference is the domain:
\toolname's samples are agent operations, its frames are semantic labels
derived from natural-language prompts, and its evaluation uses hidden
agent-trajectory labels across heterogeneous datasets.

\textbf{Agent tracing and LLM observability.}
OpenTelemetry GenAI and OpenInference standardize GenAI spans~\cite{otel,
openinference}. LangSmith, Langfuse, and Phoenix provide trace
visualization, evaluations, and dashboards~\cite{langsmith, langfuse,
phoenix}. AgentOps argues for structured agent
observability~\cite{agentops}. These systems excel at single-execution
debugging. \toolname complements them by providing aggregate profiling:
the same trace data can be imported as operations and folded across
sessions. Fixed-session drilldown is our evaluated baseline; real
OpenTelemetry span-tree imports remain future interoperability work.

\textbf{Agent failure diagnosis.}
AgentRx releases annotated failure trajectories and uses constraint
checking plus an LLM judge for root-cause
localization~\cite{agentrx}. TELBench builds span-localization benchmarks
from semantic error annotations~\cite{telbench}. These systems perform
span-level fault localization within a single execution. \toolname
performs cross-session aggregate profiling: which \emph{categories} of
work produce the most failures, consume the most budget, or generate the
most repeated system effects.

%% ===================================================================
\section{Discussion}

\textbf{Label quality.}
Semantic labels are lossy navigation frames, not ground-truth intent
classifications. The regex tagger requires manual iteration; the LLM
tagger produces noisy long-tail labels. A label-permutation test shows
that real labels carry significantly more information than random
assignments ($p = 0.001$), but human adequacy evaluation remains future
work.

\textbf{Scope.}
The evaluation shows label-scored profiler fidelity, not human
productivity gains. A user study measuring whether developers answer
questions faster with flame graphs than with timelines would strengthen
the practical claim but is not required for the profiler-mechanism
contribution.

\textbf{Profiler vs.\ debugger.}
Fixed-session drilldown finds a first positive faster on most tasks.
Profilers and debuggers are complementary: the profiler identifies
\emph{which categories} deserve attention; the debugger explains
\emph{what happened} in a specific case. \toolname supports both by
including or excluding session fields in the stack query.

\textbf{Trace compatibility.}
\toolname currently reads Codex/Claude local histories and operation
JSONL. OpenTelemetry, LangSmith, and Langfuse trace imports are
engineering work, not design obstacles: each format maps to operations
with fields. The fixed-session baseline in E3 is our evaluated
trace-tree proxy; real span-tree imports are future work.

%% ===================================================================
\section{Conclusion}

\toolname reduces agent profiling to two abstractions. Operations carry
semantic and mechanism fields; operation stacks fold those fields at a
depth chosen by the query. Intent recognition---through regex rules, a
local LLM, or clustering---restores the deterministic-label precondition
that makes flame-graph aggregation work for natural-language agent traces.

On real sessions, semantic labels separate 90\% of system-effect weight
that flat summaries merge. On public benchmarks, operation-stack profiling
locates labeled problems with 90\% less inspection work than flat
summaries and 45\% less fragmentation than fixed-session drilldown. Case
studies show budget distribution, repeated work, and security-audit
insights that no timeline view can surface. The profiler complements
existing debuggers: it answers ``where did the budget go?''---the
aggregate question that 80{,}000 spans on a timeline cannot.

1	\documentclass[sigconf]{acmart}
2	
3	\setcopyright{none}
4	\settopmatter{printacmref=false}
5	\renewcommand\footnotetextcopyrightpermission[1]{}
6	\pagestyle{plain}
7	
8	\usepackage{booktabs}
9	\usepackage{array}
10	\usepackage{xspace}
11	\usepackage{url}
12	\usepackage{graphicx}
13	
14	\newcommand{\toolname}{\textsc{AgentPProf}\xspace}
15	\newcommand{\operation}{\texttt{operation}\xspace}
16	\newcommand{\opstack}{\texttt{operation stack}\xspace}
17	
18	\begin{document}
19	
20	\title{AgentPProf: Semantic Profiling for AI Agent Traces}
21	
22	\begin{abstract}
23	AI agent observability tools can show every span, every LLM call, and every
24	tool invocation---but they cannot answer aggregate questions: which categories
25	of work consumed the most tokens, where did the budget go, and which task
26	families produce repeated failures? These tools are debuggers; agents also
27	need a profiler.
28	
29	CPU profilers solved the equivalent problem for programs: flame graphs fold
30	millions of function calls into a single chart where width equals cost.
31	The key enabler is that function names are deterministic---identical code
32	paths produce identical stack frames that merge on contact.
33	Agent traces break this assumption. Prompts are natural language:
34	nondeterministic, variable-length, multilingual. Two prompts expressing the
35	same intent produce different strings and cannot be folded.
36	
37	\toolname restores the aggregation ability that natural-language prompts
38	break. It maps free-form prompts to stable semantic labels
39	(\texttt{debug}, \texttt{review}, \texttt{test}), then folds agent traces
40	into flame graphs where width represents token count, wall-clock time, or
41	operation count. The profiler retains only two core abstractions:
42	an \emph{operation} (a weighted record carrying semantic and
43	mechanism fields) and an \emph{operation stack} (an ordered field
44	projection chosen at query time). Sessions, spans, and trace identifiers
45	are operation fields, not separate profiler objects; changing the stack
46	changes the aggregation without changing the underlying data.
47	
48	We evaluate \toolname on 15 public labeled trace families (47{,}590
49	operations) and on hundreds of real Codex/Claude sessions (183{,}714
50	system observations). On real sessions, removing semantic labels leaves
51	90.4\% of system-effect weight in mixed-intent buckets; adding prompt
52	labels reduces this to 36.7\%. On four oracle-rich public datasets (6
53	tasks, 34{,}539 operations, 3{,}699 positives), operation-stack profiling
54	inspects 9.4\% of the work to cover the top five groups versus 100\% for
55	flat summaries, and reduces median group fragmentation from 285 to 158
56	compared to fixed-session drilldown. Case studies on real flame graphs
57	show actionable budget, duplication, and security-audit insights that
58	timeline views cannot surface.
59	\end{abstract}
60	
61	\maketitle
62	
63	%% ===================================================================
64	\section{Introduction}
65	
66	AI agent systems produce execution traces that interleave prompts, LLM
67	calls, tool invocations, GUI actions, process events, and benchmark
68	labels. As agent deployments scale to hundreds of sessions and tens of
69	thousands of calls, developers need to answer aggregate questions: which
70	categories of work consume the most tokens, where do repeated failures
71	concentrate, and how does cost distribute across semantic task families?
72	Existing observability tools---LangSmith~\cite{langsmith},
73	Langfuse~\cite{langfuse}, Phoenix~\cite{phoenix}, OpenTelemetry
74	GenAI~\cite{otel}---organize events into per-execution timelines and
75	span trees, enabling developers to debug individual runs. But no existing
76	tool provides an aggregate view that folds heterogeneous events across
77	sessions into a cost or frequency distribution grouped by semantic work
78	category.
79	
80	This gap has a precise analogy in traditional software.
81	Before CPU profilers, developers diagnosed performance by reading logs
82	and instrumenting individual functions. Flame
83	graphs~\cite{flamegraphs} and profiling tools like pprof~\cite{pprof}
84	changed the practice: they compress millions of function-call samples
85	into a single chart where width represents cost, and identical call
86	stacks merge automatically. The key enabler is that function names are
87	\emph{deterministic}---the same code path always produces the same stack
88	frames. Agent traces break this assumption. Prompts are natural language:
89	nondeterministic, variable-length, and multilingual.
90	``Fix the bug'' and ``修一下这个 error'' express the same intent but
91	share no characters. If prompt text is used directly as a flame-graph
92	frame label, every prompt becomes a unique bar and no aggregation occurs.
93	The same problem affects tool calls, GUI actions, and process events,
94	which are named heterogeneously across agent families and trace formats.
95	
96	This paper presents \toolname, a profiler that restores aggregate
97	flame-graph analysis for agent traces. The core mechanism is
98	\emph{intent recognition}: mapping free-form prompts and heterogeneous
99	actions to stable semantic labels through pluggable backends (regex rules,
100	local LLM tagging, or unsupervised clustering). Once labeled, agent
101	events fold into flame graphs using the same folded-stack aggregation
102	that CPU profilers use. The profiler is built on two abstractions:
103	an \emph{operation} (a weighted record representing any measurable agent
104	activity) and an \emph{operation stack} (an ordered field projection
105	chosen at query time). Sessions, spans, and trace identifiers are
106	operation fields, not separate profiler objects; changing the stack
107	projection changes the aggregation shape without changing the underlying
108	data.
109	
110	This paper makes three contributions:
111	
112	\begin{enumerate}
113	\item \textbf{Problem: the aggregation gap.}
114	  We identify a structural gap in agent observability: existing tools
115	  provide per-execution trace debugging but not cross-session aggregate
116	  profiling. The key obstacle is that natural-language prompts lack the
117	  deterministic identifiers that enable flame-graph folding
118	  (\S\ref{sec:design}).
119	\item \textbf{Design: semantic agent profiling.}
120	  We design a profiler around two abstractions---operations and operation
121	  stacks---with pluggable intent recognition that restores flame-graph
122	  aggregation for agent traces. Four built-in views answer distinct
123	  aggregate questions about token budget, time, file access, and network
124	  activity (\S\ref{sec:design}--\S\ref{sec:impl}).
125	\item \textbf{Evaluation.}
126	  On real agent sessions, semantic labels separate 90\% of the
127	  system-effect weight that unsemantic summaries merge. On public labeled
128	  benchmarks, operation-stack profiling reduces inspection work by 90\%
129	  versus flat summaries and fragmentation by 45\% versus fixed-session
130	  drilldown. Case studies demonstrate budget, duplication, and
131	  security-audit insights invisible to timeline views
132	  (\S\ref{sec:eval}).
133	\end{enumerate}
134	
135	%% ===================================================================
136	\section{Design}
137	\label{sec:design}
138	
139	\subsection{Operations and Operation Stacks}
140	
141	A CPU flame graph has two objects: a \emph{sample} (a weighted snapshot of
142	the call stack) and a \emph{stack} (the sequence of function frames).
143	\toolname adapts these to agent traces.
144	
145	An \operation is a weighted record representing one measurable activity in
146	an agent's history: a user prompt, an LLM call, a tool invocation, a file
147	read, or a network request. Each operation carries string fields
148	(\texttt{project}, \texttt{agent}, \texttt{session}, \texttt{prompt\_tag},
149	\texttt{kind}, \texttt{model}, \texttt{path}, \texttt{domain},
150	\texttt{status}, \ldots) and additive measures (token count, duration,
151	occurrence count). Different agent families and trace formats produce
152	different fields, but every entry is an operation record.
153	
154	An \opstack is an ordered list of fields chosen at query time. Folding
155	operations by that list produces the standard folded-stack representation:
156	
157	\begin{small}
158	\begin{verbatim}
159	CPU:   main;parse;tokenize          42
160	Agent: prompt:debug;call:llm;tool:bash  4200
161	\end{verbatim}
162	\end{small}
163	
164	\noindent The critical difference from CPU profiling is that the stack is
165	not determined by execution---it is chosen by the analyst. The same
166	operations can be folded as a flat task summary, a fixed-session tree, a
167	semantic phase/action hierarchy, or a dataset-native trajectory. Changing
168	the fields changes the aggregation shape without changing the underlying
169	operations.
170	
171	A \emph{view} is a triple $(\varphi, \sigma, w)$: a predicate $\varphi$
172	selects which operations participate, a stack function $\sigma$ maps each
173	operation to a frame sequence, and a weight function $w$ assigns a
174	nonnegative measure. Evaluation produces folded stacks grouped by
175	$\sigma$ with weights summed by $w$. Four built-in views answer four
176	different questions:
177	
178	\begin{table}[t]
179	\centering\small
180	\caption{Built-in views. Each shares the same operation set
181	but selects different activities, stack structures, and weights.}
182	\label{tab:views}
183	\begin{tabular}{llll}
184	\toprule
185	View & $\varphi$ (select) & $w$ (width) & Question \\
186	\midrule
187	\texttt{tokens} & LLM calls & token count & Budget distribution? \\
188	\texttt{time} & All timed ops & duration (s) & Time distribution? \\
189	\texttt{files} & File-effect ops & event count & Repo coverage? \\
190	\texttt{network} & Net-effect ops & event count & External contacts? \\
191	\bottomrule
192	\end{tabular}
193	\end{table}
194	
195	Sessions and spans deserve explicit discussion. In existing observability
196	tools, sessions and spans define the fixed hierarchy. In \toolname, they
197	are optional operation fields. An analyst can include \texttt{session} in
198	the stack (producing a per-session drilldown equivalent to a trace tree),
199	or exclude it (producing a cross-session aggregate that no trace tool
200	provides). This is the design's central point: the same data supports
201	both debugging and profiling views, selected at query time.
202	
203	\subsection{Intent Recognition: From Prompts to Labels}
204	
205	Operations and stacks are conventional engineering; the hard problem is
206	\emph{intent recognition}. A flame graph requires short, stable,
207	repeatable frame labels. Function names provide this for CPU profiles.
208	Agent prompts do not: they are free-form, multilingual, variable-length,
209	and often contain sensitive content.
210	
211	\toolname provides a pluggable tagger framework with three backends:
212	
213	\paragraph{Regex rules with agent-assisted iteration.}
214	The production default. Rules have the form
215	\texttt{KIND:TAG=REGEX}, where \texttt{KIND} is \texttt{prompt},
216	\texttt{llm}, or \texttt{all}, \texttt{TAG} is a short lowercase label,
217	and \texttt{REGEX} is a pattern. Rules are evaluated in order; the first
218	match wins. The workflow is human--agent collaborative: run \toolname,
219	observe the unmatched rate and sample prompts, add rules, re-run, and
220	iterate until unmatched drops below 5\% with a reasonable distribution
221	(10--20 categories, no single category exceeding 50\%). This typically
222	takes 5--10 rounds of 1--2 minutes each. The resulting rule set is
223	deterministic, reproducible, and version-controllable.
224	
225	\paragraph{Local LLM tagger.}
226	For exploration or complex multilingual prompts, a local model
227	(e.g., a 3B-parameter GGUF via llama.cpp) generates a single-word label
228	per prompt. Grammar-constrained decoding ensures output validity.
229	Labels are cached; re-runs with unchanged prompts incur zero LLM calls.
230	The LLM tagger's output serves as a starting point for writing regex
231	rules.
232	
233	\paragraph{Unsupervised clustering.}
234	TF-IDF vectorization followed by K-Means discovers natural prompt groups
235	without predefined rules. This backend identifies ``what categories exist
236	in my prompt distribution'' and feeds rule authoring.
237	
238	The one-word label design is deliberate. Flame-graph frames must be
239	short; long summaries make charts unreadable. Labels serve navigation
240	and aggregation, not correctness verdicts. A label like \texttt{debug}
241	does not certify that the prompt is a debugging task; it groups prompts
242	that share debugging-related tokens so that their downstream
243	activities fold together.
244	
245	\subsection{Mapping for Structured Traces}
246	
247	For public benchmark datasets and structured trace formats, prompts are
248	already structured: action types, tool names, environment labels, and
249	quality annotations are explicit fields. \toolname supports deterministic
250	\emph{mapping rules} that derive new operation fields from existing ones
251	before stack construction. For example, desktop actions \texttt{type} and
252	\texttt{key} can map to \texttt{phase=input}, while API tool rows can map
253	to a tool-phase field. A \emph{profile spec} records the complete
254	analysis configuration---data sources, mappings, predicates, stack
255	fields, and outputs---for deterministic replay.
256	
257	This mechanism explains why \toolname handles both real agent sessions
258	(which need intent recognition) and public benchmarks (which need
259	mapping rules): both paths produce operations with fields, and the
260	stack query works identically on both.
261	
262	%% ===================================================================
263	\section{Implementation}
264	\label{sec:impl}
265	
266	\toolname is a Rust CLI. It reads Codex and Claude Code local JSONL
267	history files through the shared \texttt{agent-session} parser crate,
268	which recovers prompts, LLM calls, tool invocations, and their triggered
269	file and network effects. External datasets enter as operation JSONL.
270	Output formats include pprof protobuf (compatible with
271	\texttt{go tool pprof}), folded-stack text, standalone SVG flame graphs,
272	and JSON summaries. Profile specs support deterministic replay: the same
273	spec and input always produce the same output.
274	
275	%% ===================================================================
276	\section{Evaluation}
277	\label{sec:eval}
278	
279	We evaluate four questions: (1)~can the two-abstraction model represent
280	diverse agent traces? (2)~does semantic folding separate what flat
281	summaries mix? (3)~can profiler groups find hidden labeled problems?
282	(4)~do real flame graphs surface actionable insights?
283	
284	\subsection{E1: Generality---Can Two Abstractions Cover Heterogeneous
285	Agent Traces?}
286	
287	We import 15 public labeled trace families covering web navigation
288	(WebLINX, Mind2Web, AgentTrek, WebShop), tool and API interaction
289	(API-Bank, ToolBench, tau-bench), software engineering (SWE-agent),
290	mobile and GUI (AndroidControl, GUI-Odyssey, ScaleCUA), expert failure
291	labels (AgentRewardBench), safety labels (SATraj-OS), human-boundary
292	labels (OSWorld-Human), and desktop step quality (AgentNet).
293	Table~\ref{tab:datasets} summarizes the families.
294	
295	\begin{table*}[t]
296	\centering\small
297	\caption{Public labeled trace families. The bottom four rows provide
298	oracle labels used for the E3 hidden-label benchmark.}
299	\label{tab:datasets}
300	\begin{tabular}{p{0.18\linewidth}p{0.28\linewidth}p{0.20\linewidth}p{0.24\linewidth}}
301	\toprule
302	Family & Native labels & Access & Evaluation role \\
303	\midrule
304	WebLINX, Mind2Web, AgentTrek, WebShop & Web actions, tasks, rewards & HF / public shards & Web coverage \\
305	API-Bank, ToolBench, tau-bench & API calls, tool messages, outcomes & HF / repo JSONL & Tool/API coverage \\
306	SWE-agent & Issue trajectories, commands & HF viewer & Software coverage \\
307	AndroidControl, GUI-Odyssey, ScaleCUA & Mobile/GUI actions, history & Public/HF samples & Mobile/GUI coverage \\
308	\midrule
309	AgentRewardBench & Success, side-effect, looping, optimality & HF annotations & Failure/looping tasks \\
310	SATraj-OS & Safety, reward, attack type & HF safety config & Safety task \\
311	OSWorld-Human & Human single/grouped-action traces & GitHub JSON & Human-boundary task \\
312	AgentNet & Step correctness, redundancy & HF repo JSONL & Step-quality tasks \\
313	\bottomrule
314	\end{tabular}
315	\end{table*}
316	
317	All 15 sources produce 47{,}590 operations through mapping rules. No
318	source requires a prompt-specific, GUI-specific, or safety-specific
319	profiler object. The same 13{,}265 operations (from the four oracle-rich
320	families) fold into 9 dataset stacks, 57 phase stacks, 226 semantic
321	stacks, 455 action stacks, or 3{,}757 fixed-session stacks by changing
322	only the stack fields. A fixed-session boundary increases stack count by
323	$417\times$ relative to dataset depth. On AgentNet, a profile-spec stack
324	override folds 16{,}741 operations from 608 stacks to 83 stacks without
325	changing any input operation.
326	
327	These results support a narrow claim: the two abstractions are sufficient
328	to represent heterogeneous agent traces and to produce recursive folding
329	at multiple depths. They do not claim complete ecosystem compatibility or
330	automatic intent-boundary discovery.
331	
332	\subsection{E2: Separation---Does Semantic Folding Add Value?}
333	
334	The strongest argument against semantic profiling is that traditional
335	tools ``can already see the same information.'' We test this directly.
336	
337	On real Codex and Claude sessions (325 readable sessions, 183{,}714
338	system observations including tool calls, process events, and
339	file/network effects), we fold observations into semantic system stacks
340	and measure how many observations land in \emph{mixed-intent} buckets
341	under different projections. A bucket is mixed if it contains observations
342	from more than one semantic region.
343	
344	\begin{table}[t]
345	\centering\small
346	\caption{Semantic-axis ablation on 183{,}714 system observations.
347	All rows preserve the same total weight.}
348	\label{tab:mixing}
349	\begin{tabular}{lrrr}
350	\toprule
351	Projection & Unique stacks & Mixed weight & Residual mixed \\
352	\midrule
353	No semantic labels & 11{,}967 & 90.4\% & 44.7\% \\
354	Session label only & 15{,}027 & 84.4\% & 33.4\% \\
355	Prompt label only & 24{,}703 & 36.7\% & 7.5\% \\
356	Session + prompt & 26{,}829 & 0.0\% & 0.0\% \\
357	\bottomrule
358	\end{tabular}
359	\end{table}
360	
361	Table~\ref{tab:mixing} shows the result. Without semantic labels,
362	90.4\% of system-effect weight falls into mixed buckets: a flat
363	\texttt{cargo~test} counter shows 2{,}903 executions but cannot
364	distinguish whether they were triggered by a \texttt{review},
365	\texttt{debug}, \texttt{refactor}, or \texttt{test} prompt. Adding
366	only the prompt semantic label reduces mixed weight to 36.7\% and
367	residual mixed weight to 7.5\%. The session label alone barely helps
368	(84.4\% mixed), because many sessions contain multiple intent phases.
369	
370	A concrete example: the process/effect stack
371	\texttt{process:cargo; effect:test; status:ok} appears under 48
372	distinct prompt tags. The top tag (\texttt{refactor}) accounts for only
373	32.0\% of the weight; the remaining 68.0\% comes from \texttt{review},
374	\texttt{research}, \texttt{test}, \texttt{explain}, and others. A flat
375	summary or a traditional process audit would merge all of these into
376	a single ``cargo test'' bar.
377	
378	A label-permutation test confirms that the separation is not random.
379	Shuffling prompt tags 1{,}000 times within each session and recomputing
380	separation gives a null-distribution p95 information gain of 1.9\%; the
381	real tags achieve 8.4\% ($p = 0.001$). This supports a weighted
382	association between semantic labels and system behavior, not a claim of
383	human-verified semantic adequacy.
384	
385	\subsection{E3: Localization---Can Profiler Groups Find Hidden Problems?}
386	
387	How does one objectively evaluate a profiler without a user study? For
388	CPU profilers, one can inject known bottlenecks and check whether the
389	profiler finds them. For agent profilers, we adopt an analogous strategy:
390	public benchmark datasets provide ground-truth labels (failure, safety
391	violation, redundant step, human-task boundary). We \emph{hide} these
392	labels, run the profiler with different view configurations, rank the
393	resulting groups, and check whether the top-ranked groups contain the
394	hidden positives.
395	
396	We build six tasks: AgentRewardBench looping and side-effect, SATraj-OS
397	unsafe operation, AgentNet incorrect and redundant step, and
398	OSWorld-Human group start. Together these cover 34{,}539 operations with
399	3{,}699 positives. We compare six views: flat summary, fixed-session
400	drilldown, dataset-native hierarchy, raw-action stacks, operation stacks,
401	and label-drilldown (hidden upper bound). Four rankers score groups:
402	width, visible-risk, query-aware, and oracle upper bound. Metrics include
403	precision@5, recall@5, F1@5, average precision (AP), nDCG,
404	work-to-first-positive (WTFP), and group count.
405	
406	\begin{table*}[t]
407	\centering\small
408	\caption{E3 hidden-label localization results (medians across six tasks).
409	Hidden policies read oracle labels and serve only as upper bounds.}
410	\label{tab:localization}
411	\begin{tabular}{lrrrrrrrr}
412	\toprule
413	Policy & Hidden & AP & R@5 & F1@5 & Work@5 & R@30\% & WTFP & Groups \\
414	\midrule
415	flat:width & 0 & 0.168 & 1.000 & 0.287 & 1.000 & 0.000 & 1.000 & 1.0 \\
416	fixed-session:query-aware & 0 & 0.348 & 0.023 & 0.043 & 0.016 & 0.356 & 0.004 & 285.0 \\
417	dataset-native:query-aware & 0 & 0.357 & 0.867 & 0.282 & 0.854 & 0.338 & 0.058 & --- \\
418	raw-action:query-aware & 0 & 0.274 & 0.244 & 0.220 & 0.151 & 0.333 & 0.037 & --- \\
419	op-stack:query-aware & 0 & 0.312 & 0.188 & 0.198 & 0.094 & 0.390 & 0.038 & 157.5 \\
420	op-stack:oracle-upper & 1 & 0.599 & 0.300 & 0.403 & 0.044 & 0.564 & 0.012 & --- \\
421	label-drilldown:oracle & 1 & 1.000 & 0.670 & 0.797 & 0.115 & 1.000 & 0.038 & --- \\
422	\bottomrule
423	\end{tabular}
424	\end{table*}
425	
426	Table~\ref{tab:localization} summarizes the results.
427	Flat summaries recover all positives but only by inspecting
428	everything (Work@5\,=\,1.0).
429	Fixed-session drilldown finds a first positive quickly
430	(WTFP\,=\,0.004) but fragments the workload into 285 groups and
431	achieves only 2.3\% top-five recall.
432	Operation-stack query-aware profiling inspects 9.4\% of the work in
433	the top five groups, achieves 39.0\% budget-30 recall, and reduces
434	groups to 157.5.
435	
436	The result is a Pareto tradeoff, not dominance. Operation stacks improve
437	top-five recall over fixed-session drilldown on 5 of 6 tasks, reduce
438	median group count by 45\%, and save 90\% of inspection work versus flat
439	summaries. But fixed-session drilldown retains lower
440	work-to-first-positive on 4 of 6 tasks. The profiler and the
441	debugger are complementary, not competing.
442	
443	Bootstrap (10{,}000 resamples) and label-permutation (2{,}000 trials)
444	audits confirm that AP deltas are stable and that AP exceeds the 95\%
445	prevalence/group-size null on all six tasks.
446	
447	\subsection{E4: Qualitative Analysis---Aggregate Insights from Flame Graphs}
448	
449	E1--E3 evaluate mechanism and label-scored fidelity. This subsection
450	examines whether semantic flame graphs reveal aggregate patterns that
451	per-event timeline views structurally cannot surface. We profile a
452	real multi-month development project (the AgentSight repository) with
453	325 Codex and Claude sessions, and report four representative
454	observations.
455	
456	\paragraph{Observation 1: Budget distribution across intent categories.}
457	The \texttt{tokens} view (Figure~\ref{fig:flamegraphs}, top) reveals that
458	\texttt{review}-tagged prompts consume the largest share of the model
459	budget, followed by \texttt{git}, \texttt{code}, \texttt{edit}, and
460	\texttt{debug}. A timeline of 80{,}000 individual LLM calls cannot
461	produce this distribution without external aggregation; the flame graph
462	produces it directly. The stack structure further decomposes each
463	category: under \texttt{prompt:review}, the dominant sub-frames are
464	\texttt{call:llm/code} and \texttt{call:llm/tool}, indicating that
465	review prompts trigger both code-generation and tool-use responses.
466	
467	\paragraph{Observation 2: Cross-session duplication.}
468	The \texttt{files} view shows that \texttt{debug}-tagged prompts
469	across different sessions repeatedly access the same source files under
470	\texttt{collector/src/}. The flame graph aggregates these accesses
471	into a single wide bar whose width reflects total cross-session
472	frequency. A timeline displays each file read as an individual event in
473	its session; only the folded view makes the repetition pattern visible.
474	
475	\paragraph{Observation 3: Metric divergence across views.}
476	The \texttt{time} and \texttt{tokens} views of the same sessions share
477	only 7 of the top 10 prompt categories. \texttt{network}-tagged prompts
478	rank 8th by wall-clock time (due to I/O wait) but 93rd by token count;
479	\texttt{benchmark}-tagged prompts show the opposite pattern. This
480	divergence motivates the multi-view design: a single cost metric cannot
481	represent the full resource picture.
482	
483	\paragraph{Observation 4: External-contact and path auditing.}
484	The \texttt{network} view attributes external domain contacts to prompt
485	categories: \texttt{anthropic.com} (model inference),
486	\texttt{crates.io} (dependency resolution), \texttt{github.com} (version
487	control). The \texttt{files} view identifies accesses outside the project
488	root, bucketed as \texttt{external/home}, \texttt{external/tmp}, and
489	\texttt{external/codex}. These cross-session access patterns are
490	invisible in per-span timelines but appear as distinct flame-graph
491	branches, supporting security and compliance auditing use cases.
492	
493	% Placeholder for actual flame-graph figure
494	\begin{figure}[t]
495	\centering
496	% \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/flamegraph-tokens.png}
497	\fbox{\parbox{0.93\linewidth}{\centering\small
498	[Flame-graph screenshots: tokens view (top) and files view (bottom)
499	showing budget distribution and file-access patterns across sessions]}}
500	\caption{Real flame graphs from a development project. Top:
501	\texttt{tokens} view showing budget distribution by prompt category.
502	Bottom: \texttt{files} view showing which prompt categories touch
503	which repository regions. Width represents token count and file-operation
504	count, respectively.}
505	\Description{Two flame graphs showing token budget and file access
506	distribution across semantic prompt categories.}
507	\label{fig:flamegraphs}
508	\end{figure}
509	
510	\subsection{Reproducibility and Cost}
511	
512	All evaluation results are backed by profile specs that support
513	deterministic replay. We re-execute all 76 tracked specs twice (152
514	invocations); all 76 produce identical semantic output. Median runtime is
515	1.6\,s per spec (p95: 2.8\,s). Deterministic-output mode
516	(\texttt{--deterministic-output}) additionally stabilizes raw-byte output
517	by replacing timestamps with fixed values: 76/76 specs achieve both
518	semantic and raw-byte determinism.
519	
520	%% ===================================================================
521	\section{Related Work}
522	
523	\textbf{Profiling and flame graphs.}
524	Flame graphs and pprof establish the folded-stack lineage: profiles are
525	weighted samples attached to location hierarchies, with optional sample
526	labels that pprof can visualize as pseudo stack frames~\cite{flamegraphs,
527	pprof}. Perfetto generalizes trace ingestion and SQL-based analysis over
528	many formats and can derive new events from trace
529	contents~\cite{perfetto}. These systems are closer than a simple
530	``fixed hierarchy'' baseline. \toolname therefore does not claim novelty
531	for query-time aggregation alone. The difference is the domain:
532	\toolname's samples are agent operations, its frames are semantic labels
533	derived from natural-language prompts, and its evaluation uses hidden
534	agent-trajectory labels across heterogeneous datasets.
535	
536	\textbf{Agent tracing and LLM observability.}
537	OpenTelemetry GenAI and OpenInference standardize GenAI spans~\cite{otel,
538	openinference}. LangSmith, Langfuse, and Phoenix provide trace
539	visualization, evaluations, and dashboards~\cite{langsmith, langfuse,
540	phoenix}. AgentOps argues for structured agent
541	observability~\cite{agentops}. These systems excel at single-execution
542	debugging. \toolname complements them by providing aggregate profiling:
543	the same trace data can be imported as operations and folded across
544	sessions. Fixed-session drilldown is our evaluated baseline; real
545	OpenTelemetry span-tree imports remain future interoperability work.
546	
547	\textbf{Agent failure diagnosis.}
548	AgentRx releases annotated failure trajectories and uses constraint
549	checking plus an LLM judge for root-cause
550	localization~\cite{agentrx}. TELBench builds span-localization benchmarks
551	from semantic error annotations~\cite{telbench}. These systems perform
552	span-level fault localization within a single execution. \toolname
553	performs cross-session aggregate profiling: which \emph{categories} of
554	work produce the most failures, consume the most budget, or generate the
555	most repeated system effects.
556	
557	%% ===================================================================
558	\section{Discussion}
559	
560	\textbf{Label quality.}
561	Semantic labels are lossy navigation frames, not ground-truth intent
562	classifications. The regex tagger requires manual iteration; the LLM
563	tagger produces noisy long-tail labels. A label-permutation test shows
564	that real labels carry significantly more information than random
565	assignments ($p = 0.001$), but human adequacy evaluation remains future
566	work.
567	
568	\textbf{Scope.}
569	The evaluation shows label-scored profiler fidelity, not human
570	productivity gains. A user study measuring whether developers answer
571	questions faster with flame graphs than with timelines would strengthen
572	the practical claim but is not required for the profiler-mechanism
573	contribution.
574	
575	\textbf{Profiler vs.\ debugger.}
576	Fixed-session drilldown finds a first positive faster on most tasks.
577	Profilers and debuggers are complementary: the profiler identifies
578	\emph{which categories} deserve attention; the debugger explains
579	\emph{what happened} in a specific case. \toolname supports both by
580	including or excluding session fields in the stack query.
581	
582	\textbf{Trace compatibility.}
583	\toolname currently reads Codex/Claude local histories and operation
584	JSONL. OpenTelemetry, LangSmith, and Langfuse trace imports are
585	engineering work, not design obstacles: each format maps to operations
586	with fields. The fixed-session baseline in E3 is our evaluated
587	trace-tree proxy; real span-tree imports are future work.
588	
589	%% ===================================================================
590	\section{Conclusion}
591	
592	\toolname reduces agent profiling to two abstractions. Operations carry
593	semantic and mechanism fields; operation stacks fold those fields at a
594	depth chosen by the query. Intent recognition---through regex rules, a
595	local LLM, or clustering---restores the deterministic-label precondition
596	that makes flame-graph aggregation work for natural-language agent traces.
597	
598	On real sessions, semantic labels separate 90\% of system-effect weight
599	that flat summaries merge. On public benchmarks, operation-stack profiling
600	locates labeled problems with 90\% less inspection work than flat
601	summaries and 45\% less fragmentation than fixed-session drilldown. Case
602	studies show budget distribution, repeated work, and security-audit
603	insights that no timeline view can surface. The profiler complements
604	existing debuggers: it answers ``where did the budget go?''---the
605	aggregate question that 80{,}000 spans on a timeline cannot.
606

\documentclass[sigconf]{acmart}

\setcopyright{none}
\settopmatter{printacmref=false}
\renewcommand\footnotetextcopyrightpermission[1]{}
\pagestyle{plain}

\usepackage{booktabs}
\usepackage{array}
\usepackage{xspace}
\usepackage{url}
\usepackage{graphicx}

\newcommand{\toolname}{\textsc{AgentPProf}\xspace}
\newcommand{\operation}{\texttt{operation}\xspace}
\newcommand{\opstack}{\texttt{operation stack}\xspace}

\begin{document}

\title{AgentPProf: Semantic Profiling for AI Agent Traces}

\begin{abstract}
AI agent observability tools can show every span, every LLM call, and every
tool invocation---but they cannot answer aggregate questions: which categories
of work consumed the most tokens, where did the budget go, and which task
families produce repeated failures? These tools are debuggers; agents also
need a profiler.

CPU profilers solved the equivalent problem for programs: flame graphs fold
millions of function calls into a single chart where width equals cost.
The key enabler is that function names are deterministic---identical code
paths produce identical stack frames that merge on contact.
Agent traces break this assumption. Prompts are natural language:
nondeterministic, variable-length, multilingual. Two prompts expressing the
same intent produce different strings and cannot be folded.

\toolname restores the aggregation ability that natural-language prompts
break. It maps free-form prompts to stable semantic labels
(\texttt{debug}, \texttt{review}, \texttt{test}), then folds agent traces
into flame graphs where width represents token count, wall-clock time, or
operation count. The profiler retains only two core abstractions:
an \emph{operation} (a weighted record carrying semantic and
mechanism fields) and an \emph{operation stack} (an ordered field
projection chosen at query time). Sessions, spans, and trace identifiers
are operation fields, not separate profiler objects; changing the stack
changes the aggregation without changing the underlying data.

We evaluate \toolname on 15 public labeled trace families (47{,}590
operations) and on hundreds of real Codex/Claude sessions (183{,}714
system observations). On real sessions, removing semantic labels leaves
90.4\% of system-effect weight in mixed-intent buckets; adding prompt
labels reduces this to 36.7\%. On four oracle-rich public datasets (6
tasks, 34{,}539 operations, 3{,}699 positives), operation-stack profiling
inspects 9.4\% of the work to cover the top five groups versus 100\% for
flat summaries, and reduces median group fragmentation from 285 to 158
compared to fixed-session drilldown. Case studies on real flame graphs
show actionable budget, duplication, and security-audit insights that
timeline views cannot surface.
\end{abstract}

\maketitle

%% ===================================================================
\section{Introduction}

AI agent systems produce execution traces that interleave prompts, LLM
calls, tool invocations, GUI actions, process events, and benchmark
labels. As agent deployments scale to hundreds of sessions and tens of
thousands of calls, developers need to answer aggregate questions: which
categories of work consume the most tokens, where do repeated failures
concentrate, and how does cost distribute across semantic task families?
Existing observability tools---LangSmith~\cite{langsmith},
Langfuse~\cite{langfuse}, Phoenix~\cite{phoenix}, OpenTelemetry
GenAI~\cite{otel}---organize events into per-execution timelines and
span trees, enabling developers to debug individual runs. But no existing
tool provides an aggregate view that folds heterogeneous events across
sessions into a cost or frequency distribution grouped by semantic work
category.

This gap has a precise analogy in traditional software.
Before CPU profilers, developers diagnosed performance by reading logs
and instrumenting individual functions. Flame
graphs~\cite{flamegraphs} and profiling tools like pprof~\cite{pprof}
changed the practice: they compress millions of function-call samples
into a single chart where width represents cost, and identical call
stacks merge automatically. The key enabler is that function names are
\emph{deterministic}---the same code path always produces the same stack
frames. Agent traces break this assumption. Prompts are natural language:
nondeterministic, variable-length, and multilingual.
``Fix the bug'' and ``修一下这个 error'' express the same intent but
share no characters. If prompt text is used directly as a flame-graph
frame label, every prompt becomes a unique bar and no aggregation occurs.
The same problem affects tool calls, GUI actions, and process events,
which are named heterogeneously across agent families and trace formats.

This paper presents \toolname, a profiler that restores aggregate
flame-graph analysis for agent traces. The core mechanism is
\emph{intent recognition}: mapping free-form prompts and heterogeneous
actions to stable semantic labels through pluggable backends (regex rules,
local LLM tagging, or unsupervised clustering). Once labeled, agent
events fold into flame graphs using the same folded-stack aggregation
that CPU profilers use. The profiler is built on two abstractions:
an \emph{operation} (a weighted record representing any measurable agent
activity) and an \emph{operation stack} (an ordered field projection
chosen at query time). Sessions, spans, and trace identifiers are
operation fields, not separate profiler objects; changing the stack
projection changes the aggregation shape without changing the underlying
data.

This paper makes three contributions:

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Problem: the aggregation gap.}
  We identify a structural gap in agent observability: existing tools
  provide per-execution trace debugging but not cross-session aggregate
  profiling. The key obstacle is that natural-language prompts lack the
  deterministic identifiers that enable flame-graph folding
  (\S\ref{sec:design}).
\item \textbf{Design: semantic agent profiling.}
  We design a profiler around two abstractions---operations and operation
  stacks---with pluggable intent recognition that restores flame-graph
  aggregation for agent traces. Four built-in views answer distinct
  aggregate questions about token budget, time, file access, and network
  activity (\S\ref{sec:design}--\S\ref{sec:impl}).
\item \textbf{Evaluation.}
  On real agent sessions, semantic labels separate 90\% of the
  system-effect weight that unsemantic summaries merge. On public labeled
  benchmarks, operation-stack profiling reduces inspection work by 90\%
  versus flat summaries and fragmentation by 45\% versus fixed-session
  drilldown. Case studies demonstrate budget, duplication, and
  security-audit insights invisible to timeline views
  (\S\ref{sec:eval}).
\end{enumerate}

%% ===================================================================
\section{Design}
\label{sec:design}

\subsection{Operations and Operation Stacks}

A CPU flame graph has two objects: a \emph{sample} (a weighted snapshot of
the call stack) and a \emph{stack} (the sequence of function frames).
\toolname adapts these to agent traces.

An \operation is a weighted record representing one measurable activity in
an agent's history: a user prompt, an LLM call, a tool invocation, a file
read, or a network request. Each operation carries string fields
(\texttt{project}, \texttt{agent}, \texttt{session}, \texttt{prompt\_tag},
\texttt{kind}, \texttt{model}, \texttt{path}, \texttt{domain},
\texttt{status}, \ldots) and additive measures (token count, duration,
occurrence count). Different agent families and trace formats produce
different fields, but every entry is an operation record.

An \opstack is an ordered list of fields chosen at query time. Folding
operations by that list produces the standard folded-stack representation:

\begin{small}
\begin{verbatim}
CPU:   main;parse;tokenize          42
Agent: prompt:debug;call:llm;tool:bash  4200
\end{verbatim}
\end{small}

\noindent The critical difference from CPU profiling is that the stack is
not determined by execution---it is chosen by the analyst. The same
operations can be folded as a flat task summary, a fixed-session tree, a
semantic phase/action hierarchy, or a dataset-native trajectory. Changing
the fields changes the aggregation shape without changing the underlying
operations.

A \emph{view} is a triple $(\varphi, \sigma, w)$: a predicate $\varphi$
selects which operations participate, a stack function $\sigma$ maps each
operation to a frame sequence, and a weight function $w$ assigns a
nonnegative measure. Evaluation produces folded stacks grouped by
$\sigma$ with weights summed by $w$. Four built-in views answer four
different questions:

\begin{table}[t]
\centering\small
\caption{Built-in views. Each shares the same operation set
but selects different activities, stack structures, and weights.}
\label{tab:views}
\begin{tabular}{llll}
\toprule
View & $\varphi$ (select) & $w$ (width) & Question \\
\midrule
\texttt{tokens} & LLM calls & token count & Budget distribution? \\
\texttt{time} & All timed ops & duration (s) & Time distribution? \\
\texttt{files} & File-effect ops & event count & Repo coverage? \\
\texttt{network} & Net-effect ops & event count & External contacts? \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Sessions and spans deserve explicit discussion. In existing observability
tools, sessions and spans define the fixed hierarchy. In \toolname, they
are optional operation fields. An analyst can include \texttt{session} in
the stack (producing a per-session drilldown equivalent to a trace tree),
or exclude it (producing a cross-session aggregate that no trace tool
provides). This is the design's central point: the same data supports
both debugging and profiling views, selected at query time.

\subsection{Intent Recognition: From Prompts to Labels}

Operations and stacks are conventional engineering; the hard problem is
\emph{intent recognition}. A flame graph requires short, stable,
repeatable frame labels. Function names provide this for CPU profiles.
Agent prompts do not: they are free-form, multilingual, variable-length,
and often contain sensitive content.

\toolname provides a pluggable tagger framework with three backends:

\paragraph{Regex rules with agent-assisted iteration.}
The production default. Rules have the form
\texttt{KIND:TAG=REGEX}, where \texttt{KIND} is \texttt{prompt},
\texttt{llm}, or \texttt{all}, \texttt{TAG} is a short lowercase label,
and \texttt{REGEX} is a pattern. Rules are evaluated in order; the first
match wins. The workflow is human--agent collaborative: run \toolname,
observe the unmatched rate and sample prompts, add rules, re-run, and
iterate until unmatched drops below 5\% with a reasonable distribution
(10--20 categories, no single category exceeding 50\%). This typically
takes 5--10 rounds of 1--2 minutes each. The resulting rule set is
deterministic, reproducible, and version-controllable.

\paragraph{Local LLM tagger.}
For exploration or complex multilingual prompts, a local model
(e.g., a 3B-parameter GGUF via llama.cpp) generates a single-word label
per prompt. Grammar-constrained decoding ensures output validity.
Labels are cached; re-runs with unchanged prompts incur zero LLM calls.
The LLM tagger's output serves as a starting point for writing regex
rules.

\paragraph{Unsupervised clustering.}
TF-IDF vectorization followed by K-Means discovers natural prompt groups
without predefined rules. This backend identifies ``what categories exist
in my prompt distribution'' and feeds rule authoring.

The one-word label design is deliberate. Flame-graph frames must be
short; long summaries make charts unreadable. Labels serve navigation
and aggregation, not correctness verdicts. A label like \texttt{debug}
does not certify that the prompt is a debugging task; it groups prompts
that share debugging-related tokens so that their downstream
activities fold together.

\subsection{Mapping for Structured Traces}

For public benchmark datasets and structured trace formats, prompts are
already structured: action types, tool names, environment labels, and
quality annotations are explicit fields. \toolname supports deterministic
\emph{mapping rules} that derive new operation fields from existing ones
before stack construction. For example, desktop actions \texttt{type} and
\texttt{key} can map to \texttt{phase=input}, while API tool rows can map
to a tool-phase field. A \emph{profile spec} records the complete
analysis configuration---data sources, mappings, predicates, stack
fields, and outputs---for deterministic replay.

This mechanism explains why \toolname handles both real agent sessions
(which need intent recognition) and public benchmarks (which need
mapping rules): both paths produce operations with fields, and the
stack query works identically on both.

%% ===================================================================
\section{Implementation}
\label{sec:impl}

\toolname is a Rust CLI. It reads Codex and Claude Code local JSONL
history files through the shared \texttt{agent-session} parser crate,
which recovers prompts, LLM calls, tool invocations, and their triggered
file and network effects. External datasets enter as operation JSONL.
Output formats include pprof protobuf (compatible with
\texttt{go tool pprof}), folded-stack text, standalone SVG flame graphs,
and JSON summaries. Profile specs support deterministic replay: the same
spec and input always produce the same output.

%% ===================================================================
\section{Evaluation}
\label{sec:eval}

We evaluate four questions: (1)~can the two-abstraction model represent
diverse agent traces? (2)~does semantic folding separate what flat
summaries mix? (3)~can profiler groups find hidden labeled problems?
(4)~do real flame graphs surface actionable insights?

\subsection{E1: Generality---Can Two Abstractions Cover Heterogeneous
Agent Traces?}

We import 15 public labeled trace families covering web navigation
(WebLINX, Mind2Web, AgentTrek, WebShop), tool and API interaction
(API-Bank, ToolBench, tau-bench), software engineering (SWE-agent),
mobile and GUI (AndroidControl, GUI-Odyssey, ScaleCUA), expert failure
labels (AgentRewardBench), safety labels (SATraj-OS), human-boundary
labels (OSWorld-Human), and desktop step quality (AgentNet).
Table~\ref{tab:datasets} summarizes the families.

\begin{table*}[t]
\centering\small
\caption{Public labeled trace families. The bottom four rows provide
oracle labels used for the E3 hidden-label benchmark.}
\label{tab:datasets}
\begin{tabular}{p{0.18\linewidth}p{0.28\linewidth}p{0.20\linewidth}p{0.24\linewidth}}
\toprule
Family & Native labels & Access & Evaluation role \\
\midrule
WebLINX, Mind2Web, AgentTrek, WebShop & Web actions, tasks, rewards & HF / public shards & Web coverage \\
API-Bank, ToolBench, tau-bench & API calls, tool messages, outcomes & HF / repo JSONL & Tool/API coverage \\
SWE-agent & Issue trajectories, commands & HF viewer & Software coverage \\
AndroidControl, GUI-Odyssey, ScaleCUA & Mobile/GUI actions, history & Public/HF samples & Mobile/GUI coverage \\
\midrule
AgentRewardBench & Success, side-effect, looping, optimality & HF annotations & Failure/looping tasks \\

All 15 sources produce 47{,}590 operations through mapping rules. No
source requires a prompt-specific, GUI-specific, or safety-specific
