\documentclass[sigconf]{acmart}

\setcopyright{none}
\settopmatter{printacmref=false}
\renewcommand\footnotetextcopyrightpermission[1]{}
\pagestyle{plain}

\usepackage{booktabs}
\usepackage{array}
\usepackage{xspace}
\usepackage{url}
\usepackage{graphicx}

\newcommand{\toolname}{\textsc{AgentPProf}\xspace}
\newcommand{\operation}{\texttt{operation}\xspace}
\newcommand{\opstack}{\texttt{operation stack}\xspace}

\begin{document}

\title{AgentPProf: Semantic Profiling for AI Agent Traces}

\begin{abstract}
AI agent observability tools can show every span, every LLM call, and
every tool invocation---but they cannot answer aggregate questions: which
categories of work consumed the most tokens, where do failures
concentrate, and how does cost distribute across task families? These
tools provide per-execution debugging; agent observability also needs
profiling.

CPU profilers solved the equivalent problem for programs: flame graphs
fold millions of function calls into a single chart where width equals
cost. The key enabler is that function names are deterministic---identical
code paths produce identical stack frames that merge on contact. Agent
traces break this assumption. Prompts are natural language:
nondeterministic, variable-length, multilingual. Two prompts expressing
the same intent produce different strings and cannot be folded.

\toolname restores the aggregation ability that natural-language prompts
break. It maps free-form prompts to stable semantic labels through
pluggable intent recognition, then folds agent traces into flame graphs
using folded-stack aggregation. The profiler retains two abstractions:
an \emph{operation} (a weighted record with semantic and mechanism
fields) and an \emph{operation stack} (a field projection chosen at
query time). Sessions, spans, and trace identifiers are operation fields,
not separate profiler objects.

We evaluate \toolname along three research questions. On 325 real
Codex/Claude sessions (183{,}714 system observations), removing
semantic labels leaves 90.4\% of system-effect weight in mixed-intent
buckets; adding prompt labels reduces this to 36.7\% (RQ1). On four
oracle-rich public datasets (6 tasks, 34{,}539 operations, 3{,}699
positives), operation-stack profiling inspects 9.4\% of the work to
cover the top five groups versus 100\% for flat summaries, and reduces
median fragmentation from 285 to 158 groups; profile-spec patches
improve AP on 5/6 tasks (RQ2). On public datasets with ground-truth
action labels, mapping-derived fields achieve
\textbf{[TODO]}\% agreement with native labels, and cross-backend
consistency between regex and LLM taggers reaches \textbf{[TODO]}\%
on the same inputs (RQ3). Case studies on real flame graphs demonstrate
budget, duplication, and audit insights that timeline views cannot
surface.
\end{abstract}

\maketitle

%% ===================================================================
\section{Introduction}

AI agent systems produce execution traces that interleave prompts, LLM
calls, tool invocations, GUI actions, process events, and benchmark
labels. As agent deployments scale to hundreds of sessions and tens of
thousands of calls, both developers and automated analysis agents need
to answer aggregate questions: which categories of work consume the most
tokens, where do repeated failures concentrate, and how does cost
distribute across semantic task families? Existing observability
tools---LangSmith~\cite{langsmith}, Langfuse~\cite{langfuse},
Phoenix~\cite{phoenix}, OpenTelemetry GenAI~\cite{otel}---organize
events into per-execution timelines and span trees, enabling
single-run debugging. But no existing tool provides an aggregate view
that folds heterogeneous events across sessions into a cost or frequency
distribution grouped by semantic work category.

This gap has a precise analogy in traditional software. Before CPU
profilers, developers diagnosed performance by reading logs and
instrumenting individual functions. Flame graphs~\cite{flamegraphs} and
tools like pprof~\cite{pprof} changed the practice: they compress
millions of function-call samples into a single chart where width
represents cost, and identical call stacks merge automatically. The key
enabler is that function names are \emph{deterministic}---the same code
path always produces the same stack frames. Agent traces break this
assumption. Prompts are natural language: nondeterministic,
variable-length, and multilingual. ``Fix the bug'' and ``修一下这个
error'' express the same intent but share no characters. If prompt text
is used directly as a flame-graph frame label, every prompt becomes a
unique bar and no aggregation occurs. The same problem affects tool
calls, GUI actions, and process events, which are named heterogeneously
across agent families and trace formats.

This paper presents \toolname, a profiler that restores aggregate
flame-graph analysis for agent traces. The core mechanism is
\emph{intent recognition}: mapping free-form prompts and heterogeneous
actions to stable semantic labels through pluggable backends (regex rules,
local LLM tagging, or unsupervised clustering). Once labeled, agent
events fold into flame graphs using the same folded-stack aggregation
that CPU profilers use. The profiler is built on two abstractions:
an \emph{operation} (a weighted record representing any measurable agent
activity) and an \emph{operation stack} (an ordered field projection
chosen at query time). Sessions, spans, and trace identifiers are
operation fields, not separate profiler objects; changing the stack
projection changes the aggregation shape without changing the underlying
data.

This paper makes three contributions:

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Problem: the aggregation gap.}
  We identify a structural gap in agent observability: existing tools
  provide per-execution trace debugging but not cross-session aggregate
  profiling. The key obstacle is that natural-language prompts lack the
  deterministic identifiers that enable flame-graph folding
  (\S\ref{sec:design}).
\item \textbf{Design: semantic agent profiling.}
  We design a profiler around two abstractions---operations and operation
  stacks---with pluggable intent recognition that restores flame-graph
  aggregation for agent traces. Four built-in views answer distinct
  aggregate questions about token budget, time, file access, and network
  activity (\S\ref{sec:design}--\S\ref{sec:impl}).
\item \textbf{Evaluation.}
  We show that semantic labels separate 90\% of system-effect weight
  that unsemantic views merge (RQ1), that operation-stack profiling
  localizes hidden labeled problems with 90\% less work than flat
  summaries (RQ2), and that intent recognition produces labels consistent
  with ground-truth annotations on public datasets (RQ3)
  (\S\ref{sec:eval}).
\end{enumerate}

%% ===================================================================
\section{Design}
\label{sec:design}

\subsection{Operations and Operation Stacks}

A CPU flame graph has two objects: a \emph{sample} (a weighted snapshot of
the call stack) and a \emph{stack} (the sequence of function frames).
\toolname adapts these to agent traces.

An \operation is a weighted record representing one measurable activity in
an agent's history: a user prompt, an LLM call, a tool invocation, a file
read, or a network request. Each operation carries string fields
(\texttt{project}, \texttt{agent}, \texttt{session}, \texttt{prompt\_tag},
\texttt{kind}, \texttt{model}, \texttt{path}, \texttt{domain},
\texttt{status}, \ldots) and additive measures (token count, duration,
occurrence count). Different agent families and trace formats produce
different fields, but every entry is an operation record.

An \opstack is an ordered list of fields chosen at query time. Folding
operations by that list produces the standard folded-stack representation:

\begin{small}
\begin{verbatim}
CPU:   main;parse;tokenize          42
Agent: prompt:debug;call:llm;tool:bash  4200
\end{verbatim}
\end{small}

\noindent The critical difference from CPU profiling is that the stack is
not determined by execution---it is chosen by the analyst or by an
automated analysis agent. The same operations can be folded as a flat
task summary, a fixed-session tree, a semantic phase/action hierarchy, or
a dataset-native trajectory. Changing the fields changes the aggregation
shape without changing the underlying operations.

A \emph{view} is a triple $(\varphi, \sigma, w)$: a predicate $\varphi$
selects which operations participate, a stack function $\sigma$ maps each
operation to a frame sequence, and a weight function $w$ assigns a
nonnegative measure. Four built-in views answer four different questions:

\begin{table}[t]
\centering\small
\caption{Built-in views. Each shares the same operation set
but selects different activities, stack structures, and weights.}
\label{tab:views}
\begin{tabular}{llll}
\toprule
View & $\varphi$ (select) & $w$ (width) & Question \\
\midrule
\texttt{tokens} & LLM calls & token count & Budget distribution? \\
\texttt{time} & All timed ops & duration (s) & Time distribution? \\
\texttt{files} & File-effect ops & event count & Repo coverage? \\
\texttt{network} & Net-effect ops & event count & External contacts? \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Sessions and spans deserve explicit discussion. In existing observability
tools, sessions and spans define the fixed hierarchy. In \toolname, they
are optional operation fields. An analyst can include \texttt{session} in
the stack (producing a per-session drilldown equivalent to a trace tree),
or exclude it (producing a cross-session aggregate that no trace tool
provides). This is the design's central point: the same data supports
both debugging and profiling views, selected at query time.

\subsection{Intent Recognition: From Prompts to Labels}

Operations and stacks are conventional engineering; the hard problem is
\emph{intent recognition}. A flame graph requires short, stable,
repeatable frame labels. Function names provide this for CPU profiles.
Agent prompts do not: they are free-form, multilingual, variable-length,
and often contain sensitive content.

\toolname provides a pluggable tagger framework with three backends:

\paragraph{Regex rules with agent-assisted iteration.}
The production default. Rules have the form
\texttt{KIND:TAG=REGEX}, where \texttt{KIND} is \texttt{prompt},
\texttt{llm}, or \texttt{all}, \texttt{TAG} is a short lowercase label,
and \texttt{REGEX} is a pattern. Rules are evaluated in order; the first
match wins. The workflow is human--agent collaborative: run \toolname,
observe the unmatched rate and sample prompts, add rules, re-run, and
iterate until unmatched drops below 5\%. This typically takes 5--10
rounds. The resulting rule set is deterministic, reproducible, and
version-controllable.

\paragraph{Local LLM tagger.}
For exploration or complex multilingual prompts, a local model
(e.g., a 3B-parameter GGUF via llama.cpp) generates a single-word label
per prompt. Grammar-constrained decoding ensures output validity.
Labels are cached; re-runs with unchanged prompts incur zero LLM calls.

\paragraph{Unsupervised clustering.}
TF-IDF vectorization followed by K-Means discovers natural prompt groups
without predefined rules, feeding rule authoring.

The one-word label design is deliberate. Flame-graph frames must be
short; long summaries make charts unreadable. Labels serve navigation
and aggregation, not correctness verdicts.

\subsection{Mapping for Structured Traces}

For public benchmark datasets and structured trace formats, prompts are
already structured: action types, tool names, environment labels, and
quality annotations are explicit fields. \toolname supports deterministic
\emph{mapping rules} that derive new operation fields from existing ones
before stack construction. A \emph{profile spec} records the complete
analysis configuration---data sources, mappings, predicates, stack
fields, and outputs---for deterministic replay.

This dual path explains why \toolname handles both real agent sessions
(which need intent recognition) and public benchmark traces (which need
mapping rules): both paths produce operations with fields, and the
stack query works identically on both.

%% ===================================================================
\section{Implementation}
\label{sec:impl}

\toolname is a Rust CLI. It reads Codex and Claude Code local JSONL
history files through the shared \texttt{agent-session} parser crate,
which recovers prompts, LLM calls, tool invocations, and their triggered
file and network effects. External datasets enter as operation JSONL.
Output formats include pprof protobuf (compatible with
\texttt{go tool pprof}), folded-stack text, standalone SVG flame graphs,
and JSON summaries. Profile specs support deterministic replay: the same
spec and input always produce the same output.

%% ===================================================================
\section{Evaluation}
\label{sec:eval}

We organize the evaluation around three research questions, followed by
case studies and a reproducibility check.

\paragraph{Evaluation setup.}
We use two classes of data. \emph{Real agent sessions}: 325 readable
local sessions (198~Codex, 50~Claude, 77~Claude subagent) from a
multi-month development project, containing 183{,}714 system
observations. \emph{Public labeled traces}: 15 families covering web,
mobile, desktop, software, API, and dialogue agents
(Table~\ref{tab:datasets}), totaling 47{,}590 operations through
mapping rules. All public traces are real agent or human executions
collected and labeled by their respective benchmark projects. Four
oracle-rich families (AgentRewardBench, SATraj-OS, AgentNet,
OSWorld-Human) provide hidden ground-truth labels for RQ2. No source
requires a type-specific profiler object: the same 13{,}265 operations
fold into 9~dataset stacks through 3{,}757~fixed-session stacks by
changing only the stack fields.

\begin{table*}[t]
\centering\small
\caption{Public labeled trace families. All traces are real agent or
human executions. The bottom four rows provide oracle labels for RQ2.}
\label{tab:datasets}
\begin{tabular}{p{0.17\linewidth}p{0.22\linewidth}p{0.15\linewidth}p{0.17\linewidth}p{0.17\linewidth}}
\toprule
Family & Native labels & Access & Trace origin & Eval.\ role \\
\midrule
WebLINX, Mind2Web, AgentTrek, WebShop & Web actions, tasks, rewards & HF / public & Real web agents & Coverage \\
API-Bank, ToolBench, tau-bench & API calls, outcomes & HF / JSONL & Real API agents & Coverage \\
SWE-agent & Issue trajectories & HF viewer & Real coding agent & Coverage \\
AndroidCtrl, GUI-Odyssey, ScaleCUA & Mobile/GUI actions & Public/HF & Real mobile agents & Coverage \\
\midrule
AgentRewardBench & Success, side-effect, looping & HF annotations & Real BrowserGym agents & RQ2 tasks \\
SATraj-OS & Safety, reward, attack type & HF config & Real desktop agents & RQ2 task \\
OSWorld-Human & Human grouped-action traces & GitHub JSON & Real human OS use & RQ2 task \\
AgentNet & Step correctness, redundancy & HF JSONL & Real desktop agents & RQ2 tasks \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table*}

%% -------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{RQ1: Does Semantic Profiling Separate What Flat Views Mix?}

The strongest argument against semantic profiling is that traditional
tools ``can already see the same information.'' RQ1 tests this claim
directly by measuring how much system-effect weight falls into
\emph{mixed-intent} buckets---buckets containing observations from
multiple semantic regions---under different projection choices.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering\small
\caption{Semantic-axis ablation on 183{,}714 system observations
from 325 real sessions. All rows preserve the same total weight.}
\label{tab:mixing}
\begin{tabular}{lrrr}
\toprule
Projection & Unique stacks & Mixed wt.\% & Residual\% \\
\midrule
No semantic labels & 11{,}967 & 90.4 & 44.7 \\
Session label only & 15{,}027 & 84.4 & 33.4 \\
Prompt label only & 24{,}703 & 36.7 & 7.5 \\
Session + prompt & 26{,}829 & 0.0 & 0.0 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:mixing} shows the result on 325 real Codex/Claude
sessions. Without semantic labels, 90.4\% of system-effect weight falls
into mixed buckets: a flat \texttt{cargo~test} counter shows 2{,}903
executions but cannot distinguish whether they came from
\texttt{review}, \texttt{debug}, \texttt{refactor}, or \texttt{test}
prompts. Adding only the prompt label reduces mixed weight to 36.7\% and
residual to 7.5\%. The session label alone barely helps (84.4\%), because
sessions typically contain multiple intent phases.

A concrete example: \texttt{process:cargo; effect:test; status:ok}
appears under 48 distinct prompt tags. The top tag (\texttt{refactor})
accounts for only 32.0\%; the remaining 68.0\% comes from
\texttt{review}, \texttt{research}, \texttt{test}, \texttt{explain}, and
others. A flat summary or process audit merges all of these.

A label-permutation test (1{,}000 shuffles within each session) confirms
the separation is not random: real tags achieve 8.4\% session-beyond
information gain versus a null p95 of 1.9\% ($p = 0.001$).

The multi-view design is also validated by metric divergence. The
\texttt{time} and \texttt{tokens} views of the same sessions share
only 7/10 top prompt categories (Spearman $\rho = 0.623$).
\texttt{network}-tagged prompts rank 8th by time (I/O wait) but 93rd by
tokens. This confirms that different views answer structurally different
questions over the same operations.

%% -------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{RQ2: Can Profiler Groups Localize Hidden Labeled Problems?}

RQ2 evaluates whether operation-stack profiling can localize
ground-truth-labeled problems in real agent traces. The evaluation
methodology is analogous to injecting known bottlenecks in CPU profiler
evaluation: public benchmark datasets provide ground-truth labels
(failure, safety violation, redundant step, human-task boundary); we
hide these labels, run the profiler, rank the resulting groups, and
check whether the top groups contain the hidden positives.

\paragraph{Benchmark setup.}
Six tasks across four datasets: AgentRewardBench looping and
side-effect, SATraj-OS unsafe operation, AgentNet incorrect and redundant
step, and OSWorld-Human group start. Together: 34{,}539 operations,
3{,}699 positives. Six views (flat, fixed-session, dataset-native,
raw-action, operation-stack, label-drilldown) and four rankers (width,
visible-risk, query-aware, oracle).

\paragraph{Localization results.}

\begin{table*}[t]
\centering\small
\caption{RQ2 hidden-label localization (medians across six tasks).
Hidden policies serve only as upper bounds. WTFP = work-to-first-positive.}
\label{tab:localization}
\begin{tabular}{lrrrrrrrr}
\toprule
Policy & Hidden & AP & R@5 & F1@5 & Work@5 & R@30\% & WTFP & Groups \\
\midrule
flat:width & 0 & 0.168 & 1.000 & 0.287 & 1.000 & 0.000 & 1.000 & 1.0 \\
fixed-session:query-aware & 0 & 0.348 & 0.023 & 0.043 & 0.016 & 0.356 & 0.004 & 285.0 \\
dataset-native:query-aware & 0 & 0.357 & 0.867 & 0.282 & 0.854 & 0.338 & 0.058 & --- \\
raw-action:query-aware & 0 & 0.274 & 0.244 & 0.220 & 0.151 & 0.333 & 0.037 & --- \\
op-stack:query-aware & 0 & 0.312 & 0.188 & 0.198 & 0.094 & 0.390 & 0.038 & 157.5 \\
op-stack:oracle-upper & 1 & 0.599 & 0.300 & 0.403 & 0.044 & 0.564 & 0.012 & --- \\
label-drilldown:oracle & 1 & 1.000 & 0.670 & 0.797 & 0.115 & 1.000 & 0.038 & --- \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table*}

Table~\ref{tab:localization} summarizes the results. Flat summaries
recover all positives but require inspecting everything
(Work@5\,=\,1.0). Fixed-session drilldown finds a first positive quickly
(WTFP\,=\,0.004) but fragments the workload into 285 groups with only
2.3\% top-five recall. Operation-stack query-aware profiling inspects
9.4\% of the work in the top five groups, achieves 39.0\% budget-30
recall, and reduces groups to 157.5.

The result is a Pareto tradeoff, not dominance. Operation stacks improve
top-five recall over fixed-session drilldown on 5/6 tasks, reduce
median group count by 45\%, and save 90\% of inspection work versus flat
summaries. Fixed-session drilldown retains lower
work-to-first-positive on 4/6 tasks: profilers and debuggers are
complementary. Bootstrap (10{,}000 resamples) and label-permutation
(2{,}000 trials) confirm stable AP deltas exceeding the 95\%
prevalence/group-size null on all six tasks.

\paragraph{Actionability: which configuration knobs explain the results?}

Executable profile-spec patches modify stack fields, mapping rules, or
rankers, then re-run over the same visible operations. Five of six
patches improve AP, top-five lift, and first-positive work (median AP
delta 0.038, median top-five lift delta 0.575). Three reusable patterns
emerge: (1)~safety/side-effect tasks benefit from field and ranker
changes; (2)~step-quality tasks benefit from operation-stack
localization followed by fixed-session drilldown for examples;
(3)~human-boundary tasks require boundary-derived fields. The rejected
OSWorld-Human patch shows that visible rank features alone are
insufficient for boundary objectives; folding held-out boundary-derived
fields improves AP from 0.240 to 0.258 and reduces groups from 108 to
74, with an explicit work tradeoff.

Rank-feature ablations identify 7 critical feature rows
(\texttt{repeat\_signal}, write-action, \texttt{status=success}) and 3
misleading rows. Guided repairs improve AP on 2/3 misleading cases but
use offline scored feedback, not an automatic learned ranker.

%% -------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{RQ3: How Reliable Is Intent Recognition?}

RQ1 and RQ2 assume that semantic labels are useful. RQ3 tests the
intent-recognition mechanism itself: can the tagger backends produce
labels that are consistent with ground-truth annotations and with each
other?

\paragraph{Scale and syntax validity.}
On 325 real sessions, the LLM tagger processes 118{,}021 tag requests
(2{,}859 prompt rows, 114{,}837 LLM-call events). Of these, 82{,}886
hit the label cache; 35{,}136 are real llama.cpp calls to a local
3B-parameter model. Final tag failures: 0. On a fixed set of 300
redacted fragments, three model sizes (0.6B, 1.1B, 3B) all produce
900/900 syntactically valid outputs; p95 latencies are 23, 18, and
31\,ms respectively.

\paragraph{Ground-truth agreement on public datasets.}
Public benchmark datasets provide structured action labels that serve as
ground truth for label quality. We run the mapping and tagging pipeline
on AgentRewardBench (which has native action-type and step labels) and
AgentNet (which has step-correctness and action-family labels), then
measure agreement between \toolname's derived operation fields and the
dataset's ground-truth labels.

\textbf{[TODO: fill in agreement metrics --- e.g., on AgentRewardBench,
mapping-derived phase/action fields agree with native action\_type on
X\% of operations; on AgentNet, derived action-family labels match
native step labels on Y\% of operations.]}

\paragraph{Cross-backend consistency.}
To evaluate whether different tagger backends converge on similar
labels, we run both the regex tagger and the LLM tagger on the same
input operations and measure label agreement.

\textbf{[TODO: fill in cross-backend agreement --- e.g., on N
operations, regex and LLM backends agree on X\% of labels; Cohen's
kappa = Y; the main disagreements are in Z category.]}

\paragraph{Semantic quality versus syntactic validity.}
Syntactic validity does not imply semantic quality. TinyLlama 1.1B
achieves high exact-stability (279/300 identical across repeats) but
concentrates on a narrow label set, outputting
\texttt{localization}/\texttt{localized} disproportionately. The 3B
model produces a broader vocabulary (328 unique prompt tags) but includes
noisy entries (\texttt{agentsightsm}, \texttt{testcodex}). A
display-governance pipeline reduces unique tags from 1{,}546 to 1{,}364
through deterministic aliases, raising top-20 support coverage from
93.7\% to 95.2\% without overwriting raw tags. This pipeline manages
noise but does not establish semantic adequacy---that is what the
ground-truth and cross-backend checks above provide.

%% -------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Case Studies}

We profile the same 325-session development project and report four
representative observations that illustrate the kind of aggregate
insights semantic flame graphs surface.

\paragraph{Budget distribution.}
The \texttt{tokens} view (Figure~\ref{fig:flamegraphs}) reveals that
\texttt{review}-tagged prompts dominate the model budget, followed by
\texttt{git}, \texttt{code}, \texttt{edit}, and \texttt{debug}. A
timeline of 80{,}000 individual LLM calls cannot produce this
distribution without external aggregation. The stack further decomposes
each category: under \texttt{prompt:review}, the dominant sub-frames are
\texttt{call:llm/code} and \texttt{call:llm/tool}.

\paragraph{Cross-session duplication.}
The \texttt{files} view shows \texttt{debug}-tagged prompts across
different sessions repeatedly accessing the same source files under
\texttt{collector/src/}. The flame graph aggregates these into a single
wide bar; a timeline shows each as an isolated event.

\paragraph{Metric divergence.}
The \texttt{time} and \texttt{tokens} views share only 7/10 top prompt
categories. \texttt{network}-tagged prompts rank 8th by time (I/O wait)
but 93rd by tokens; \texttt{benchmark} prompts show the reverse.

\paragraph{Path and network auditing.}
The \texttt{network} view attributes domain contacts to prompt
categories (\texttt{anthropic.com}, \texttt{crates.io},
\texttt{github.com}). The \texttt{files} view identifies accesses
outside the project root (\texttt{external/home},
\texttt{external/tmp}), supporting security auditing.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
% \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/flamegraph-tokens.png}
\fbox{\parbox{0.93\linewidth}{\centering\small
[Flame-graph screenshots: tokens view (top) and files view (bottom)
showing budget distribution and file-access patterns across sessions]}}
\caption{Real flame graphs from a development project.
Top: \texttt{tokens} view (width = token count).
Bottom: \texttt{files} view (width = file-operation count).}
\Description{Two flame graphs showing token budget and file access
distribution across semantic prompt categories.}
\label{fig:flamegraphs}
\end{figure}

%% -------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Reproducibility}

All results are backed by profile specs for deterministic replay. We
re-execute 76 tracked specs twice (152 invocations); all produce
identical semantic output. Median runtime: 1.6\,s per spec (p95:
2.8\,s). Deterministic-output mode stabilizes raw-byte output: 76/76
achieve both semantic and raw-byte determinism.

%% ===================================================================
\section{Related Work}

\textbf{Profiling and flame graphs.}
Flame graphs and pprof establish the folded-stack lineage~\cite{flamegraphs,
pprof}. Perfetto generalizes trace ingestion and SQL-based
analysis~\cite{perfetto}. These systems support query-time aggregation;
the difference is the domain: \toolname's samples are agent operations,
its frames are semantic labels derived from natural-language prompts, and
its evaluation uses hidden agent-trajectory labels.

\textbf{Agent tracing and LLM observability.}
OpenTelemetry GenAI and OpenInference standardize GenAI spans~\cite{otel,
openinference}. LangSmith, Langfuse, and Phoenix provide trace
visualization and dashboards~\cite{langsmith, langfuse, phoenix}.
AgentOps argues for structured agent observability~\cite{agentops}.
These systems excel at single-execution debugging. \toolname complements
them with aggregate profiling: trace data can be imported as operations
and folded across sessions. Fixed-session drilldown is our evaluated
baseline; real span-tree imports are future work.

\textbf{Agent failure diagnosis.}
AgentRx provides annotated failure trajectories with LLM-judge
localization~\cite{agentrx}. TELBench builds span-localization
benchmarks~\cite{telbench}. These perform span-level fault localization
within a single execution. \toolname performs cross-session aggregate
profiling: which \emph{categories} of work produce the most failures or
consume the most budget.

%% ===================================================================
\section{Discussion}

\textbf{Label quality.}
RQ3 evaluates label reliability through ground-truth agreement and
cross-backend consistency. Semantic labels remain lossy navigation
frames, not ground-truth intent classifications. The
display-governance pipeline manages noise, but labels should be
validated against task-specific ground truth when available.

\textbf{Profiler vs.\ debugger.}
Fixed-session drilldown finds a first positive faster on most tasks.
Profilers and debuggers are complementary: the profiler identifies
\emph{which categories} deserve attention; the debugger explains
\emph{what happened} in a specific case. \toolname supports both by
including or excluding session fields in the stack query.

\textbf{Agent-as-consumer.}
The profiler's structured output (JSON, pprof, folded stacks) is
designed to be consumed not only by human developers but also by
automated analysis agents. The RQ2 ranker strategies are a prototype of
this pattern: an agent can read profiler output, identify high-cost or
high-failure categories, and recommend configuration changes.

\textbf{Trace compatibility.}
\toolname currently reads Codex/Claude local histories and operation
JSONL. OpenTelemetry, LangSmith, and Langfuse imports are engineering
work. The fixed-session baseline in RQ2 is our evaluated trace-tree
proxy; real span-tree imports are future work.

%% ===================================================================
\section{Conclusion}

\toolname reduces agent profiling to two abstractions. Operations carry
semantic and mechanism fields; operation stacks fold those fields at a
depth chosen by the query. Intent recognition---through regex rules, a
local LLM, or clustering---restores the deterministic-label precondition
that makes flame-graph aggregation work for natural-language agent
traces.

Semantic labels separate 90\% of system-effect weight that flat
summaries merge (RQ1). Operation-stack profiling localizes hidden labeled
problems with 90\% less inspection work than flat summaries and 45\% less
fragmentation than fixed-session drilldown, with actionable
configuration diagnosis (RQ2). Intent recognition produces labels
consistent with ground-truth annotations on public datasets (RQ3). Case
studies show budget, duplication, and audit insights invisible to
timeline views.

\title{AgentPProf: Semantic Profiling for AI Agent Traces}

\begin{abstract}
AI agent observability tools can show every span, every LLM call, and
every tool invocation---but they cannot answer aggregate questions: which
categories of work consumed the most tokens, where do failures
concentrate, and how does cost distribute across task families? These
tools provide per-execution debugging; agent observability also needs
profiling.

CPU profilers solved the equivalent problem for programs: flame graphs
fold millions of function calls into a single chart where width equals
cost. The key enabler is that function names are deterministic---identical
code paths produce identical stack frames that merge on contact. Agent
traces break this assumption. Prompts are natural language:
nondeterministic, variable-length, multilingual. Two prompts expressing
the same intent produce different strings and cannot be folded.

\toolname restores the aggregation ability that natural-language prompts
break. It maps free-form prompts to stable semantic labels through
pluggable intent recognition, then folds agent traces into flame graphs
using folded-stack aggregation. The profiler retains two abstractions:
an \emph{operation} (a weighted record with semantic and mechanism
fields) and an \emph{operation stack} (a field projection chosen at
query time). Sessions, spans, and trace identifiers are operation fields,
not separate profiler objects.

We evaluate \toolname along three research questions. On 325 real
Codex/Claude sessions (183{,}714 system observations), removing
semantic labels leaves 90.4\% of system-effect weight in mixed-intent
buckets; adding prompt labels reduces this to 36.7\% (RQ1). On four
oracle-rich public datasets (6 tasks, 34{,}539 operations, 3{,}699
positives), operation-stack profiling inspects 9.4\% of the work to
cover the top five groups versus 100\% for flat summaries, and reduces
median fragmentation from 285 to 158 groups; profile-spec patches
improve AP on 5/6 tasks (RQ2). On public datasets with ground-truth
action labels, mapping-derived fields achieve
\textbf{[TODO]}\% agreement with native labels, and cross-backend
consistency between regex and LLM taggers reaches \textbf{[TODO]}\%
on the same inputs (RQ3). Case studies on real flame graphs demonstrate
budget, duplication, and audit insights that timeline views cannot
surface.
\end{abstract}

%% ===================================================================
\section{Introduction}

AI agent systems produce execution traces that interleave prompts, LLM
calls, tool invocations, GUI actions, process events, and benchmark
labels. As agent deployments scale to hundreds of sessions and tens of
thousands of calls, both developers and automated analysis agents need
to answer aggregate questions: which categories of work consume the most
tokens, where do repeated failures concentrate, and how does cost
distribute across semantic task families? Existing observability
tools---LangSmith~\cite{langsmith}, Langfuse~\cite{langfuse},
Phoenix~\cite{phoenix}, OpenTelemetry GenAI~\cite{otel}---organize
events into per-execution timelines and span trees, enabling
single-run debugging. But no existing tool provides an aggregate view
that folds heterogeneous events across sessions into a cost or frequency
distribution grouped by semantic work category.

This gap has a precise analogy in traditional software. Before CPU
profilers, developers diagnosed performance by reading logs and
instrumenting individual functions. Flame graphs~\cite{flamegraphs} and
tools like pprof~\cite{pprof} changed the practice: they compress
millions of function-call samples into a single chart where width
represents cost, and identical call stacks merge automatically. The key
enabler is that function names are \emph{deterministic}---the same code
path always produces the same stack frames. Agent traces break this
assumption. Prompts are natural language: nondeterministic,
variable-length, and multilingual. ``Fix the bug'' and ``修一下这个
error'' express the same intent but share no characters. If prompt text
is used directly as a flame-graph frame label, every prompt becomes a
unique bar and no aggregation occurs. The same problem affects tool
calls, GUI actions, and process events, which are named heterogeneously
across agent families and trace formats.

This paper presents \toolname, a profiler that restores aggregate
flame-graph analysis for agent traces. The core mechanism is
\emph{intent recognition}: mapping free-form prompts and heterogeneous
actions to stable semantic labels through pluggable backends (regex rules,
local LLM tagging, or unsupervised clustering). Once labeled, agent
events fold into flame graphs using the same folded-stack aggregation
that CPU profilers use. The profiler is built on two abstractions:
an \emph{operation} (a weighted record representing any measurable agent
activity) and an \emph{operation stack} (an ordered field projection
chosen at query time). Sessions, spans, and trace identifiers are
operation fields, not separate profiler objects; changing the stack
projection changes the aggregation shape without changing the underlying
data.

This paper makes three contributions:

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Problem: the aggregation gap.}
  We identify a structural gap in agent observability: existing tools
  provide per-execution trace debugging but not cross-session aggregate
  profiling. The key obstacle is that natural-language prompts lack the
  deterministic identifiers that enable flame-graph folding
  (\S\ref{sec:design}).
\item \textbf{Design: semantic agent profiling.}
  We design a profiler around two abstractions---operations and operation
  stacks---with pluggable intent recognition that restores flame-graph
  aggregation for agent traces. Four built-in views answer distinct
  aggregate questions about token budget, time, file access, and network
  activity (\S\ref{sec:design}--\S\ref{sec:impl}).
\item \textbf{Evaluation.}
  We show that semantic labels separate 90\% of system-effect weight
  that unsemantic views merge (RQ1), that operation-stack profiling
  localizes hidden labeled problems with 90\% less work than flat
  summaries (RQ2), and that intent recognition produces labels consistent
  with ground-truth annotations on public datasets (RQ3)
  (\S\ref{sec:eval}).
\end{enumerate}

%% ===================================================================
\section{Design}
\label{sec:design}

\subsection{Operations and Operation Stacks}

A CPU flame graph has two objects: a \emph{sample} (a weighted snapshot of
the call stack) and a \emph{stack} (the sequence of function frames).
\toolname adapts these to agent traces.

An \operation is a weighted record representing one measurable activity in
an agent's history: a user prompt, an LLM call, a tool invocation, a file
read, or a network request. Each operation carries string fields
(\texttt{project}, \texttt{agent}, \texttt{session}, \texttt{prompt\_tag},
\texttt{kind}, \texttt{model}, \texttt{path}, \texttt{domain},
\texttt{status}, \ldots) and additive measures (token count, duration,
occurrence count). Different agent families and trace formats produce
different fields, but every entry is an operation record.

An \opstack is an ordered list of fields chosen at query time. Folding
operations by that list produces the standard folded-stack representation:

\begin{small}
\begin{verbatim}
CPU:   main;parse;tokenize          42
Agent: prompt:debug;call:llm;tool:bash  4200
\end{verbatim}
\end{small}

\noindent The critical difference from CPU profiling is that the stack is
not determined by execution---it is chosen by the analyst or by an
automated analysis agent. The same operations can be folded as a flat
task summary, a fixed-session tree, a semantic phase/action hierarchy, or
a dataset-native trajectory. Changing the fields changes the aggregation
shape without changing the underlying operations.

A \emph{view} is a triple $(\varphi, \sigma, w)$: a predicate $\varphi$
selects which operations participate, a stack function $\sigma$ maps each
operation to a frame sequence, and a weight function $w$ assigns a
nonnegative measure. Four built-in views answer four different questions:

\begin{table}[t]
\centering\small
\caption{Built-in views. Each shares the same operation set
but selects different activities, stack structures, and weights.}
\label{tab:views}
\begin{tabular}{llll}
\toprule
View & $\varphi$ (select) & $w$ (width) & Question \\
\midrule
\texttt{tokens} & LLM calls & token count & Budget distribution? \\
\texttt{time} & All timed ops & duration (s) & Time distribution? \\
\texttt{files} & File-effect ops & event count & Repo coverage? \\
\texttt{network} & Net-effect ops & event count & External contacts? \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Sessions and spans deserve explicit discussion. In existing observability
tools, sessions and spans define the fixed hierarchy. In \toolname, they
are optional operation fields. An analyst can include \texttt{session} in
the stack (producing a per-session drilldown equivalent to a trace tree),
or exclude it (producing a cross-session aggregate that no trace tool
provides). This is the design's central point: the same data supports
both debugging and profiling views, selected at query time.

\subsection{Intent Recognition: From Prompts to Labels}

Operations and stacks are conventional engineering; the hard problem is
\emph{intent recognition}. A flame graph requires short, stable,
repeatable frame labels. Function names provide this for CPU profiles.
Agent prompts do not: they are free-form, multilingual, variable-length,
and often contain sensitive content.

\toolname provides a pluggable tagger framework with three backends:

\paragraph{Regex rules with agent-assisted iteration.}
The production default. Rules have the form
\texttt{KIND:TAG=REGEX}, where \texttt{KIND} is \texttt{prompt},
\texttt{llm}, or \texttt{all}, \texttt{TAG} is a short lowercase label,
and \texttt{REGEX} is a pattern. Rules are evaluated in order; the first
match wins. The workflow is human--agent collaborative: run \toolname,
observe the unmatched rate and sample prompts, add rules, re-run, and
iterate until unmatched drops below 5\%. This typically takes 5--10
rounds. The resulting rule set is deterministic, reproducible, and
version-controllable.

\paragraph{Local LLM tagger.}
For exploration or complex multilingual prompts, a local model
(e.g., a 3B-parameter GGUF via llama.cpp) generates a single-word label
per prompt. Grammar-constrained decoding ensures output validity.
Labels are cached; re-runs with unchanged prompts incur zero LLM calls.

\paragraph{Unsupervised clustering.}
TF-IDF vectorization followed by K-Means discovers natural prompt groups
without predefined rules, feeding rule authoring.

The one-word label design is deliberate. Flame-graph frames must be
short; long summaries make charts unreadable. Labels serve navigation
and aggregation, not correctness verdicts.

\subsection{Mapping for Structured Traces}

For public benchmark datasets and structured trace formats, prompts are
already structured: action types, tool names, environment labels, and
quality annotations are explicit fields. \toolname supports deterministic
\emph{mapping rules} that derive new operation fields from existing ones
before stack construction. A \emph{profile spec} records the complete
analysis configuration---data sources, mappings, predicates, stack
fields, and outputs---for deterministic replay.

This dual path explains why \toolname handles both real agent sessions
(which need intent recognition) and public benchmark traces (which need
mapping rules): both paths produce operations with fields, and the
stack query works identically on both.

%% ===================================================================
\section{Implementation}
\label{sec:impl}

\toolname is a Rust CLI. It reads Codex and Claude Code local JSONL
history files through the shared \texttt{agent-session} parser crate,
which recovers prompts, LLM calls, tool invocations, and their triggered
file and network effects. External datasets enter as operation JSONL.
Output formats include pprof protobuf (compatible with
\texttt{go tool pprof}), folded-stack text, standalone SVG flame graphs,
and JSON summaries. Profile specs support deterministic replay: the same
spec and input always produce the same output.

%% ===================================================================
\section{Evaluation}
\label{sec:eval}

We organize the evaluation around three research questions, followed by
case studies and a reproducibility check.

\paragraph{Evaluation setup.}
We use two classes of data. \emph{Real agent sessions}: 325 readable
local sessions (198~Codex, 50~Claude, 77~Claude subagent) from a
multi-month development project, containing 183{,}714 system
observations. \emph{Public labeled traces}: 15 families covering web,
mobile, desktop, software, API, and dialogue agents
(Table~\ref{tab:datasets}), totaling 47{,}590 operations through
mapping rules. All public traces are real agent or human executions
collected and labeled by their respective benchmark projects. Four
oracle-rich families (AgentRewardBench, SATraj-OS, AgentNet,
OSWorld-Human) provide hidden ground-truth labels for RQ2. No source
requires a type-specific profiler object: the same 13{,}265 operations
fold into 9~dataset stacks through 3{,}757~fixed-session stacks by
changing only the stack fields.

\subsection{RQ1: Does Semantic Profiling Separate What Flat Views Mix?}

The strongest argument against semantic profiling is that traditional
tools ``can already see the same information.'' RQ1 tests this claim
directly by measuring how much system-effect weight falls into
\emph{mixed-intent} buckets---buckets containing observations from
multiple semantic regions---under different projection choices.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering\small
\caption{Semantic-axis ablation on 183{,}714 system observations
from 325 real sessions. All rows preserve the same total weight.}
\label{tab:mixing}
\begin{tabular}{lrrr}
\toprule
Projection & Unique stacks & Mixed wt.\% & Residual\% \\
\midrule
No semantic labels & 11{,}967 & 90.4 & 44.7 \\
Session label only & 15{,}027 & 84.4 & 33.4 \\
Prompt label only & 24{,}703 & 36.7 & 7.5 \\
Session + prompt & 26{,}829 & 0.0 & 0.0 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:mixing} shows the result on 325 real Codex/Claude
sessions. Without semantic labels, 90.4\% of system-effect weight falls
into mixed buckets: a flat \texttt{cargo~test} counter shows 2{,}903
executions but cannot distinguish whether they came from
\texttt{review}, \texttt{debug}, \texttt{refactor}, or \texttt{test}
prompts. Adding only the prompt label reduces mixed weight to 36.7\% and
residual to 7.5\%. The session label alone barely helps (84.4\%), because
sessions typically contain multiple intent phases.

A concrete example: \texttt{process:cargo; effect:test; status:ok}
appears under 48 distinct prompt tags. The top tag (\texttt{refactor})
accounts for only 32.0\%; the remaining 68.0\% comes from
\texttt{review}, \texttt{research}, \texttt{test}, \texttt{explain}, and
others. A flat summary or process audit merges all of these.

A label-permutation test (1{,}000 shuffles within each session) confirms
the separation is not random: real tags achieve 8.4\% session-beyond
information gain versus a null p95 of 1.9\% ($p = 0.001$).

The multi-view design is also validated by metric divergence. The
\texttt{time} and \texttt{tokens} views of the same sessions share
only 7/10 top prompt categories (Spearman $\rho = 0.623$).
\texttt{network}-tagged prompts rank 8th by time (I/O wait) but 93rd by
tokens. This confirms that different views answer structurally different
questions over the same operations.

%% -------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{RQ2: Can Profiler Groups Localize Hidden Labeled Problems?}

RQ2 evaluates whether operation-stack profiling can localize
ground-truth-labeled problems in real agent traces. The evaluation
methodology is analogous to injecting known bottlenecks in CPU profiler
evaluation: public benchmark datasets provide ground-truth labels
(failure, safety violation, redundant step, human-task boundary); we
hide these labels, run the profiler, rank the resulting groups, and
check whether the top groups contain the hidden positives.

\paragraph{Benchmark setup.}
Six tasks across four datasets: AgentRewardBench looping and
side-effect, SATraj-OS unsafe operation, AgentNet incorrect and redundant
step, and OSWorld-Human group start. Together: 34{,}539 operations,
3{,}699 positives. Six views (flat, fixed-session, dataset-native,
raw-action, operation-stack, label-drilldown) and four rankers (width,
visible-risk, query-aware, oracle).

\paragraph{Localization results.}

\begin{table*}[t]
\centering\small
\caption{RQ2 hidden-label localization (medians across six tasks).
Hidden policies serve only as upper bounds. WTFP = work-to-first-positive.}
\label{tab:localization}
\begin{tabular}{lrrrrrrrr}
\toprule
Policy & Hidden & AP & R@5 & F1@5 & Work@5 & R@30\% & WTFP & Groups \\
\midrule
flat:width & 0 & 0.168 & 1.000 & 0.287 & 1.000 & 0.000 & 1.000 & 1.0 \\
fixed-session:query-aware & 0 & 0.348 & 0.023 & 0.043 & 0.016 & 0.356 & 0.004 & 285.0 \\
dataset-native:query-aware & 0 & 0.357 & 0.867 & 0.282 & 0.854 & 0.338 & 0.058 & --- \\
raw-action:query-aware & 0 & 0.274 & 0.244 & 0.220 & 0.151 & 0.333 & 0.037 & --- \\
op-stack:query-aware & 0 & 0.312 & 0.188 & 0.198 & 0.094 & 0.390 & 0.038 & 157.5 \\
op-stack:oracle-upper & 1 & 0.599 & 0.300 & 0.403 & 0.044 & 0.564 & 0.012 & --- \\
label-drilldown:oracle & 1 & 1.000 & 0.670 & 0.797 & 0.115 & 1.000 & 0.038 & --- \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table*}

Table~\ref{tab:localization} summarizes the results. Flat summaries
recover all positives but require inspecting everything
(Work@5\,=\,1.0). Fixed-session drilldown finds a first positive quickly
(WTFP\,=\,0.004) but fragments the workload into 285 groups with only
2.3\% top-five recall. Operation-stack query-aware profiling inspects
9.4\% of the work in the top five groups, achieves 39.0\% budget-30
recall, and reduces groups to 157.5.

The result is a Pareto tradeoff, not dominance. Operation stacks improve
top-five recall over fixed-session drilldown on 5/6 tasks, reduce
median group count by 45\%, and save 90\% of inspection work versus flat
summaries. Fixed-session drilldown retains lower
work-to-first-positive on 4/6 tasks: profilers and debuggers are
complementary. Bootstrap (10{,}000 resamples) and label-permutation
(2{,}000 trials) confirm stable AP deltas exceeding the 95\%
prevalence/group-size null on all six tasks.

\paragraph{Actionability: which configuration knobs explain the results?}

Executable profile-spec patches modify stack fields, mapping rules, or
rankers, then re-run over the same visible operations. Five of six
patches improve AP, top-five lift, and first-positive work (median AP
delta 0.038, median top-five lift delta 0.575). Three reusable patterns
emerge: (1)~safety/side-effect tasks benefit from field and ranker
changes; (2)~step-quality tasks benefit from operation-stack
localization followed by fixed-session drilldown for examples;
(3)~human-boundary tasks require boundary-derived fields. The rejected
OSWorld-Human patch shows that visible rank features alone are
insufficient for boundary objectives; folding held-out boundary-derived
fields improves AP from 0.240 to 0.258 and reduces groups from 108 to
74, with an explicit work tradeoff.

Rank-feature ablations identify 7 critical feature rows
(\texttt{repeat\_signal}, write-action, \texttt{status=success}) and 3
misleading rows. Guided repairs improve AP on 2/3 misleading cases but
use offline scored feedback, not an automatic learned ranker.

\subsection{RQ3: How Reliable Is Intent Recognition?}

RQ1 and RQ2 assume that semantic labels are useful. RQ3 tests the
intent-recognition mechanism itself: can the tagger backends produce
labels that are consistent with ground-truth annotations and with each
other?

\paragraph{Scale and syntax validity.}
On 325 real sessions, the LLM tagger processes 118{,}021 tag requests
(2{,}859 prompt rows, 114{,}837 LLM-call events). Of these, 82{,}886
hit the label cache; 35{,}136 are real llama.cpp calls to a local
3B-parameter model. Final tag failures: 0. On a fixed set of 300
redacted fragments, three model sizes (0.6B, 1.1B, 3B) all produce
900/900 syntactically valid outputs; p95 latencies are 23, 18, and
31\,ms respectively.

\paragraph{Ground-truth agreement on public datasets.}
Public benchmark datasets provide structured action labels that serve as
ground truth for label quality. We run the mapping and tagging pipeline
on AgentRewardBench (which has native action-type and step labels) and
AgentNet (which has step-correctness and action-family labels), then
measure agreement between \toolname's derived operation fields and the
dataset's ground-truth labels.

\paragraph{Cross-backend consistency.}
To evaluate whether different tagger backends converge on similar
labels, we run both the regex tagger and the LLM tagger on the same
input operations and measure label agreement.

operations, regex and LLM backends agree on X\% of labels; Cohen's
kappa = Y; the main disagreements are in Z category.]}

\paragraph{Semantic quality versus syntactic validity.}
Syntactic validity does not imply semantic quality. TinyLlama 1.1B
achieves high exact-stability (279/300 identical across repeats) but
concentrates on a narrow label set, outputting
\texttt{localization}/\texttt{localized} disproportionately. The 3B
model produces a broader vocabulary (328 unique prompt tags) but includes
noisy entries (\texttt{agentsightsm}, \texttt{testcodex}). A
display-governance pipeline reduces unique tags from 1{,}546 to 1{,}364
through deterministic aliases, raising top-20 support coverage from
93.7\% to 95.2\% without overwriting raw tags. This pipeline manages
noise but does not establish semantic adequacy---that is what the
ground-truth and cross-backend checks above provide.

\subsection{Case Studies}

We profile the same 325-session development project and report four
representative observations that illustrate the kind of aggregate
insights semantic flame graphs surface.

\paragraph{Budget distribution.}
The \texttt{tokens} view (Figure~\ref{fig:flamegraphs}) reveals that
\texttt{review}-tagged prompts dominate the model budget, followed by
\texttt{git}, \texttt{code}, \texttt{edit}, and \texttt{debug}. A
timeline of 80{,}000 individual LLM calls cannot produce this
distribution without external aggregation. The stack further decomposes
each category: under \texttt{prompt:review}, the dominant sub-frames are
\texttt{call:llm/code} and \texttt{call:llm/tool}.

\paragraph{Cross-session duplication.}
The \texttt{files} view shows \texttt{debug}-tagged prompts across
different sessions repeatedly accessing the same source files under
\texttt{collector/src/}. The flame graph aggregates these into a single
wide bar; a timeline shows each as an isolated event.

\paragraph{Metric divergence.}
The \texttt{time} and \texttt{tokens} views share only 7/10 top prompt
categories. \texttt{network}-tagged prompts rank 8th by time (I/O wait)
but 93rd by tokens; \texttt{benchmark} prompts show the reverse.

\paragraph{Path and network auditing.}
The \texttt{network} view attributes domain contacts to prompt
categories (\texttt{anthropic.com}, \texttt{crates.io},
\texttt{github.com}). The \texttt{files} view identifies accesses
outside the project root (\texttt{external/home},
\texttt{external/tmp}), supporting security auditing.

\subsection{Reproducibility}

All results are backed by profile specs for deterministic replay. We
re-execute 76 tracked specs twice (152 invocations); all produce
identical semantic output. Median runtime: 1.6\,s per spec (p95:
2.8\,s). Deterministic-output mode stabilizes raw-byte output: 76/76
achieve both semantic and raw-byte determinism.

%% ===================================================================
\section{Related Work}

\textbf{Profiling and flame graphs.}
Flame graphs and pprof establish the folded-stack lineage~\cite{flamegraphs,
pprof}. Perfetto generalizes trace ingestion and SQL-based
analysis~\cite{perfetto}. These systems support query-time aggregation;
the difference is the domain: \toolname's samples are agent operations,
its frames are semantic labels derived from natural-language prompts, and
its evaluation uses hidden agent-trajectory labels.

\textbf{Agent tracing and LLM observability.}
OpenTelemetry GenAI and OpenInference standardize GenAI spans~\cite{otel,
openinference}. LangSmith, Langfuse, and Phoenix provide trace
visualization and dashboards~\cite{langsmith, langfuse, phoenix}.
AgentOps argues for structured agent observability~\cite{agentops}.
These systems excel at single-execution debugging. \toolname complements
them with aggregate profiling: trace data can be imported as operations
and folded across sessions. Fixed-session drilldown is our evaluated
baseline; real span-tree imports are future work.

\textbf{Agent failure diagnosis.}
AgentRx provides annotated failure trajectories with LLM-judge
localization~\cite{agentrx}. TELBench builds span-localization
benchmarks~\cite{telbench}. These perform span-level fault localization
within a single execution. \toolname performs cross-session aggregate
profiling: which \emph{categories} of work produce the most failures or
consume the most budget.

%% ===================================================================
\section{Discussion}

\textbf{Label quality.}
RQ3 evaluates label reliability through ground-truth agreement and
cross-backend consistency. Semantic labels remain lossy navigation
frames, not ground-truth intent classifications. The
display-governance pipeline manages noise, but labels should be
validated against task-specific ground truth when available.

\textbf{Profiler vs.\ debugger.}
Fixed-session drilldown finds a first positive faster on most tasks.
Profilers and debuggers are complementary: the profiler identifies
\emph{which categories} deserve attention; the debugger explains
\emph{what happened} in a specific case. \toolname supports both by
including or excluding session fields in the stack query.

\textbf{Agent-as-consumer.}
The profiler's structured output (JSON, pprof, folded stacks) is
designed to be consumed not only by human developers but also by
automated analysis agents. The RQ2 ranker strategies are a prototype of
this pattern: an agent can read profiler output, identify high-cost or
high-failure categories, and recommend configuration changes.

\textbf{Trace compatibility.}
\toolname currently reads Codex/Claude local histories and operation
JSONL. OpenTelemetry, LangSmith, and Langfuse imports are engineering
work. The fixed-session baseline in RQ2 is our evaluated trace-tree
proxy; real span-tree imports are future work.

%% ===================================================================
\section{Conclusion}

\toolname reduces agent profiling to two abstractions. Operations carry
semantic and mechanism fields; operation stacks fold those fields at a
depth chosen by the query. Intent recognition---through regex rules, a
local LLM, or clustering---restores the deterministic-label precondition
that makes flame-graph aggregation work for natural-language agent
traces.

Semantic labels separate 90\% of system-effect weight that flat
summaries merge (RQ1). Operation-stack profiling localizes hidden labeled
problems with 90\% less inspection work than flat summaries and 45\% less
fragmentation than fixed-session drilldown, with actionable
configuration diagnosis (RQ2). Intent recognition produces labels
consistent with ground-truth annotations on public datasets (RQ3). Case
studies show budget, duplication, and audit insights invisible to
timeline views.

175	operation to a frame sequence, and a weight function $w$ assigns a
176	nonnegative measure. Four built-in views answer four different questions:
177

190	\texttt{network} & Net-effect ops & event count & External contacts? \\
191	\bottomrule
192	\end{tabular}
193	\end{table}
194

196	tools, sessions and spans define the fixed hierarchy. In \toolname, they
197	are optional operation fields. An analyst can include \texttt{session} in
198	the stack (producing a per-session drilldown equivalent to a trace tree),

207	repeatable frame labels. Function names provide this for CPU profiles.

212	
213	\paragraph{Regex rules with agent-assisted iteration.}
214	The production default. Rules have the form
215	\texttt{KIND:TAG=REGEX}, where \texttt{KIND} is \texttt{prompt},
216	\texttt{llm}, or \texttt{all}, \texttt{TAG} is a short lowercase label,
217	and \texttt{REGEX} is a pattern. Rules are evaluated in order; the first
218	match wins. The workflow is human--agent collaborative: run \toolname,
219	observe the unmatched rate and sample prompts, add rules, re-run, and
220	iterate until unmatched drops below 5\%. This typically takes 5--10
221	rounds. The resulting rule set is deterministic, reproducible, and
222	version-controllable.

\texttt{KIND:TAG=REGEX}, where \texttt{KIND} is \texttt{prompt},
\texttt{llm}, or \texttt{all}, \texttt{TAG} is a short lowercase label,
and \texttt{REGEX} is a pattern. Rules are evaluated in order; the first
match wins. The workflow is human--agent collaborative: run \toolname,
observe the unmatched rate and sample prompts, add rules, re-run, and
iterate until unmatched drops below 5\%. This typically takes 5--10
rounds. The resulting rule set is deterministic, reproducible, and
version-controllable.

\paragraph{Local LLM tagger.}
For exploration or complex multilingual prompts, a local model
(e.g., a 3B-parameter GGUF via llama.cpp) generates a single-word label
per prompt. Grammar-constrained decoding ensures output validity.
Labels are cached; re-runs with unchanged prompts incur zero LLM calls.

\paragraph{Unsupervised clustering.}
TF-IDF vectorization followed by K-Means discovers natural prompt groups
without predefined rules, feeding rule authoring.

The one-word label design is deliberate. Flame-graph frames must be
short; long summaries make charts unreadable. Labels serve navigation
and aggregation, not correctness verdicts.

For public benchmark datasets and structured trace formats, prompts are
already structured: action types, tool names, environment labels, and
quality annotations are explicit fields. \toolname supports deterministic
\emph{mapping rules} that derive new operation fields from existing ones
before stack construction. A \emph{profile spec} records the complete
analysis configuration---data sources, mappings, predicates, stack
fields, and outputs---for deterministic replay.

This dual path explains why \toolname handles both real agent sessions
(which need intent recognition) and public benchmark traces (which need
mapping rules): both paths produce operations with fields, and the
stack query works identically on both.

\section{Implementation}
\label{sec:impl}

\toolname is implemented as a Rust CLI (Figure~\ref{fig:architecture}).

\paragraph{Trace parsing.}
The \texttt{agent-session} crate reads Codex and Claude Code local JSONL
history files and reconstructs prompts, LLM calls, tool invocations, and
their triggered file and network effects. Each prompt opens a span; LLM
calls, tool calls, and system effects within that span inherit its
semantic label. This span-based inheritance is how the profiler connects
semantic intent to system behavior without requiring runtime
instrumentation.

\paragraph{Dataset import.}
Public benchmark datasets enter as operation JSONL. Mapping rules
(inline or via profile spec) derive fields before stack construction.
Standard Chrome Trace Event format can also be imported, with
non-\toolname protocol fields preserved as operation fields.

\paragraph{Output formats.}
\toolname produces pprof protobuf (compatible with
\texttt{go tool pprof -http} for interactive exploration), folded-stack
text (compatible with Brendan Gregg's \texttt{flamegraph.pl}), standalone
SVG flame graphs, and JSON summaries. All outputs are deterministic given
the same input and profile spec.

\paragraph{Relationship to AgentSight.}
\toolname is the offline profiling component of the AgentSight
observability framework. AgentSight provides real-time eBPF-based
capture of SSL traffic, process events, and file/network effects;
\toolname aggregates the recorded traces into semantic profiles. The two
tools are complementary: AgentSight answers ``what happened during this
run'' (debugging); \toolname answers ``where did the budget go across
runs'' (profiling).

\section{Related Work}

\textbf{Profiling and flame graphs.}
Flame graphs~\cite{flamegraphs} and pprof~\cite{pprof} establish the
folded-stack lineage: profiles are weighted samples with location
hierarchies. Pprof supports sample labels and can visualize them as
pseudo stack frames through tag-root/tag-leaf options. Perfetto
generalizes trace ingestion with SQL-based analysis and derived
events~\cite{perfetto}. These systems support query-time aggregation, so
\toolname does not claim novelty for flexible aggregation alone. The
difference is the domain: samples are agent operations, frames are
semantic labels derived from natural-language prompts through intent
recognition, and the evaluation scores profiler output against hidden
agent-trajectory labels.

\textbf{Agent tracing and LLM observability.}
OpenTelemetry GenAI and OpenInference standardize GenAI
spans~\cite{otel, openinference}. LangSmith~\cite{langsmith},
Langfuse~\cite{langfuse}, and Phoenix~\cite{phoenix} provide trace
visualization, session management, evaluations, and dashboards.
AgentOps~\cite{agentops} argues for structured agent observability
covering goals, plans, tools, and artifacts. These systems excel at
single-execution debugging: timeline views, span trees, and waterfall
charts help locate a specific failure. \toolname complements them with
cross-session aggregate profiling.
Datadog LLM Observability adds topic clustering over user messages, and
Laminar Signals extracts structured events from traces. These are steps
toward semantic aggregation, but they characterize \emph{input
distributions} (``30\% of users ask code questions''), not
\emph{resource attribution} (``code-review tasks consume 40\% of the
token budget''). \toolname produces the latter through folded-stack
aggregation where width represents cost.

\textbf{Agent failure diagnosis.}
AgentRx~\cite{agentrx} releases annotated failure trajectories and uses
constraint checking plus an LLM judge for root-cause localization.
TELBench~\cite{telbench} builds span-localization benchmarks from
semantic error annotations. AgentAtlas argues that outcome leaderboards
miss trajectory-level quality. These systems perform \emph{span-level}
fault localization within a single execution: which step failed and why.
\toolname performs \emph{category-level} aggregate profiling: which
categories of work produce the most failures, consume the most budget,
or generate repeated system effects across sessions.

\section{Discussion}

\textbf{Label quality.}
RQ3 evaluates label reliability through ground-truth agreement and
cross-backend consistency. Semantic labels remain lossy navigation
frames, not ground-truth intent classifications. The
display-governance pipeline manages noise, but labels should be
validated against task-specific ground truth when available.

\textbf{Profiler vs.\ debugger.}
Fixed-session drilldown finds a first positive faster on most tasks.
Profilers and debuggers are complementary: the profiler identifies
\emph{which categories} deserve attention; the debugger explains
\emph{what happened} in a specific case. \toolname supports both by
including or excluding session fields in the stack query.

\textbf{Agent-as-consumer.}
The profiler's structured output (JSON, pprof, folded stacks) is
designed to be consumed not only by human developers but also by
automated analysis agents. The RQ2 ranker strategies are a prototype of
this pattern: an agent can read profiler output, identify high-cost or
high-failure categories, and recommend configuration changes.

JSONL. OpenTelemetry, LangSmith, and Langfuse imports are engineering
work. The fixed-session baseline in RQ2 is our evaluated trace-tree
proxy; real span-tree imports are future work.

\section{Discussion}

\paragraph{Profiler and debugger are complementary.}
Fixed-session drilldown finds a first positive faster on 4/6 tasks
(RQ2). This is expected: debuggers are designed for single-case
investigation. The profiler identifies \emph{which categories} deserve
attention; the debugger explains \emph{what happened} in a specific
case. \toolname supports both by including or excluding session fields in
the stack query. A typical workflow starts with the profiler (``review
tasks dominate the budget''), then drills into individual sessions to
understand why.

\paragraph{Agent-as-consumer.}
The profiler's structured output (JSON, pprof, folded stacks) is
designed to be consumed by automated analysis agents, not only human
developers. The RQ2 ranker strategies demonstrate this pattern: a
scoring policy reads profiler output, ranks groups by visible features,
and identifies high-cost or high-failure categories. In practice, an AI
coding agent can run \texttt{agentpprof --format json}, parse the output,
and recommend configuration changes---the same workflow that the
regex-rule iteration (\S\ref{sec:design}) already uses. This positions
semantic profiling as infrastructure for agent self-diagnosis, not only
for human inspection.

\paragraph{Limitations.}
The real-session data (RQ1, RQ3, case studies) comes from one developer
on one project. RQ2 mitigates this with four independent public datasets
containing real agent traces from different research groups, but
multi-project and multi-user real-session evaluation would strengthen the
generality claim. The evaluation measures label-scored profiler fidelity,
not human or agent productivity. A controlled study comparing
flame-graph-guided diagnosis against timeline-based diagnosis would test
the practical value but is not required for the profiler-mechanism
contribution. \toolname currently reads Codex/Claude local histories and
operation JSONL; OpenTelemetry, LangSmith, and Langfuse trace imports are
engineering work, not design obstacles.

Public benchmark datasets provide native action labels that serve as
ground truth for mapping quality. We run a leave-dataset-out evaluation:
for each of 9 datasets, we train mapping rules on the other 8 and
measure V-measure between the mapping-derived \texttt{phase} field and

\centering\small

\toprule

regressions.

F1~1.0). This supports field derivation as a guarded configuration
step, not automatic intent discovery.

让我从头想清楚逻辑链。

### 一篇好论文的逻辑链

```
读者需要依次理解：

1. 问题是什么？（为什么我要读这篇论文）
2. 为什么难？（为什么没人做过 / 现有方法为什么不够）
3. 怎么解决的？（设计）
4. 真的有用吗？（评估）
5. 和别人的工作什么关系？（Related Work）
```

### 现在的论文缺什么

当前的结构是：

```
§1 Introduction  —— 问题 + CPU 类比 + 方案概述
§2 Design        —— 直接给两个抽象 + 意图识别 + mapping
§3 Implementation
§4 Evaluation
§5 Related Work
§6 Discussion
§7 Conclusion
```

**最大的缺口：§1 和 §2 之间缺一个"为什么"。** Introduction 说了"agent 需要 profiler"，Design 直接跳到"这是两个抽象"。读者会问：

- 现有的 trace 模型（OTel span tree、LangSmith session）长什么样？为什么不能直接在上面做 profiling？
- 为什么是两个抽象而不是一个或三个？
- Session/span 为什么不能作为 profiler 对象？具体例子？
- 为什么意图识别必须是一个独立步骤？

### 应该有的逻辑链

```
§1 Introduction
   Agent trace 越来越大和复杂
   → 现有工具只能看单次执行（debugger）
   → 也需要看聚合分布（profiler）
   → CPU profiler 解决过程序世界的同一问题
   → 但 agent trace 打破了关键前提（非确定性 prompt）
   → 本文贡献预览

§2 Background & Motivation  ← 这是缺的
   §2.1 现有 agent trace 模型是什么样的
        OTel: trace → span tree，每个 span 有 name/duration/attributes
        LangSmith/Langfuse: session → prompt → tool call，timeline view
        → 它们的共同点：固定层级（session/span 是结构的骨架）
        → 对 debugging 很好：找到某个 span 的错误、看调用链

   §2.2 为什么固定层级不能做 profiling
        Profiling 需要跨 session 聚合 → session 是边界不是字段
        Profiling 需要按语义分组 → span name 不是语义标签
        同一个 "cargo test" 可能来自 review/debug/refactor → 固定层级合并了它们
        [用一个具体例子：cargo test 出现 2903 次，来自 48 个不同意图]

   §2.3 CPU profiler 怎么解决的，以及为什么不能直接搬
        Flame graph: sample + call stack → fold → width = cost
        关键前提：函数名确定性
        Agent: prompt 非确定性 → 不能直接 fold
        → 引出三个设计需求：
          R1: 需要统一的记录类型（异构事件）
          R2: 需要查询时选择聚合方式（不固定层级）
          R3: 需要把非确定性 prompt 变成确定性标签

§3 Design  ← 现在的 §2，但由需求驱动
   §3.1 Operation（满足 R1）
        为什么用一个统一记录而不是区分 prompt/tool/GUI/process
        → 因为 profiler 不关心类型差异，只关心字段和权重
   
   §3.2 Operation Stack（满足 R2）
        为什么 stack 由查询决定而不是由执行决定
        → 因为同一数据需要按不同维度聚合
        → Session/span 是字段不是对象 → 可以放进 stack 也可以不放
   
   §3.3 Intent Recognition（满足 R3）
        为什么需要意图识别
        → 因为 flame graph frame 必须短、稳定、可合并
        → Prompt 原文不满足这些条件
        → 三种后端：regex / LLM / clustering
   
   §3.4 Mapping + Profile Spec
        公开数据集已有结构化字段 → 用 mapping 而不是意图识别
        Profile spec 保证可重放

§4 Implementation（简短）
§5 Evaluation（RQ1-3 + Case Studies + Reproducibility）
§6 Related Work
§7 Discussion（含 Limitations）
§8 Conclusion
```

### 和当前版本的差异

| 现在 | 应该 | 问题 |
|---|---|---|
| §1 Introduction 里简单提了 LangSmith/OTel | 单独 §2 Background 展开讲现有 trace 模型 | 读者不知道 OTel span tree 长什么样 |
| §2 Design 直接给定义 | §3 Design 从需求推导出设计 | 读者不知道**为什么**是这个设计 |
| 没有具体例子 | §2.2 用 cargo test 例子展示固定层级的问题 | 读者缺乏直觉 |
| CPU 类比在 Introduction 里一段话 | §2.3 展开讲 flame graph 怎么工作 | 对不熟悉 profiling 的读者不够 |

**核心改动：加一个 §2 Background & Motivation，把"为什么"讲清楚，然后 Design 变成"因为这些需求，所以这样设计"。**
