1	\documentclass[sigconf]{acmart}
2	
3	\setcopyright{none}
4	\settopmatter{printacmref=false}
5	\renewcommand\footnotetextcopyrightpermission[1]{}
6	\pagestyle{plain}
7	
8	\usepackage{booktabs}
9	\usepackage{array}
10	\usepackage{xspace}
11	\usepackage{url}
12	\usepackage{graphicx}
13	
14	\newcommand{\toolname}{\textsc{AgentPProf}\xspace}
15	\newcommand{\operation}{\texttt{operation}\xspace}
16	\newcommand{\opstack}{\texttt{operation stack}\xspace}
17	
18	\begin{document}
19	
20	\title{AgentPProf: Semantic Profiling for AI Agent Traces}
21	
22	\begin{abstract}
23	AI agent observability tools can show every span, every LLM call, and
24	every tool invocation---but they cannot answer aggregate questions: which
25	categories of work consumed the most tokens, where do failures
26	concentrate, and how does cost distribute across task families? These
27	tools provide per-execution debugging; agent observability also needs
28	profiling.
29	
30	CPU profilers solved the equivalent problem for programs: flame graphs
31	fold millions of function calls into a single chart where width equals
32	cost. The key enabler is that function names are deterministic---identical
33	code paths produce identical stack frames that merge on contact. Agent
34	traces break this assumption. Prompts are natural language:
35	nondeterministic, variable-length, multilingual. Two prompts expressing
36	the same intent produce different strings and cannot be folded.
37	
38	\toolname restores the aggregation ability that natural-language prompts
39	break. It maps free-form prompts to stable semantic labels through
40	pluggable intent recognition, then folds agent traces into flame graphs
41	using folded-stack aggregation. The profiler retains two abstractions:
42	an \emph{operation} (a weighted record with semantic and mechanism
43	fields) and an \emph{operation stack} (a field projection chosen at
44	query time). Sessions, spans, and trace identifiers are operation fields,
45	not separate profiler objects.
46	
47	We evaluate \toolname along three research questions. On 325 real
48	Codex/Claude sessions (183{,}714 system observations), removing
49	semantic labels leaves 90.4\% of system-effect weight in mixed-intent
50	buckets; adding prompt labels reduces this to 36.7\% (RQ1). On four
51	oracle-rich public datasets (6 tasks, 34{,}539 operations, 3{,}699
52	positives), operation-stack profiling inspects 9.4\% of the work to
53	cover the top five groups versus 100\% for flat summaries, and reduces
54	median fragmentation from 285 to 158 groups; profile-spec patches
55	improve AP on 5/6 tasks (RQ2). On public datasets with ground-truth action labels, leave-dataset-out
56	mapping achieves V-measure above 0.7 on 7/9 held-out datasets, and
57	learned boundary derivation beats simple baselines on 4/5 families
58	(RQ3). Case studies on real flame graphs demonstrate
59	budget, duplication, and audit insights that timeline views cannot
60	surface.
61	\end{abstract}
62	
63	\maketitle
64	
65	%% ===================================================================
66	\section{Introduction}
67	
68	AI agent systems produce execution traces that interleave prompts, LLM
69	calls, tool invocations, GUI actions, process events, and benchmark
70	labels. As agent deployments scale to hundreds of sessions and tens of
71	thousands of calls, both developers and automated analysis agents need
72	to answer aggregate questions: which categories of work consume the most
73	tokens, where do repeated failures concentrate, and how does cost
74	distribute across semantic task families? Existing observability
75	tools---LangSmith~\cite{langsmith}, Langfuse~\cite{langfuse},
76	Phoenix~\cite{phoenix}, OpenTelemetry GenAI~\cite{otel}---organize
77	events into per-execution timelines and span trees, enabling
78	single-run debugging. But no existing tool provides an aggregate view
79	that folds heterogeneous events across sessions into a cost or frequency
80	distribution grouped by semantic work category.
81	
82	This gap has a precise analogy in traditional software. Before CPU
83	profilers, developers diagnosed performance by reading logs and
84	instrumenting individual functions. Flame graphs~\cite{flamegraphs} and
85	tools like pprof~\cite{pprof} changed the practice: they compress
86	millions of function-call samples into a single chart where width
87	represents cost, and identical call stacks merge automatically. The key
88	enabler is that function names are \emph{deterministic}---the same code
89	path always produces the same stack frames. Agent traces break this
90	assumption. Prompts are natural language: nondeterministic,
91	variable-length, and multilingual. ``Fix the bug'' and ``修一下这个
92	error'' express the same intent but share no characters. If prompt text
93	is used directly as a flame-graph frame label, every prompt becomes a
94	unique bar and no aggregation occurs. The same problem affects tool
95	calls, GUI actions, and process events, which are named heterogeneously
96	across agent families and trace formats.
97	
98	This paper presents \toolname, a profiler that restores aggregate
99	flame-graph analysis for agent traces. The core mechanism is
100	\emph{intent recognition}: mapping free-form prompts and heterogeneous
101	actions to stable semantic labels through pluggable backends (regex rules,
102	local LLM tagging, or unsupervised clustering). Once labeled, agent
103	events fold into flame graphs using the same folded-stack aggregation
104	that CPU profilers use. The profiler is built on two abstractions:
105	an \emph{operation} (a weighted record representing any measurable agent
106	activity) and an \emph{operation stack} (an ordered field projection
107	chosen at query time). Sessions, spans, and trace identifiers are
108	operation fields, not separate profiler objects; changing the stack
109	projection changes the aggregation shape without changing the underlying
110	data.
111	
112	This paper makes three contributions:
113	
114	\begin{enumerate}
115	\item \textbf{Problem: the aggregation gap.}
116	  We identify a structural gap in agent observability: existing tools
117	  provide per-execution trace debugging but not cross-session aggregate
118	  profiling. The key obstacle is that natural-language prompts lack the
119	  deterministic identifiers that enable flame-graph folding
120	  (\S\ref{sec:design}).
121	\item \textbf{Design: semantic agent profiling.}
122	  We design a profiler around two abstractions---operations and operation
123	  stacks---with pluggable intent recognition that restores flame-graph
124	  aggregation for agent traces. Four built-in views answer distinct
125	  aggregate questions about token budget, time, file access, and network
126	  activity (\S\ref{sec:design}--\S\ref{sec:impl}).
127	\item \textbf{Evaluation.}
128	  We show that semantic labels separate 90\% of system-effect weight
129	  that unsemantic views merge (RQ1), that operation-stack profiling
130	  localizes hidden labeled problems with 90\% less work than flat
131	  summaries (RQ2), and that intent recognition produces labels
132	  consistent with ground-truth annotations on 7/9 public datasets (RQ3)
133	  (\S\ref{sec:eval}).
134	\end{enumerate}
135	
136	%% ===================================================================
137	\section{Design}
138	\label{sec:design}
139	
140	\subsection{Operations and Operation Stacks}
141	
142	A CPU flame graph has two objects: a \emph{sample} (a weighted snapshot of
143	the call stack) and a \emph{stack} (the sequence of function frames).
144	\toolname adapts these to agent traces.
145	
146	An \operation is a weighted record representing one measurable activity in
147	an agent's history: a user prompt, an LLM call, a tool invocation, a file
148	read, or a network request. Each operation carries string fields
149	(\texttt{project}, \texttt{agent}, \texttt{session}, \texttt{prompt\_tag},
150	\texttt{kind}, \texttt{model}, \texttt{path}, \texttt{domain},
151	\texttt{status}, \ldots) and additive measures (token count, duration,
152	occurrence count). Different agent families and trace formats produce
153	different fields, but every entry is an operation record.
154	
155	An \opstack is an ordered list of fields chosen at query time. Folding
156	operations by that list produces the standard folded-stack representation:
157	
158	\begin{small}
159	\begin{verbatim}
160	CPU:   main;parse;tokenize          42
161	Agent: prompt:debug;call:llm;tool:bash  4200
162	\end{verbatim}
163	\end{small}
164	
165	\noindent The critical difference from CPU profiling is that the stack is
166	not determined by execution---it is chosen by the analyst or by an
167	automated analysis agent. The same operations can be folded as a flat
168	task summary, a fixed-session tree, a semantic phase/action hierarchy, or
169	a dataset-native trajectory. Changing the fields changes the aggregation
170	shape without changing the underlying operations.
171	
172	A \emph{view} is a triple $(\varphi, \sigma, w)$: a predicate $\varphi$
173	selects which operations participate, a stack function $\sigma$ maps each
174	operation to a frame sequence, and a weight function $w$ assigns a
175	nonnegative measure. Four built-in views answer four different questions:
176	
177	\begin{table}[t]
178	\centering\small
179	\caption{Built-in views. Each shares the same operation set
180	but selects different activities, stack structures, and weights.}
181	\label{tab:views}
182	\begin{tabular}{llll}
183	\toprule
184	View & $\varphi$ (select) & $w$ (width) & Question \\
185	\midrule
186	\texttt{tokens} & LLM calls & token count & Budget distribution? \\
187	\texttt{time} & All timed ops & duration (s) & Time distribution? \\
188	\texttt{files} & File-effect ops & event count & Repo coverage? \\
189	\texttt{network} & Net-effect ops & event count & External contacts? \\
190	\bottomrule
191	\end{tabular}
192	\end{table}
193	
194	Sessions and spans deserve explicit discussion. In existing observability
195	tools, sessions and spans define the fixed hierarchy. In \toolname, they
196	are optional operation fields. An analyst can include \texttt{session} in
197	the stack (producing a per-session drilldown equivalent to a trace tree),
198	or exclude it (producing a cross-session aggregate that no trace tool
199	provides). This is the design's central point: the same data supports
200	both debugging and profiling views, selected at query time.
201	
202	\begin{figure}[t]
203	\centering
204	% \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig-architecture.pdf}
205	\fbox{\parbox{0.93\linewidth}{\centering\small
206	[Architecture: Agent trace files (Codex/Claude JSONL, benchmark JSONL)
207	$\to$ Parser / Importer $\to$ Intent Recognition (regex / LLM / clustering)
208	or Mapping Rules $\to$ Operations with fields $\to$ Stack query
209	$(\varphi, \sigma, w)$ $\to$ Folded stacks $\to$ Flame graph / pprof /
210	JSON]}}
211	\caption{System architecture. Local agent histories enter through
212	\texttt{agent-session} parsing; public datasets enter as operation JSONL.
213	Both paths produce operations; the stack query and output are identical.}
214	\Description{Data flow from agent traces through parsing and intent
215	recognition to folded-stack flame graphs.}
216	\label{fig:architecture}
217	\end{figure}
218	
219	\subsection{Intent Recognition: From Prompts to Labels}
220	
221	Operations and stacks are conventional engineering; the hard problem is
222	\emph{intent recognition}. A flame graph requires short, stable,
223	repeatable frame labels. Function names provide this for CPU profiles.
224	Agent prompts do not: they are free-form, multilingual, variable-length,
225	and often contain sensitive content.
226	
227	\toolname provides a pluggable tagger framework with three backends:
228	
229	\paragraph{Regex rules with agent-assisted iteration.}
230	The production default. Rules have the form
231	\texttt{KIND:TAG=REGEX}, where \texttt{KIND} is \texttt{prompt},
232	\texttt{llm}, or \texttt{all}, \texttt{TAG} is a short lowercase label,
233	and \texttt{REGEX} is a pattern. Rules are evaluated in order; the first
234	match wins. The workflow is human--agent collaborative: run \toolname,
235	observe the unmatched rate and sample prompts, add rules, re-run, and
236	iterate until unmatched drops below 5\%. This typically takes 5--10
237	rounds. The resulting rule set is deterministic, reproducible, and
238	version-controllable.
239	
240	\paragraph{Local LLM tagger.}
241	For exploration or complex multilingual prompts, a local model
242	(e.g., a 3B-parameter GGUF via llama.cpp) generates a single-word label
243	per prompt. Grammar-constrained decoding ensures output validity.
244	Labels are cached; re-runs with unchanged prompts incur zero LLM calls.
245	
246	\paragraph{Unsupervised clustering.}
247	TF-IDF vectorization followed by K-Means discovers natural prompt groups
248	without predefined rules, feeding rule authoring.
249	
250	The one-word label design is deliberate. Flame-graph frames must be
251	short; long summaries make charts unreadable. Labels serve navigation
252	and aggregation, not correctness verdicts.
253	
254	\subsection{Mapping for Structured Traces}
255	
256	For public benchmark datasets and structured trace formats, prompts are
257	already structured: action types, tool names, environment labels, and
258	quality annotations are explicit fields. \toolname supports deterministic
259	\emph{mapping rules} that derive new operation fields from existing ones
260	before stack construction. A \emph{profile spec} records the complete
261	analysis configuration---data sources, mappings, predicates, stack
262	fields, and outputs---for deterministic replay.
263	
264	This dual path explains why \toolname handles both real agent sessions
265	(which need intent recognition) and public benchmark traces (which need
266	mapping rules): both paths produce operations with fields, and the
267	stack query works identically on both.
268	
269	%% ===================================================================
270	\section{Implementation}
271	\label{sec:impl}
272	
273	\toolname is implemented as a Rust CLI (Figure~\ref{fig:architecture}).
274	
275	\paragraph{Trace parsing.}
276	The \texttt{agent-session} crate reads Codex and Claude Code local JSONL
277	history files and reconstructs prompts, LLM calls, tool invocations, and
278	their triggered file and network effects. Each prompt opens a span; LLM
279	calls, tool calls, and system effects within that span inherit its
280	semantic label. This span-based inheritance is how the profiler connects
281	semantic intent to system behavior without requiring runtime
282	instrumentation.
283	
284	\paragraph{Dataset import.}
285	Public benchmark datasets enter as operation JSONL. Mapping rules
286	(inline or via profile spec) derive fields before stack construction.
287	Standard Chrome Trace Event format can also be imported, with
288	non-\toolname protocol fields preserved as operation fields.
289	
290	\paragraph{Output formats.}
291	\toolname produces pprof protobuf (compatible with
292	\texttt{go tool pprof -http} for interactive exploration), folded-stack
293	text (compatible with Brendan Gregg's \texttt{flamegraph.pl}), standalone
294	SVG flame graphs, and JSON summaries. All outputs are deterministic given
295	the same input and profile spec.
296	
297	\paragraph{Relationship to AgentSight.}
298	\toolname is the offline profiling component of the AgentSight
299	observability framework. AgentSight provides real-time eBPF-based
300	capture of SSL traffic, process events, and file/network effects;
301	\toolname aggregates the recorded traces into semantic profiles. The two
302	tools are complementary: AgentSight answers ``what happened during this
303	run'' (debugging); \toolname answers ``where did the budget go across
304	runs'' (profiling).
305	
306	%% ===================================================================
307	\section{Evaluation}
308	\label{sec:eval}
309	
310	We organize the evaluation around three research questions, followed by
311	case studies and a reproducibility check.
312	
313	\paragraph{Evaluation setup.}
314	We use two classes of data. \emph{Real agent sessions}: 325 readable
315	local sessions (198~Codex, 50~Claude, 77~Claude subagent) from a
316	multi-month development project, containing 183{,}714 system
317	observations. \emph{Public labeled traces}: 15 families covering web,
318	mobile, desktop, software, API, and dialogue agents
319	(Table~\ref{tab:datasets}), totaling 47{,}590 operations through
320	mapping rules. All public traces are real agent or human executions
321	collected and labeled by their respective benchmark projects. Four
322	oracle-rich families (AgentRewardBench, SATraj-OS, AgentNet,
323	OSWorld-Human) provide hidden ground-truth labels for RQ2. No source
324	requires a type-specific profiler object: the same 13{,}265 operations
325	fold into 9~dataset stacks through 3{,}757~fixed-session stacks by
326	changing only the stack fields.
327	
328	\begin{table*}[t]
329	\centering\small
330	\caption{Public labeled trace families. All traces are real agent or
331	human executions. The bottom four rows provide oracle labels for RQ2.}
332	\label{tab:datasets}
333	\begin{tabular}{p{0.17\linewidth}p{0.22\linewidth}p{0.15\linewidth}p{0.17\linewidth}p{0.17\linewidth}}
334	\toprule
335	Family & Native labels & Access & Trace origin & Eval.\ role \\
336	\midrule
337	WebLINX, Mind2Web, AgentTrek, WebShop & Web actions, tasks, rewards & HF / public & Real web agents & Coverage \\
338	API-Bank, ToolBench, tau-bench & API calls, outcomes & HF / JSONL & Real API agents & Coverage \\
339	SWE-agent & Issue trajectories & HF viewer & Real coding agent & Coverage \\
340	AndroidCtrl, GUI-Odyssey, ScaleCUA & Mobile/GUI actions & Public/HF & Real mobile agents & Coverage \\
341	\midrule
342	AgentRewardBench & Success, side-effect, looping & HF annotations & Real BrowserGym agents & RQ2 tasks \\
343	SATraj-OS & Safety, reward, attack type & HF config & Real desktop agents & RQ2 task \\

347	\end{tabular}

349	
350	%% -------------------------------------------------------------------
351	\subsection{RQ1: Does Semantic Profiling Separate What Flat Views Mix?}
352	
353	The strongest argument against semantic profiling is that traditional
354	tools ``can already see the same information.'' RQ1 tests this claim
355	directly by measuring how much system-effect weight falls into
356	\emph{mixed-intent} buckets---buckets containing observations from
357	multiple semantic regions---under different projection choices.
358	
359	\begin{table}[t]
360	\centering\small
361	\caption{Semantic-axis ablation on 183{,}714 system observations
362	from 325 real sessions. All rows preserve the same total weight.}
363	\label{tab:mixing}
364	\begin{tabular}{lrrr}
365	\toprule
366	Projection & Unique stacks & Mixed wt.\% & Residual\% \\
367	\midrule
368	No semantic labels & 11{,}967 & 90.4 & 44.7 \\
369	Session label only & 15{,}027 & 84.4 & 33.4 \\
370	Prompt label only & 24{,}703 & 36.7 & 7.5 \\
371	Session + prompt & 26{,}829 & 0.0 & 0.0 \\
372	\bottomrule
373	\end{tabular}
374	\end{table}
375	
376	Table~\ref{tab:mixing} shows the result on 325 real Codex/Claude
377	sessions. Without semantic labels, 90.4\% of system-effect weight falls
378	into mixed buckets: a flat \texttt{cargo~test} counter shows 2{,}903
379	executions but cannot distinguish whether they came from
380	\texttt{review}, \texttt{debug}, \texttt{refactor}, or \texttt{test}
381	prompts. Adding only the prompt label reduces mixed weight to 36.7\% and
382	residual to 7.5\%. The session label alone barely helps (84.4\%), because
383	sessions typically contain multiple intent phases.
384	
385	A concrete example: \texttt{process:cargo; effect:test; status:ok}
386	appears under 48 distinct prompt tags. The top tag (\texttt{refactor})
387	accounts for only 32.0\%; the remaining 68.0\% comes from
388	\texttt{review}, \texttt{research}, \texttt{test}, \texttt{explain}, and
389	others. A flat summary or process audit merges all of these.
390	
391	A label-permutation test (1{,}000 shuffles within each session) confirms
392	the separation is not random: real tags achieve 8.4\% session-beyond
393	information gain versus a null p95 of 1.9\% ($p = 0.001$).
394	
395	The multi-view design is also validated by metric divergence. The
396	\texttt{time} and \texttt{tokens} views of the same sessions share
397	only 7/10 top prompt categories (Spearman $\rho = 0.623$).
398	\texttt{network}-tagged prompts rank 8th by time (I/O wait) but 93rd by
399	tokens. This confirms that different views answer structurally different
400	questions over the same operations.
401	
402	%% -------------------------------------------------------------------
403	\subsection{RQ2: Can Profiler Groups Localize Hidden Labeled Problems?}
404	
405	RQ2 evaluates whether operation-stack profiling can localize
406	ground-truth-labeled problems in real agent traces. The evaluation
407	methodology is analogous to injecting known bottlenecks in CPU profiler
408	evaluation: public benchmark datasets provide ground-truth labels
409	(failure, safety violation, redundant step, human-task boundary); we
410	hide these labels, run the profiler, rank the resulting groups, and
411	check whether the top groups contain the hidden positives.
412	
413	\paragraph{Benchmark setup.}
414	Six tasks across four datasets: AgentRewardBench looping and
415	side-effect, SATraj-OS unsafe operation, AgentNet incorrect and redundant
416	step, and OSWorld-Human group start. Together: 34{,}539 operations,
417	3{,}699 positives. Six views (flat, fixed-session, dataset-native,
418	raw-action, operation-stack, label-drilldown) and four rankers (width,
419	visible-risk, query-aware, oracle).
420	
421	\paragraph{Localization results.}
422	
423	\begin{table*}[t]
424	\centering\small
425	\caption{RQ2 hidden-label localization (medians across six tasks).
426	Hidden policies serve only as upper bounds. WTFP = work-to-first-positive.}
427	\label{tab:localization}
428	\begin{tabular}{lrrrrrrrr}
429	\toprule
430	Policy & Hidden & AP & R@5 & F1@5 & Work@5 & R@30\% & WTFP & Groups \\
431	\midrule
432	flat:width & 0 & 0.168 & 1.000 & 0.287 & 1.000 & 0.000 & 1.000 & 1.0 \\
433	fixed-session:query-aware & 0 & 0.348 & 0.023 & 0.043 & 0.016 & 0.356 & 0.004 & 285.0 \\
434	dataset-native:query-aware & 0 & 0.357 & 0.867 & 0.282 & 0.854 & 0.338 & 0.058 & --- \\
435	raw-action:query-aware & 0 & 0.274 & 0.244 & 0.220 & 0.151 & 0.333 & 0.037 & --- \\
436	op-stack:query-aware & 0 & 0.312 & 0.188 & 0.198 & 0.094 & 0.390 & 0.038 & 157.5 \\
437	op-stack:oracle-upper & 1 & 0.599 & 0.300 & 0.403 & 0.044 & 0.564 & 0.012 & --- \\
438	label-drilldown:oracle & 1 & 1.000 & 0.670 & 0.797 & 0.115 & 1.000 & 0.038 & --- \\
439	\bottomrule
440	\end{tabular}
441	\end{table*}
442	
443	Table~\ref{tab:localization} summarizes the results. Flat summaries
444	recover all positives but require inspecting everything
445	(Work@5\,=\,1.0). Fixed-session drilldown finds a first positive quickly
446	(WTFP\,=\,0.004) but fragments the workload into 285 groups with only
447	2.3\% top-five recall. Operation-stack query-aware profiling inspects
448	9.4\% of the work in the top five groups, achieves 39.0\% budget-30
449	recall, and reduces groups to 157.5.
450	
451	The result is a Pareto tradeoff, not dominance. Operation stacks improve
452	top-five recall over fixed-session drilldown on 5/6 tasks, reduce
453	median group count by 45\%, and save 90\% of inspection work versus flat
454	summaries. Fixed-session drilldown retains lower
455	work-to-first-positive on 4/6 tasks: profilers and debuggers are
456	complementary. Bootstrap (10{,}000 resamples) and label-permutation
457	(2{,}000 trials) confirm stable AP deltas exceeding the 95\%
458	prevalence/group-size null on all six tasks.
459	
460	\paragraph{Actionability: which configuration knobs explain the results?}
461	
462	Executable profile-spec patches modify stack fields, mapping rules, or
463	rankers, then re-run over the same visible operations. Five of six
464	patches improve AP, top-five lift, and first-positive work (median AP
465	delta 0.038, median top-five lift delta 0.575). Three reusable patterns
466	emerge: (1)~safety/side-effect tasks benefit from field and ranker
467	changes; (2)~step-quality tasks benefit from operation-stack
468	localization followed by fixed-session drilldown for examples;
469	(3)~human-boundary tasks require boundary-derived fields. The rejected
470	OSWorld-Human patch shows that visible rank features alone are
471	insufficient for boundary objectives; folding held-out boundary-derived
472	fields improves AP from 0.240 to 0.258 and reduces groups from 108 to
473	74, with an explicit work tradeoff.
474	
475	Rank-feature ablations identify 7 critical feature rows
476	(\texttt{repeat\_signal}, write-action, \texttt{status=success}) and 3
477	misleading rows. Guided repairs improve AP on 2/3 misleading cases but
478	use offline scored feedback, not an automatic learned ranker.
479	
480	%% -------------------------------------------------------------------
481	\subsection{RQ3: How Reliable Is Intent Recognition?}
482	
483	RQ1 and RQ2 assume that semantic labels are useful. RQ3 tests the
484	intent-recognition mechanism itself: can the tagger backends produce
485	labels that are consistent with ground-truth annotations and with each
486	other?
487	
488	\paragraph{Scale and syntax validity.}
489	On 325 real sessions, the LLM tagger processes 118{,}021 tag requests
490	(2{,}859 prompt rows, 114{,}837 LLM-call events). Of these, 82{,}886
491	hit the label cache; 35{,}136 are real llama.cpp calls to a local
492	3B-parameter model. Final tag failures: 0. On a fixed set of 300
493	redacted fragments, three model sizes (0.6B, 1.1B, 3B) all produce
494	900/900 syntactically valid outputs; p95 latencies are 23, 18, and
495	31\,ms respectively.
496	
497	\paragraph{Ground-truth agreement on public datasets.}
498	Public benchmark datasets provide native action labels that serve as
499	ground truth for mapping quality. We run a leave-dataset-out evaluation:
500	for each of 9 datasets, we train mapping rules on the other 8 and
501	measure V-measure between the mapping-derived \texttt{phase} field and
502	the dataset's native \texttt{action} labels, plus boundary F1 between
503	mapped phase boundaries and native action boundaries.
504	
505	\begin{table}[t]
506	\centering\small
507	\caption{Leave-dataset-out mapping quality. V-measure between
508	mapping-derived \texttt{phase} and native \texttt{action} labels.
509	13{,}265 total operations across 9 held-out evaluations.}
510	\label{tab:vmeasure}
511	\begin{tabular}{lrrr}
512	\toprule
513	Held-out dataset & Ops & V-measure & Boundary F1 \\
514	\midrule
515	mind2web & 774 & 1.000 & 1.000 \\
516	webshop-expert & 2{,}504 & 1.000 & 1.000 \\
517	swe-agent & 496 & 0.926 & 0.962 \\
518	weblinx-chat & 500 & 0.872 & 0.860 \\
519	agenttrek & 200 & 0.862 & --- \\
520	gui-odyssey & 7{,}868 & 0.811 & 0.842 \\
521	android-control & 9 & 0.716 & 0.727 \\
522	toolbench & 866 & 0.134 & 0.353 \\
523	api-bank & 48 & 0.000 & --- \\
524	\bottomrule
525	\end{tabular}
526	\end{table}
527	
528	Table~\ref{tab:vmeasure} shows the results. On 7/9 datasets, V-measure
529	exceeds 0.7, indicating strong agreement between mapping-derived and
530	native labels. The two low-scoring datasets (toolbench, api-bank) have
531	atypical action vocabularies that the held-out mapping rules do not
532	cover. Mapping reduces unique stacks on 6/9 datasets with zero negative
533	regressions.
534	
535	A supervised boundary-derivation backend further validates the field
536	pipeline. On OSWorld-Human held-out adjacent pairs, a learned boundary
537	predictor achieves F1~0.77, beating the best simple baseline
538	(\texttt{always\_boundary}, F1~0.71). Learned backends beat simple
539	baselines on 4/5 tested boundary families, while AgentRewardBench
540	looping is fully explained by \texttt{repeat\_signal\_change} (baseline
541	F1~1.0). This supports field derivation as a guarded configuration
542	step, not automatic intent discovery.
543	
544	\paragraph{Cross-backend consistency.}
545	\textbf{[TODO: run regex and LLM taggers on the same public-dataset
546	operations and measure inter-backend agreement. This experiment does not
547	yet exist in the artifact set.]}
548	
549	\paragraph{Semantic quality versus syntactic validity.}
550	Syntactic validity does not imply semantic quality. TinyLlama 1.1B
551	achieves high exact-stability (279/300 identical across repeats) but
552	concentrates on a narrow label set, outputting
553	\texttt{localization}/\texttt{localized} disproportionately. The 3B
554	model produces a broader vocabulary (328 unique prompt tags) but includes
555	noisy entries (\texttt{agentsightsm}, \texttt{testcodex}). A
556	display-governance pipeline reduces unique tags from 1{,}546 to 1{,}364
557	through deterministic aliases, raising top-20 support coverage from
558	93.7\% to 95.2\% without overwriting raw tags. This pipeline manages
559	noise but does not establish semantic adequacy---that is what the
560	ground-truth and cross-backend checks above provide.
561	
562	%% -------------------------------------------------------------------
563	\subsection{Case Studies}
564	
565	We profile the same 325-session development project and report four
566	representative observations that illustrate the kind of aggregate
567	insights semantic flame graphs surface.
568	
569	\paragraph{Budget distribution.}
570	The \texttt{tokens} view (Figure~\ref{fig:flamegraphs}) reveals that
571	\texttt{review}-tagged prompts dominate the model budget, followed by
572	\texttt{git}, \texttt{code}, \texttt{edit}, and \texttt{debug}. A
573	timeline of 80{,}000 individual LLM calls cannot produce this
574	distribution without external aggregation. The stack further decomposes
575	each category: under \texttt{prompt:review}, the dominant sub-frames are
576	\texttt{call:llm/code} and \texttt{call:llm/tool}.
577	
578	\paragraph{Cross-session duplication.}
579	The \texttt{files} view shows \texttt{debug}-tagged prompts across
580	different sessions repeatedly accessing the same source files under
581	\texttt{collector/src/}. The flame graph aggregates these into a single
582	wide bar; a timeline shows each as an isolated event.
583	
584	\paragraph{Metric divergence.}
585	The \texttt{time} and \texttt{tokens} views share only 7/10 top prompt
586	categories. \texttt{network}-tagged prompts rank 8th by time (I/O wait)
587	but 93rd by tokens; \texttt{benchmark} prompts show the reverse.
588	
589	\paragraph{Path and network auditing.}
590	The \texttt{network} view attributes domain contacts to prompt
591	categories (\texttt{anthropic.com}, \texttt{crates.io},
592	\texttt{github.com}). The \texttt{files} view identifies accesses
593	outside the project root (\texttt{external/home},
594	\texttt{external/tmp}), supporting security auditing.
595	
596	\begin{figure}[t]
597	\centering
598	% \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/flamegraph-tokens.png}
599	\fbox{\parbox{0.93\linewidth}{\centering\small
600	[Flame-graph screenshots: tokens view (top) and files view (bottom)
601	showing budget distribution and file-access patterns across sessions]}}
602	\caption{Real flame graphs from a development project.
603	Top: \texttt{tokens} view (width = token count).
604	Bottom: \texttt{files} view (width = file-operation count).}
605	\Description{Two flame graphs showing token budget and file access
606	distribution across semantic prompt categories.}
607	\label{fig:flamegraphs}
608	\end{figure}
609	
610	%% -------------------------------------------------------------------
611	\subsection{Reproducibility}
612	
613	All results are backed by profile specs for deterministic replay. We
614	re-execute 76 tracked specs twice (152 invocations); all produce
615	identical semantic output. Median runtime: 1.6\,s per spec (p95:
616	2.8\,s). Deterministic-output mode stabilizes raw-byte output: 76/76
617	achieve both semantic and raw-byte determinism.
618	
619	%% ===================================================================
620	\section{Related Work}
621	
622	\textbf{Profiling and flame graphs.}
623	Flame graphs~\cite{flamegraphs} and pprof~\cite{pprof} establish the
624	folded-stack lineage: profiles are weighted samples with location
625	hierarchies. Pprof supports sample labels and can visualize them as
626	pseudo stack frames through tag-root/tag-leaf options. Perfetto
627	generalizes trace ingestion with SQL-based analysis and derived
628	events~\cite{perfetto}. These systems support query-time aggregation, so
629	\toolname does not claim novelty for flexible aggregation alone. The
630	difference is the domain: samples are agent operations, frames are
631	semantic labels derived from natural-language prompts through intent
632	recognition, and the evaluation scores profiler output against hidden
633	agent-trajectory labels.
634	
635	\textbf{Agent tracing and LLM observability.}
636	OpenTelemetry GenAI and OpenInference standardize GenAI
637	spans~\cite{otel, openinference}. LangSmith~\cite{langsmith},
638	Langfuse~\cite{langfuse}, and Phoenix~\cite{phoenix} provide trace
639	visualization, session management, evaluations, and dashboards.
640	AgentOps~\cite{agentops} argues for structured agent observability
641	covering goals, plans, tools, and artifacts. These systems excel at
642	single-execution debugging: timeline views, span trees, and waterfall
643	charts help locate a specific failure. \toolname complements them with
644	cross-session aggregate profiling.
645	Datadog LLM Observability adds topic clustering over user messages, and
646	Laminar Signals extracts structured events from traces. These are steps
647	toward semantic aggregation, but they characterize \emph{input
648	distributions} (``30\% of users ask code questions''), not
649	\emph{resource attribution} (``code-review tasks consume 40\% of the
650	token budget''). \toolname produces the latter through folded-stack
651	aggregation where width represents cost.
652	
653	\textbf{Agent failure diagnosis.}
654	AgentRx~\cite{agentrx} releases annotated failure trajectories and uses
655	constraint checking plus an LLM judge for root-cause localization.
656	TELBench~\cite{telbench} builds span-localization benchmarks from
657	semantic error annotations. AgentAtlas argues that outcome leaderboards
658	miss trajectory-level quality. These systems perform \emph{span-level}
659	fault localization within a single execution: which step failed and why.
660	\toolname performs \emph{category-level} aggregate profiling: which
661	categories of work produce the most failures, consume the most budget,
662	or generate repeated system effects across sessions.
663	
664	%% ===================================================================
665	\section{Discussion}
666	
667	\paragraph{Profiler and debugger are complementary.}
668	Fixed-session drilldown finds a first positive faster on 4/6 tasks
669	(RQ2). This is expected: debuggers are designed for single-case
670	investigation. The profiler identifies \emph{which categories} deserve
671	attention; the debugger explains \emph{what happened} in a specific
672	case. \toolname supports both by including or excluding session fields in
673	the stack query. A typical workflow starts with the profiler (``review
674	tasks dominate the budget''), then drills into individual sessions to
675	understand why.
676	
677	\paragraph{Agent-as-consumer.}
678	The profiler's structured output (JSON, pprof, folded stacks) is
679	designed to be consumed by automated analysis agents, not only human
680	developers. The RQ2 ranker strategies demonstrate this pattern: a
681	scoring policy reads profiler output, ranks groups by visible features,
682	and identifies high-cost or high-failure categories. In practice, an AI
683	coding agent can run \texttt{agentpprof --format json}, parse the output,
684	and recommend configuration changes---the same workflow that the
685	regex-rule iteration (\S\ref{sec:design}) already uses. This positions
686	semantic profiling as infrastructure for agent self-diagnosis, not only
687	for human inspection.
688	
689	\paragraph{Limitations.}
690	The real-session data (RQ1, RQ3, case studies) comes from one developer
691	on one project. RQ2 mitigates this with four independent public datasets
692	containing real agent traces from different research groups, but
693	multi-project and multi-user real-session evaluation would strengthen the
694	generality claim. The evaluation measures label-scored profiler fidelity,
695	not human or agent productivity. A controlled study comparing
696	flame-graph-guided diagnosis against timeline-based diagnosis would test
697	the practical value but is not required for the profiler-mechanism
698	contribution. \toolname currently reads Codex/Claude local histories and
699	operation JSONL; OpenTelemetry, LangSmith, and Langfuse trace imports are
700	engineering work, not design obstacles.
701	
702	%% ===================================================================
703	\section{Conclusion}
704	
705	\toolname reduces agent profiling to two abstractions. Operations carry
706	semantic and mechanism fields; operation stacks fold those fields at a
707	depth chosen by the query. Intent recognition---through regex rules, a
708	local LLM, or clustering---restores the deterministic-label precondition
709	that makes flame-graph aggregation work for natural-language agent
710	traces.
711	
712	Semantic labels separate 90\% of system-effect weight that flat
713	summaries merge (RQ1). Operation-stack profiling localizes hidden labeled
714	problems with 90\% less inspection work than flat summaries and 45\% less
715	fragmentation than fixed-session drilldown, with actionable
716	configuration diagnosis (RQ2). Intent recognition produces labels that agree with ground-truth
717	annotations on 7/9 public datasets (V-measure ${>}0.7$), with learned
718	boundary derivation beating simple baselines on 4/5 families (RQ3). Case
719	studies show budget, duplication, and audit insights invisible to
720	timeline views.

\title{AgentPProf: Semantic Profiling for AI Agent Traces}

\begin{abstract}
AI agent observability tools can show every span, every LLM call, and
every tool invocation---but they cannot answer aggregate questions: which
categories of work consumed the most tokens, where do failures
concentrate, and how does cost distribute across task families? These
tools provide per-execution debugging; agent observability also needs
profiling.

CPU profilers solved the equivalent problem for programs: flame graphs
fold millions of function calls into a single chart where width equals
cost. The key enabler is that function names are deterministic---identical
code paths produce identical stack frames that merge on contact. Agent
traces break this assumption. Prompts are natural language:
nondeterministic, variable-length, multilingual. Two prompts expressing
the same intent produce different strings and cannot be folded.

\toolname restores the aggregation ability that natural-language prompts
break. It maps free-form prompts to stable semantic labels through
pluggable intent recognition, then folds agent traces into flame graphs
using folded-stack aggregation. The profiler retains two abstractions:
an \emph{operation} (a weighted record with semantic and mechanism
fields) and an \emph{operation stack} (a field projection chosen at
query time). Sessions, spans, and trace identifiers are operation fields,
not separate profiler objects.

We evaluate \toolname along three research questions. On 325 real
Codex/Claude sessions (183{,}714 system observations), removing
semantic labels leaves 90.4\% of system-effect weight in mixed-intent
buckets; adding prompt labels reduces this to 36.7\% (RQ1). On four
oracle-rich public datasets (6 tasks, 34{,}539 operations, 3{,}699
positives), operation-stack profiling inspects 9.4\% of the work to
cover the top five groups versus 100\% for flat summaries, and reduces
median fragmentation from 285 to 158 groups; profile-spec patches
improve AP on 5/6 tasks (RQ2). On public datasets with ground-truth action labels, leave-dataset-out
mapping achieves V-measure above 0.7 on 7/9 held-out datasets, and
learned boundary derivation beats simple baselines on 4/5 families
(RQ3). Case studies on real flame graphs demonstrate
budget, duplication, and audit insights that timeline views cannot
surface.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}

AI agent systems produce execution traces that interleave prompts, LLM
calls, tool invocations, GUI actions, process events, and benchmark
labels. As agent deployments scale to hundreds of sessions and tens of
thousands of calls, both developers and automated analysis agents need
to answer aggregate questions: which categories of work consume the most
tokens, where do repeated failures concentrate, and how does cost
distribute across semantic task families? Existing observability
tools---LangSmith~\cite{langsmith}, Langfuse~\cite{langfuse},
Phoenix~\cite{phoenix}, OpenTelemetry GenAI~\cite{otel}---organize
events into per-execution timelines and span trees, enabling
single-run debugging. But no existing tool provides an aggregate view
that folds heterogeneous events across sessions into a cost or frequency
distribution grouped by semantic work category.

This gap has a precise analogy in traditional software. Before CPU
profilers, developers diagnosed performance by reading logs and
instrumenting individual functions. Flame graphs~\cite{flamegraphs} and
tools like pprof~\cite{pprof} changed the practice: they compress
millions of function-call samples into a single chart where width
represents cost, and identical call stacks merge automatically. The key
enabler is that function names are \emph{deterministic}---the same code
path always produces the same stack frames. Agent traces break this
assumption. Prompts are natural language: nondeterministic,
variable-length, and multilingual. ``Fix the bug'' and ``修一下这个
error'' express the same intent but share no characters. If prompt text
is used directly as a flame-graph frame label, every prompt becomes a
unique bar and no aggregation occurs. The same problem affects tool
calls, GUI actions, and process events, which are named heterogeneously
across agent families and trace formats.

This paper presents \toolname, a profiler that restores aggregate
flame-graph analysis for agent traces. The core mechanism is
\emph{intent recognition}: mapping free-form prompts and heterogeneous
actions to stable semantic labels through pluggable backends (regex rules,
local LLM tagging, or unsupervised clustering). Once labeled, agent
events fold into flame graphs using the same folded-stack aggregation
that CPU profilers use. The profiler is built on two abstractions:
an \emph{operation} (a weighted record representing any measurable agent
activity) and an \emph{operation stack} (an ordered field projection
chosen at query time). Sessions, spans, and trace identifiers are
operation fields, not separate profiler objects; changing the stack
projection changes the aggregation shape without changing the underlying
data.

This paper makes three contributions:

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Problem: the aggregation gap.}
  We identify a structural gap in agent observability: existing tools
  provide per-execution trace debugging but not cross-session aggregate
  profiling. The key obstacle is that natural-language prompts lack the
  deterministic identifiers that enable flame-graph folding
  (\S\ref{sec:design}).
\item \textbf{Design: semantic agent profiling.}
  We design a profiler around two abstractions---operations and operation
  stacks---with pluggable intent recognition that restores flame-graph
  aggregation for agent traces. Four built-in views answer distinct
  aggregate questions about token budget, time, file access, and network
  activity (\S\ref{sec:design}--\S\ref{sec:impl}).
\item \textbf{Evaluation.}
  We show that semantic labels separate 90\% of system-effect weight
  that unsemantic views merge (RQ1), that operation-stack profiling
  localizes hidden labeled problems with 90\% less work than flat
  summaries (RQ2), and that intent recognition produces labels
  consistent with ground-truth annotations on 7/9 public datasets (RQ3)
  (\S\ref{sec:eval}).
\end{enumerate}

\section{Design}
\label{sec:design}

\subsection{Operations and Operation Stacks}

A CPU flame graph has two objects: a \emph{sample} (a weighted snapshot of
the call stack) and a \emph{stack} (the sequence of function frames).
\toolname adapts these to agent traces.

An \operation is a weighted record representing one measurable activity in
an agent's history: a user prompt, an LLM call, a tool invocation, a file
read, or a network request. Each operation carries string fields
(\texttt{project}, \texttt{agent}, \texttt{session}, \texttt{prompt\_tag},
\texttt{kind}, \texttt{model}, \texttt{path}, \texttt{domain},
\texttt{status}, \ldots) and additive measures (token count, duration,
occurrence count). Different agent families and trace formats produce
different fields, but every entry is an operation record.

An \opstack is an ordered list of fields chosen at query time. Folding
operations by that list produces the standard folded-stack representation:

\begin{small}
\begin{verbatim}
CPU:   main;parse;tokenize          42
Agent: prompt:debug;call:llm;tool:bash  4200
\end{verbatim}
\end{small}

\noindent The critical difference from CPU profiling is that the stack is
not determined by execution---it is chosen by the analyst or by an
automated analysis agent. The same operations can be folded as a flat
task summary, a fixed-session tree, a semantic phase/action hierarchy, or
a dataset-native trajectory. Changing the fields changes the aggregation
shape without changing the underlying operations.

A \emph{view} is a triple $(\varphi, \sigma, w)$: a predicate $\varphi$
selects which operations participate, a stack function $\sigma$ maps each
operation to a frame sequence, and a weight function $w$ assigns a
nonnegative measure. Four built-in views answer four different questions:

\begin{table}[t]
\centering\small
\caption{Built-in views. Each shares the same operation set
but selects different activities, stack structures, and weights.}
\label{tab:views}
\begin{tabular}{llll}
\toprule
View & $\varphi$ (select) & $w$ (width) & Question \\
\midrule
\texttt{tokens} & LLM calls & token count & Budget distribution? \\
\texttt{time} & All timed ops & duration (s) & Time distribution? \\
\texttt{files} & File-effect ops & event count & Repo coverage? \\
\texttt{network} & Net-effect ops & event count & External contacts? \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Sessions and spans deserve explicit discussion. In existing observability
tools, sessions and spans define the fixed hierarchy. In \toolname, they
are optional operation fields. An analyst can include \texttt{session} in
the stack (producing a per-session drilldown equivalent to a trace tree),
or exclude it (producing a cross-session aggregate that no trace tool
provides). This is the design's central point: the same data supports
both debugging and profiling views, selected at query time.

\subsection{Intent Recognition: From Prompts to Labels}

Operations and stacks are conventional engineering; the hard problem is
\emph{intent recognition}. A flame graph requires short, stable,
repeatable frame labels. Function names provide this for CPU profiles.
Agent prompts do not: they are free-form, multilingual, variable-length,
and often contain sensitive content.

\toolname provides a pluggable tagger framework with three backends:

\paragraph{Regex rules with agent-assisted iteration.}
The production default. Rules have the form
\texttt{KIND:TAG=REGEX}, where \texttt{KIND} is \texttt{prompt},
\texttt{llm}, or \texttt{all}, \texttt{TAG} is a short lowercase label,
and \texttt{REGEX} is a pattern. Rules are evaluated in order; the first
match wins. The workflow is human--agent collaborative: run \toolname,
observe the unmatched rate and sample prompts, add rules, re-run, and
iterate until unmatched drops below 5\%. This typically takes 5--10
rounds. The resulting rule set is deterministic, reproducible, and
version-controllable.

\paragraph{Local LLM tagger.}
For exploration or complex multilingual prompts, a local model
(e.g., a 3B-parameter GGUF via llama.cpp) generates a single-word label
per prompt. Grammar-constrained decoding ensures output validity.
Labels are cached; re-runs with unchanged prompts incur zero LLM calls.

\paragraph{Unsupervised clustering.}
TF-IDF vectorization followed by K-Means discovers natural prompt groups
without predefined rules, feeding rule authoring.

The one-word label design is deliberate. Flame-graph frames must be
short; long summaries make charts unreadable. Labels serve navigation
and aggregation, not correctness verdicts.

\subsection{Mapping for Structured Traces}

For public benchmark datasets and structured trace formats, prompts are
already structured: action types, tool names, environment labels, and
quality annotations are explicit fields. \toolname supports deterministic
\emph{mapping rules} that derive new operation fields from existing ones
before stack construction. A \emph{profile spec} records the complete
analysis configuration---data sources, mappings, predicates, stack
fields, and outputs---for deterministic replay.

This dual path explains why \toolname handles both real agent sessions
(which need intent recognition) and public benchmark traces (which need
mapping rules): both paths produce operations with fields, and the
stack query works identically on both.

\section{Implementation}
\label{sec:impl}

\toolname is implemented as a Rust CLI (Figure~\ref{fig:architecture}).

\paragraph{Trace parsing.}
The \texttt{agent-session} crate reads Codex and Claude Code local JSONL
history files and reconstructs prompts, LLM calls, tool invocations, and
their triggered file and network effects. Each prompt opens a span; LLM
calls, tool calls, and system effects within that span inherit its
semantic label. This span-based inheritance is how the profiler connects
semantic intent to system behavior without requiring runtime
instrumentation.

\paragraph{Dataset import.}
Public benchmark datasets enter as operation JSONL. Mapping rules
(inline or via profile spec) derive fields before stack construction.
Standard Chrome Trace Event format can also be imported, with
non-\toolname protocol fields preserved as operation fields.

\paragraph{Output formats.}
\toolname produces pprof protobuf (compatible with
\texttt{go tool pprof -http} for interactive exploration), folded-stack
text (compatible with Brendan Gregg's \texttt{flamegraph.pl}), standalone
SVG flame graphs, and JSON summaries. All outputs are deterministic given
the same input and profile spec.

\paragraph{Relationship to AgentSight.}
\toolname is the offline profiling component of the AgentSight
observability framework. AgentSight provides real-time eBPF-based
capture of SSL traffic, process events, and file/network effects;
\toolname aggregates the recorded traces into semantic profiles. The two
tools are complementary: AgentSight answers ``what happened during this
run'' (debugging); \toolname answers ``where did the budget go across
runs'' (profiling).

\paragraph{Evaluation setup.}

\subsection{RQ1: Does Semantic Profiling Separate What Flat Views Mix?}

The strongest argument against semantic profiling is that traditional
tools ``can already see the same information.'' RQ1 tests this claim
directly by measuring how much system-effect weight falls into
\emph{mixed-intent} buckets---buckets containing observations from
multiple semantic regions---under different projection choices.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering\small
\caption{Semantic-axis ablation on 183{,}714 system observations
from 325 real sessions. All rows preserve the same total weight.}
\label{tab:mixing}
\begin{tabular}{lrrr}
\toprule
Projection & Unique stacks & Mixed wt.\% & Residual\% \\
\midrule
No semantic labels & 11{,}967 & 90.4 & 44.7 \\
Session label only & 15{,}027 & 84.4 & 33.4 \\
Prompt label only & 24{,}703 & 36.7 & 7.5 \\
Session + prompt & 26{,}829 & 0.0 & 0.0 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:mixing} shows the result on 325 real Codex/Claude
sessions. Without semantic labels, 90.4\% of system-effect weight falls
into mixed buckets: a flat \texttt{cargo~test} counter shows 2{,}903
executions but cannot distinguish whether they came from
\texttt{review}, \texttt{debug}, \texttt{refactor}, or \texttt{test}
prompts. Adding only the prompt label reduces mixed weight to 36.7\% and
residual to 7.5\%. The session label alone barely helps (84.4\%), because
sessions typically contain multiple intent phases.

A concrete example: \texttt{process:cargo; effect:test; status:ok}
appears under 48 distinct prompt tags. The top tag (\texttt{refactor})
accounts for only 32.0\%; the remaining 68.0\% comes from
\texttt{review}, \texttt{research}, \texttt{test}, \texttt{explain}, and
others. A flat summary or process audit merges all of these.

A label-permutation test (1{,}000 shuffles within each session) confirms
the separation is not random: real tags achieve 8.4\% session-beyond
information gain versus a null p95 of 1.9\% ($p = 0.001$).

The multi-view design is also validated by metric divergence. The
\texttt{time} and \texttt{tokens} views of the same sessions share
only 7/10 top prompt categories (Spearman $\rho = 0.623$).
\texttt{network}-tagged prompts rank 8th by time (I/O wait) but 93rd by
tokens. This confirms that different views answer structurally different
questions over the same operations.

\subsection{RQ2: Can Profiler Groups Localize Hidden Labeled Problems?}

RQ2 evaluates whether operation-stack profiling can localize
ground-truth-labeled problems in real agent traces. The evaluation
methodology is analogous to injecting known bottlenecks in CPU profiler
evaluation: public benchmark datasets provide ground-truth labels
(failure, safety violation, redundant step, human-task boundary); we
hide these labels, run the profiler, rank the resulting groups, and
check whether the top groups contain the hidden positives.

\paragraph{Benchmark setup.}
Six tasks across four datasets: AgentRewardBench looping and
side-effect, SATraj-OS unsafe operation, AgentNet incorrect and redundant
step, and OSWorld-Human group start. Together: 34{,}539 operations,
3{,}699 positives. Six views (flat, fixed-session, dataset-native,
raw-action, operation-stack, label-drilldown) and four rankers (width,
visible-risk, query-aware, oracle).

\paragraph{Localization results.}

Hidden policies serve only as upper bounds. WTFP = work-to-first-positive.}
\label{tab:localization}

\toprule
Policy & Hidden & AP & R@5 & F1@5 & Work@5 & R@30\% & WTFP & Groups \\
\midrule

fixed-session:query-aware & 0 & 0.348 & 0.023 & 0.043 & 0.016 & 0.356 & 0.004 & 285.0 \\

Table~\ref{tab:localization} summarizes the results. Flat summaries
recover all positives but require inspecting everything
(Work@5\,=\,1.0). Fixed-session drilldown finds a first positive quickly
(WTFP\,=\,0.004) but fragments the workload into 285 groups with only
2.3\% top-five recall. Operation-stack query-aware profiling inspects
9.4\% of the work in the top five groups, achieves 39.0\% budget-30
recall, and reduces groups to 157.5.

The result is a Pareto tradeoff, not dominance. Operation stacks improve
top-five recall over fixed-session drilldown on 5/6 tasks, reduce
median group count by 45\%, and save 90\% of inspection work versus flat
summaries. Fixed-session drilldown retains lower
work-to-first-positive on 4/6 tasks: profilers and debuggers are
complementary. Bootstrap (10{,}000 resamples) and label-permutation
(2{,}000 trials) confirm stable AP deltas exceeding the 95\%
prevalence/group-size null on all six tasks.

\paragraph{Actionability: which configuration knobs explain the results?}

Executable profile-spec patches modify stack fields, mapping rules, or
rankers, then re-run over the same visible operations. Five of six
patches improve AP, top-five lift, and first-positive work (median AP
delta 0.038, median top-five lift delta 0.575). Three reusable patterns
emerge: (1)~safety/side-effect tasks benefit from field and ranker
changes; (2)~step-quality tasks benefit from operation-stack
localization followed by fixed-session drilldown for examples;
(3)~human-boundary tasks require boundary-derived fields. The rejected
OSWorld-Human patch shows that visible rank features alone are
insufficient for boundary objectives; folding held-out boundary-derived
fields improves AP from 0.240 to 0.258 and reduces groups from 108 to
74, with an explicit work tradeoff.

Rank-feature ablations identify 7 critical feature rows
(\texttt{repeat\_signal}, write-action, \texttt{status=success}) and 3
misleading rows. Guided repairs improve AP on 2/3 misleading cases but
use offline scored feedback, not an automatic learned ranker.

\subsection{RQ3: How Reliable Is Intent Recognition?}

RQ1 and RQ2 assume that semantic labels are useful. RQ3 tests the
intent-recognition mechanism itself: can the tagger backends produce
labels that are consistent with ground-truth annotations and with each
other?

\paragraph{Scale and syntax validity.}
On 325 real sessions, the LLM tagger processes 118{,}021 tag requests
(2{,}859 prompt rows, 114{,}837 LLM-call events). Of these, 82{,}886
hit the label cache; 35{,}136 are real llama.cpp calls to a local
3B-parameter model. Final tag failures: 0. On a fixed set of 300
redacted fragments, three model sizes (0.6B, 1.1B, 3B) all produce
900/900 syntactically valid outputs; p95 latencies are 23, 18, and
31\,ms respectively.

\paragraph{Ground-truth agreement on public datasets.}
Public benchmark datasets provide native action labels that serve as
ground truth for mapping quality. We run a leave-dataset-out evaluation:
for each of 9 datasets, we train mapping rules on the other 8 and
measure V-measure between the mapping-derived \texttt{phase} field and
the dataset's native \texttt{action} labels, plus boundary F1 between
mapped phase boundaries and native action boundaries.

Table~\ref{tab:vmeasure} shows the results. On 7/9 datasets, V-measure
exceeds 0.7, indicating strong agreement between mapping-derived and
native labels. The two low-scoring datasets (toolbench, api-bank) have
atypical action vocabularies that the held-out mapping rules do not
cover. Mapping reduces unique stacks on 6/9 datasets with zero negative
regressions.

A supervised boundary-derivation backend further validates the field
pipeline. On OSWorld-Human held-out adjacent pairs, a learned boundary
predictor achieves F1~0.77, beating the best simple baseline
(\texttt{always\_boundary}, F1~0.71). Learned backends beat simple
baselines on 4/5 tested boundary families, while AgentRewardBench
looping is fully explained by \texttt{repeat\_signal\_change} (baseline
F1~1.0). This supports field derivation as a guarded configuration
step, not automatic intent discovery.

\paragraph{Semantic quality versus syntactic validity.}
Syntactic validity does not imply semantic quality. TinyLlama 1.1B
achieves high exact-stability (279/300 identical across repeats) but
concentrates on a narrow label set, outputting
\texttt{localization}/\texttt{localized} disproportionately. The 3B
model produces a broader vocabulary (328 unique prompt tags) but includes
noisy entries (\texttt{agentsightsm}, \texttt{testcodex}). A
display-governance pipeline reduces unique tags from 1{,}546 to 1{,}364
through deterministic aliases, raising top-20 support coverage from
93.7\% to 95.2\% without overwriting raw tags. This pipeline manages
noise but does not establish semantic adequacy---that is what the
ground-truth and cross-backend checks above provide.

\subsection{Case Studies}

We profile the same 325-session development project and report four
representative observations that illustrate the kind of aggregate
insights semantic flame graphs surface.

\paragraph{Budget distribution.}
The \texttt{tokens} view (Figure~\ref{fig:flamegraphs}) reveals that
\texttt{review}-tagged prompts dominate the model budget, followed by
\texttt{git}, \texttt{code}, \texttt{edit}, and \texttt{debug}. A
timeline of 80{,}000 individual LLM calls cannot produce this
distribution without external aggregation. The stack further decomposes
each category: under \texttt{prompt:review}, the dominant sub-frames are
\texttt{call:llm/code} and \texttt{call:llm/tool}.

\paragraph{Cross-session duplication.}
The \texttt{files} view shows \texttt{debug}-tagged prompts across
different sessions repeatedly accessing the same source files under
\texttt{collector/src/}. The flame graph aggregates these into a single
wide bar; a timeline shows each as an isolated event.

\paragraph{Metric divergence.}
The \texttt{time} and \texttt{tokens} views share only 7/10 top prompt
categories. \texttt{network}-tagged prompts rank 8th by time (I/O wait)
but 93rd by tokens; \texttt{benchmark} prompts show the reverse.

\paragraph{Path and network auditing.}
The \texttt{network} view attributes domain contacts to prompt
categories (\texttt{anthropic.com}, \texttt{crates.io},
\texttt{github.com}). The \texttt{files} view identifies accesses
outside the project root (\texttt{external/home},
\texttt{external/tmp}), supporting security auditing.

\subsection{Reproducibility}

All results are backed by profile specs for deterministic replay. We
re-execute 76 tracked specs twice (152 invocations); all produce
identical semantic output. Median runtime: 1.6\,s per spec (p95:
2.8\,s). Deterministic-output mode stabilizes raw-byte output: 76/76
achieve both semantic and raw-byte determinism.

\section{Related Work}

\textbf{Profiling and flame graphs.}
Flame graphs~\cite{flamegraphs} and pprof~\cite{pprof} establish the
folded-stack lineage: profiles are weighted samples with location
hierarchies. Pprof supports sample labels and can visualize them as
pseudo stack frames through tag-root/tag-leaf options. Perfetto
generalizes trace ingestion with SQL-based analysis and derived
events~\cite{perfetto}. These systems support query-time aggregation, so
\toolname does not claim novelty for flexible aggregation alone. The
difference is the domain: samples are agent operations, frames are
semantic labels derived from natural-language prompts through intent
recognition, and the evaluation scores profiler output against hidden
agent-trajectory labels.

\textbf{Agent tracing and LLM observability.}
OpenTelemetry GenAI and OpenInference standardize GenAI
spans~\cite{otel, openinference}. LangSmith~\cite{langsmith},
Langfuse~\cite{langfuse}, and Phoenix~\cite{phoenix} provide trace
visualization, session management, evaluations, and dashboards.
AgentOps~\cite{agentops} argues for structured agent observability
covering goals, plans, tools, and artifacts. These systems excel at
single-execution debugging: timeline views, span trees, and waterfall
charts help locate a specific failure. \toolname complements them with
cross-session aggregate profiling.
Datadog LLM Observability adds topic clustering over user messages, and
Laminar Signals extracts structured events from traces. These are steps
toward semantic aggregation, but they characterize \emph{input
distributions} (``30\% of users ask code questions''), not
\emph{resource attribution} (``code-review tasks consume 40\% of the
token budget''). \toolname produces the latter through folded-stack
aggregation where width represents cost.

\textbf{Agent failure diagnosis.}
AgentRx~\cite{agentrx} releases annotated failure trajectories and uses
constraint checking plus an LLM judge for root-cause localization.
TELBench~\cite{telbench} builds span-localization benchmarks from
semantic error annotations. AgentAtlas argues that outcome leaderboards
miss trajectory-level quality. These systems perform \emph{span-level}
fault localization within a single execution: which step failed and why.
\toolname performs \emph{category-level} aggregate profiling: which
categories of work produce the most failures, consume the most budget,
or generate repeated system effects across sessions.

%% ===================================================================
\section{Discussion}

\paragraph{Profiler and debugger are complementary.}
Fixed-session drilldown finds a first positive faster on 4/6 tasks
(RQ2). This is expected: debuggers are designed for single-case
investigation. The profiler identifies \emph{which categories} deserve
attention; the debugger explains \emph{what happened} in a specific
case. \toolname supports both by including or excluding session fields in
the stack query. A typical workflow starts with the profiler (``review
tasks dominate the budget''), then drills into individual sessions to
understand why.

\paragraph{Agent-as-consumer.}
The profiler's structured output (JSON, pprof, folded stacks) is
designed to be consumed by automated analysis agents, not only human
developers. The RQ2 ranker strategies demonstrate this pattern: a
scoring policy reads profiler output, ranks groups by visible features,
and identifies high-cost or high-failure categories. In practice, an AI
coding agent can run \texttt{agentpprof --format json}, parse the output,
and recommend configuration changes---the same workflow that the
regex-rule iteration (\S\ref{sec:design}) already uses. This positions
semantic profiling as infrastructure for agent self-diagnosis, not only
for human inspection.

\paragraph{Limitations.}
The real-session data (RQ1, RQ3, case studies) comes from one developer
on one project. RQ2 mitigates this with four independent public datasets
containing real agent traces from different research groups, but
multi-project and multi-user real-session evaluation would strengthen the
generality claim. The evaluation measures label-scored profiler fidelity,
not human or agent productivity. A controlled study comparing
flame-graph-guided diagnosis against timeline-based diagnosis would test
the practical value but is not required for the profiler-mechanism
contribution. \toolname currently reads Codex/Claude local histories and
operation JSONL; OpenTelemetry, LangSmith, and Langfuse trace imports are
engineering work, not design obstacles.

%% ===================================================================
\section{Conclusion}

\toolname reduces agent profiling to two abstractions. Operations carry
semantic and mechanism fields; operation stacks fold those fields at a
depth chosen by the query. Intent recognition---through regex rules, a
local LLM, or clustering---restores the deterministic-label precondition
that makes flame-graph aggregation work for natural-language agent
traces.

Semantic labels separate 90\% of system-effect weight that flat
summaries merge (RQ1). Operation-stack profiling localizes hidden labeled
problems with 90\% less inspection work than flat summaries and 45\% less
fragmentation than fixed-session drilldown, with actionable
configuration diagnosis (RQ2). Intent recognition produces labels that agree with ground-truth
annotations on 7/9 public datasets (V-measure ${>}0.7$), with learned
boundary derivation beating simple baselines on 4/5 families (RQ3). Case
studies show budget, duplication, and audit insights invisible to
timeline views.

%% ===================================================================
\section{Background and Motivation}
\label{sec:background}

\subsection{How Existing Agent Trace Models Work}

Current agent observability tools organize traces around fixed
hierarchies. OpenTelemetry represents an execution as a \emph{trace}
containing a tree of \emph{spans}, each with a name, duration, and
key-value attributes. LangSmith and Langfuse group spans into
\emph{sessions} and display them as timelines or waterfall charts.
Phoenix and OpenInference add GenAI-specific span types for LLM calls,
tool invocations, retrieval steps, and agent reasoning.

These models share a structural property: the session or span tree is the
skeleton of the data. Every event belongs to exactly one span, and spans
nest in a fixed parent-child hierarchy determined at execution time.
This design is effective for debugging: a developer can locate a failing
span, inspect its attributes, and trace its parent chain to understand
the execution context.

\subsection{Why Fixed Hierarchies Cannot Profile}

Profiling requires a fundamentally different operation: \emph{folding}
events across executions by semantic category so that width represents
aggregate cost. Fixed session/span hierarchies obstruct this in three
ways.

\paragraph{Sessions are boundaries, not categories.}
A session groups events by execution, not by intent. A single session
may contain review, debugging, and refactoring phases; splitting by
session assigns all of them to the same bucket. Conversely, two sessions
performing the same task produce two separate buckets that cannot be
merged without external logic.

\paragraph{Span names are not semantic labels.}
Span names describe mechanisms (\texttt{LLMCall}, \texttt{ToolInvoke},
\texttt{ChatCompletion}), not user intent (\texttt{review},
\texttt{debug}, \texttt{test}). Grouping by span name tells you how many
LLM calls occurred, not which categories of work consumed the budget.

\paragraph{Concrete example.}
In a real development project, the system effect
\texttt{process:cargo; effect:test; status:ok} appears 2{,}903 times
across 325 sessions. A flat process summary or a span-grouped view shows
a single ``cargo test'' counter. But this counter aggregates tests
triggered by 48 distinct prompt intents: \texttt{refactor} accounts for
only 32\% of the weight; the remaining 68\% comes from \texttt{review},
\texttt{research}, \texttt{test}, \texttt{explain}, and others. No
existing trace tool disaggregates this automatically.

\subsection{Why CPU Profiling Does Not Directly Apply}

CPU profilers solve the equivalent aggregation problem for programs.
A flame graph~\cite{flamegraphs} represents a profile as a set of
weighted \emph{samples}, each attached to a \emph{call stack} (an
ordered list of function frames). Identical stacks merge; width
represents aggregate cost. The key enabler is that function names are
\emph{deterministic}: the same code path always produces the same
frames.

Agent traces break this precondition. Prompts are natural language:
``Fix the bug'' and ``修一下这个 error'' express the same intent but
share no characters. Tool calls, GUI actions, and process events are
named heterogeneously across agent families. If raw event names are
used as flame-graph frames, every prompt produces a unique bar and
folding collapses.

These observations yield three design requirements:

\begin{description}
\item[R1: Uniform record type.]
  Agent traces mix prompts, LLM calls, tool invocations, GUI actions,
  process events, and benchmark labels. The profiler needs a single
  record type that can represent all of them without type-specific
  objects.
\item[R2: Query-time aggregation.]
  The same data must support multiple aggregation shapes---by task,
  phase, action, session, or dataset---without rebuilding the trace.
  Sessions and spans must be fields, not fixed hierarchy nodes.
\item[R3: Deterministic labels for folding.]
  Free-form prompts must be mapped to short, stable, repeatable labels
  before folding. This \emph{intent recognition} step has no analogue in
  CPU profiling, where function names are already deterministic.
\end{description}

%% ===================================================================
\section{Design}
\label{sec:design}

The three requirements from \S\ref{sec:background} drive the design.

\subsection{Operations (R1: Uniform Record Type)}

A profiler should not distinguish between prompts, tool calls, and
process events at the object-model level. \toolname uses a single
abstraction: an \operation is a weighted record with string fields and
additive measures.

An \operation is a weighted record representing one measurable activity in
an agent's history: a user prompt, an LLM call, a tool invocation, a file
read, or a network request. Each operation carries string fields
(\texttt{project}, \texttt{agent}, \texttt{session}, \texttt{prompt\_tag},
\texttt{kind}, \texttt{model}, \texttt{path}, \texttt{domain},
\texttt{status}, \ldots) and additive measures (token count, duration,
occurrence count). Different agent families and trace formats produce
different fields, but every entry is an operation record.

An \opstack is an ordered list of fields chosen at query time. Folding
operations by that list produces the standard folded-stack representation:

\begin{small}
\begin{verbatim}
CPU:   main;parse;tokenize          42
Agent: prompt:debug;call:llm;tool:bash  4200
\end{verbatim}
\end{small}

\noindent The critical difference from CPU profiling is that the stack is
not determined by execution---it is chosen by the analyst or by an
automated analysis agent. The same operations can be folded as a flat
task summary, a fixed-session tree, a semantic phase/action hierarchy, or
a dataset-native trajectory. Changing the fields changes the aggregation
shape without changing the underlying operations.

A \emph{view} is a triple $(\varphi, \sigma, w)$: a predicate $\varphi$
selects which operations participate, a stack function $\sigma$ maps each
operation to a frame sequence, and a weight function $w$ assigns a
nonnegative measure. Four built-in views answer four different questions:

\begin{table}[t]
\centering\small
\caption{Built-in views. Each shares the same operation set
but selects different activities, stack structures, and weights.}
\label{tab:views}
\begin{tabular}{llll}
\toprule
View & $\varphi$ (select) & $w$ (width) & Question \\
\midrule
\texttt{tokens} & LLM calls & token count & Budget distribution? \\
\texttt{time} & All timed ops & duration (s) & Time distribution? \\
\texttt{files} & File-effect ops & event count & Repo coverage? \\
\texttt{network} & Net-effect ops & event count & External contacts? \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Sessions and spans deserve explicit discussion. In existing observability
tools, sessions and spans define the fixed hierarchy. In \toolname, they
are optional operation fields. An analyst can include \texttt{session} in
the stack (producing a per-session drilldown equivalent to a trace tree),
or exclude it (producing a cross-session aggregate that no trace tool
provides). This is the design's central point: the same data supports
both debugging and profiling views, selected at query time.

- agentpprof/src/ — look for test code that compares tagger outputs

Report everything you find, even if it's only partially relevant.

# Iterative Paper Refinement

Orchestrate multi-round review-fix cycles on a systems paper. Subagents review, the main agent (you) fixes. The user steers direction.

## First Step

Read the paper (`main.tex` or the file the user specifies). Then read `references/common-pitfalls.md` for patterns the user has flagged before.

**Always run the full cycle.** Do not stop after a diagnostic, do not ask "should I continue?", do not skip phases because the paper "looks clean." Launch Phase 0 immediately after reading, then proceed through Phase 1-3 without pausing. The only pause point is after Phase 0 findings, where the user must confirm framing/scope direction before you apply fixes.

## Two Phases

### Phase 0 — Specialized Pre-checks (run before general refinement)

These catch fundamental problems that waste cycles if found late. Launch as parallel fork subagents, each read-only:

| Agent | Question it answers | Skill to use |
|-------|-------------------|--------------|
| **Framing** | Is the motivation single-dimensional? Does it cover all relevant dimensions (e.g., security + safety + efficiency)? Is the paper framed as a tool paper or an insight paper? | `critique-like-senior-systems-reviewer` with framing focus |
| **Scope** | What is the fundamental contribution? Is the scope too narrow or too broad? What problem does the system solve at the highest level? | `critique-like-senior-systems-reviewer` with scope focus |
| **Structure** | Is the section structure standard? Is design separated from implementation? Does the abstract follow context→problem→system→results? | `audit-paper-consistency` |

Process findings as they arrive — apply fixes immediately when a subagent completes, don't wait for all three. Pause for user direction only on framing/scope disagreements that require a judgment call. For clear fixes, apply directly.

### Phase 1-3 — General Refinement (3 rounds, serial)

Only enter after Phase 0 issues are resolved. Create tasks to track progress.

**Round 1 — Logic and Claims.** Fork subagent uses `critique-like-senior-systems-reviewer` on the full paper. Checks: thesis clarity, claim-evidence alignment, motivation completeness, evaluation coverage. Reports Must-fix / Should-fix / Consider. You apply fixes, compile, verify.

**Round 2 — Consistency.** Fork subagent uses `audit-paper-consistency`. Checks: cross-refs, terminology drift, design goals ↔ contributions alignment, abstract ↔ intro ↔ body coherence. You apply fixes, compile, verify.

**Round 3 — Language.** Fork subagent reviews against `paper-writing-style` checklist. Checks: semicolons, fragments, subject-verb distance, weak openings, jargon inflation. You apply fixes, compile, verify page count, deliver PDF.

## Subagent Rules

- Fork subagents inherit your context — use `subagent_type: "fork"` for reviews.
- Every review subagent prompt must end with: **"Do NOT edit the file — only report findings as Must-fix / Should-fix / Consider with section, problem, and concrete fix suggestion."**
- Never launch multiple subagents that edit the same file.
- After each round, compile (`make` or `latexmk`) and check for errors before starting the next round.

## Quality Gates

Stop iterating when:
- No Must-fix items remain
- Should-fix items are cosmetic, not structural
- Paper compiles cleanly with correct page count
- The user is satisfied with framing and scope

## Reference Files

- `references/common-pitfalls.md` — Patterns the user has corrected before. Read at the start of every run.
- For skill-specific review criteria, read the target skill's own SKILL.md (e.g., `paper-writing-style`, `critique-like-senior-systems-reviewer`).
Let me start the iterative refinement. First, read the paper and the common pitfalls reference.

22	\begin{abstract}
23	AI agent observability tools can show every span, every LLM call, and
24	every tool invocation---but they cannot answer aggregate questions: which
25	categories of work consumed the most tokens, where do failures
26	concentrate, and how does cost distribute across task families? These

30	CPU profilers solved the equivalent problem for programs: flame graphs

33	code paths produce identical stack frames that merge on contact. Agent
34	traces break this assumption. Prompts are natural language:
